1.1.title: The exam in numbers
1.1.text:
| Property | Value |
|:----------------------|:------------------------------------------------------------|
| Length | **2 hours** |
| Items | **50–60**, multiple choice (one answer) and multiple select (the item says how many) |
| Cut score | **Not published.** About 70% is the working convention |
| Penalty for a wrong answer | None — never leave an item blank |
| Price | $125 plus tax (*verify*) |
| Languages | English, Japanese, Spanish, Portuguese |
| Delivery | Online-proctored, or at a testing centre |
| Validity | **3 years**. A shorter renewal exam (1 hour, 20 items) is available near expiry |
| Recommended experience | 6+ months hands-on with Google Cloud |

**Time budget.** 120 minutes over 50–60 items is roughly two minutes each. A practical rhythm: one pass answering
everything you know and flagging anything over 90 seconds; a second pass on the flagged items; a last pass on
every multiple-select item and every answer you changed.

> **A multiple-select item says "Choose two" (or three).** Selecting the wrong *number* of answers scores zero, and so
> does a single answer on a two-answer item. Read the instruction line before the options.

1.2.title: The four sections, and what moved in June 2026
1.2.text:
The exam guide that went live on **30 June 2026** has four sections:

| Section | Weight | What it covers |
|:----------------------------------|:------|:--------------------------------------------------------------|
| **1** Setting up a cloud solution environment | ~20% | Hierarchy, org policy, identities and groups, APIs, quotas, observability set-up, standalone orgs, networking set-up, locations, Asset Inventory, Workforce Identity Federation, billing |
| **2** Planning and implementing a cloud solution | ~30% | Choosing and deploying compute (VMs, MIGs, GKE, serverless, agents, GPUs/TPUs), storage and data products, networking, IaC and AI-assisted tooling |
| **3** Ensuring successful operation | ~30% | Day-2 work on compute, GKE, Cloud Run, storage and databases, networking, monitoring and logging, AI/dev platforms |
| **4** Configuring access and security | ~20% | IAM policies and roles, inheritance, service accounts, impersonation, short-lived credentials, Workload Identity Federation |

The previous guide had five sections (20 / 17.5 / 25 / 20 / 17.5) with "planning" and "deploying" separate. They
are now one 30% section, and "operating" grew from 20% to 30%. **Day-2 operations is now as heavy as building.**

> New in the June 2026 guide — the list to check yourself against
>
> **Setup:** standalone organizations · setting up cloud networking · verifying product availability by location ·
> Cloud Asset Inventory and Gemini Cloud Assist · **Workforce Identity Federation**.
> **Planning:** Agent Runtime on Gemini Enterprise Agent Platform · Hyperdisk · **GPUs vs TPUs** · Managed Service for
> Apache Kafka · Memorystore · Filestore, NetApp Volumes, Managed Lustre · multi-region redundancy · **Cloud NGFW
> policies and secure tags** · Cloud Interconnect · Fabric FAST · **AI-assisted tooling** (Gemini CLI, Google
> Antigravity, Gemini Cloud Assist, Application Design Center).
> **Operations:** Autopilot Pod resource requests · traffic splitting across Cloud Run, functions *and GKE* ·
> attaching GPUs/TPUs · deploying agents · Workbench and BigQuery notebooks · Cloud Workstations · Database Center ·
> **CMEK** · custom static routes · VPC Flow Logs and firewall logs · Query Insights and index advisor ·
> **Personalized Service Health** · Active Assist · **Cloud Hub**.
> **Security:** policy inheritance in the hierarchy · Google-managed service accounts · service accounts for GKE
> applications · provisioning Workload Identity Federation.

**What left the guide:** Cloud Run for Anthos and GKE Enterprise are no longer named, and *Cloud Functions* is now
**Cloud Run functions**. App Engine is not named at all, but it still exists and still appears as a distractor;
[§6.12](https://nirmata78.github.io/gcp-ace-simulator/theory/06-containers-serverless.html#s6-12) covers it in one page.

1.3.title: How ACE items are written
1.3.text:
The exam is scenario-based: a short story, a requirement, and four options that all *work* to some degree. It is
testing whether you pick the one Google would recommend. Five preferences run through almost every item:

1. **Managed over assembled.** If a product exists for the job, the answer is that product, not a VM running
   open-source software that does the same thing.
2. **Least privilege, at the smallest sufficient scope.** A predefined role on one resource beats a broad role on a
   project; a group binding beats per-user bindings.
3. **No long-lived secrets.** An attached service account, impersonation or federation beats a downloaded key every
   time a keyless option exists.
4. **The fewest moving parts that satisfy every clause.** One command, one object, one resource — unless the
   requirement genuinely needs two constructs (alerting is the classic case, [§9.3](https://nirmata78.github.io/gcp-ace-simulator/theory/09-operations.html#s9-3)).
5. **Cost matters, but never above a stated requirement.** "Cheapest" only decides between options that all meet
   the availability, latency and compliance clauses.

> **Find the deciding clause first.** Most stems contain one phrase that eliminates three options — *"without
> changing the application"*, *"including project owners"*, *"no key material"*, *"must survive a zone failure"*,
> *"scale to zero"*. Underline it mentally before reading the options, and check each option against it.

1.4.title: Locations: regions, zones and what lives where
1.4.text:
A **region** is a geographic area (`europe-central2`, Warsaw). A **zone** is an isolated failure domain inside it
(`europe-central2-a`); most regions have three. A **multi-region** is a continent-scale location (`US`, `EU`,
`ASIA`) used by storage and analytics products. Some products add **dual-regions** (a named pair).

Every resource has a scope, and the scope decides what survives what:

| Scope | Examples | Survives |
|:-----------|:------------------------------------------------------------------|:------------------|
| **Zonal** | VM instances, zonal Persistent Disks, zonal MIGs, zonal GKE clusters, TPU VMs | Nothing beyond its zone |
| **Regional** | Subnets, regional disks, regional MIGs, Cloud SQL instances (HA ones span two zones), Cloud Run services, regional load balancers, Cloud Router, Cloud NAT, Artifact Registry repositories, regional GKE clusters | A zone failure (if spread) |
| **Multi-regional / global** | VPC networks, firewall rules, routes, images, snapshots (by default), global instance templates, global load balancers, Cloud DNS, Pub/Sub topics, IAM | A region failure |

**Two consequences worth holding:** a **VPC is global while its subnets are regional**, so one VPC spans every
region with no peering; and **images and snapshots are global**, so a disk in one zone can be recreated in any
other zone or region from them.

### Verifying that a product is available where you need it

Not every product, machine series, GPU or TPU type exists in every region — and within a region, not in every
zone. The exam frames this as *"the deployment failed in zone X"* or *"which regions can host workload Y"*.


The **Cloud locations** page and each product's *locations* page are the documentation answers. For a data-residency
requirement the enforcement answer is different: the `gcp.resourceLocations` organization-policy constraint
([§3.7](https://nirmata78.github.io/gcp-ace-simulator/theory/03-identity-access.html#s3-7)), which stops anyone creating resources outside approved locations.

> **Available versus allowed.** *"Is the A3 machine series offered in this zone?"* is a catalogue question —
> `machine-types list` / `accelerator-types list`. *"Make sure nobody can create resources outside the EU"* is a
> governance question — the `gcp.resourceLocations` organization policy. Neither answers the other.

1.5.title: The interfaces: Console, gcloud, Cloud Shell, SDKs
1.5.text:
| Interface | Use it for |
|:----------------------|:----------------------------------------------------------------|
| Google Cloud console | Point and click; some features and every Gemini Cloud Assist panel appear here first |
| `gcloud` | The CLI for almost every service |
| `gcloud storage` | Cloud Storage — **replaces `gsutil`**; prefer it in any new answer |
| `bq` | BigQuery |
| `kubectl` | Kubernetes objects **inside** a cluster — never to create the cluster itself |
| `cbt` | Bigtable data-plane operations |
| Cloud Shell | A browser terminal with all of the above pre-installed and already authenticated |
| Client libraries | Application code, using Application Default Credentials ([§3.11](https://nirmata78.github.io/gcp-ace-simulator/theory/03-identity-access.html#s3-11)) |

### gcloud grammar and configurations

The grammar is regular: `gcloud [GROUP] [SUBGROUP] VERB NAME --flags`, with scope expressed as `--zone`,
`--region` or `--global` (newer groups use `--location`). Two flags work almost everywhere: **`--format`**
(`json`, `yaml`, `table(...)`, `value(...)`) to shape output, and **`--filter`** to select server-side.

**`gcloud beta ...` and `gcloud alpha ...` are release tracks, not typos.** A command that exists only on those
tracks must be typed with the prefix: in the current SDK that includes `beta projects move`, the whole
`beta quotas` group and `beta services identity create`, and `alpha resource-manager liens`. Everything else in this booklet is GA and takes no prefix. Exam options sometimes
drop the prefix — judge the *verb and flags*, not the track.

A **configuration** is a named bundle of properties — account, project, default region and zone. It is the
answer to *"switch between work contexts in one command"*:

| Task | Command |
|:------------------------------------|:----------------------------------------------------------------------|
| First-time set-up | `gcloud init` |
| Create / switch a named context | `gcloud config configurations create prod` · `gcloud config configurations activate prod` |
| Default project and region | `gcloud config set project P` · `gcloud config set compute/region R` |
| Credentials for the CLI (a human) | `gcloud auth login` |
| Credentials for local application code (ADC) | `gcloud auth application-default login` |
| Add kubectl to a local SDK | `gcloud components install kubectl` |

> **`gcloud auth login` versus `gcloud auth application-default login`.** The first gives **the gcloud CLI** your
> credentials. The second writes **Application Default Credentials** that client libraries — your own code —
> pick up. A program that says "could not find default credentials" on a laptop where `gcloud` works fine needs
> the second. And the Docker daemon is a third client again (`gcloud auth configure-docker`, [§6.7](https://nirmata78.github.io/gcp-ace-simulator/theory/06-containers-serverless.html#s6-7)).

### Cloud Shell

| Property | Value |
|:----------------------|:----------------------------------------------------------|
| What it is | A small VM, provisioned per user on demand, reached from the console |
| Persistent storage | **5 GB mounted at `$HOME`** — the only thing that survives |
| Everything else | Ephemeral: packages installed outside `$HOME` vanish when the VM is recycled |
| Keeping tools | Install into `$HOME`, or re-install at start from `~/.customize_environment` |
| Inactivity | The session ends after idle time; an unused home disk is eventually deleted (*verify* the window) |
| Pre-installed | `gcloud`, `kubectl`, `docker`, `terraform`, `helm`, language runtimes, an editor, web preview |

> **"Only `$HOME` persists" is the whole Cloud Shell topic.** Options that claim the VM is permanently yours, that
> nothing persists, or that system paths like `/usr/local/bin` persist are each a near-miss of that one fact.

2.1.title: The resource hierarchy
2.1.text:
```
Organization                 the root: one per Cloud Identity / Workspace customer, or a standalone org
  +-- Folder                 optional, nestable (up to 10 levels): departments, environments, teams
  |     +-- Folder
  |     |     +-- Project    the unit of billing, quota, API enablement and default isolation
  |     |           +-- Resource   VM, bucket, Cloud SQL instance, cluster, topic ...
  |     +-- Project
  +-- Project                projects may hang directly off the organization
```

**Four rules follow from the tree, and each is examined directly:**

1. **IAM allow policies are inherited downward and are additive.** A grant on a folder is effective on every
   project in it, including projects created later. There is no "more specific wins" ([§3.3](https://nirmata78.github.io/gcp-ace-simulator/theory/03-identity-access.html#s3-3)).
2. **Organization policies are inherited downward too.** The **constraint** is the rule type Google defines
   (`compute.vmExternalIpAccess`); the **organization policy** is your setting of that constraint on a node. Descendants inherit the policy; a lower node can **replace** it, or for
   list constraints **merge** with it ([§3.7](https://nirmata78.github.io/gcp-ace-simulator/theory/03-identity-access.html#s3-7)). Unlike IAM, it binds Owners too.
3. **The project is the boundary** for billing linkage, quota, API enablement and, by default, networking.
   *"Stop one team exhausting another's quota"* means separate projects.
4. **Grant at the smallest node that covers the requirement, including its future.** *"All of Finance's projects,
   including new ones"* is one binding on the Finance folder — not forty project bindings.

### Project identifiers

| Identifier | Mutable? | Notes |
|:--------------|:--------|:--------------------------------------------------------------|
| Project **ID** | **No** | Globally unique, chosen at creation (6–30 characters, lowercase, digits, hyphens). What almost every command takes |
| Project **name** | Yes | A display label; not unique |
| Project **number** | No | Assigned by Google; appears in default and Google-managed service account addresses |

`gcloud` accepts the ID or the number, never the display name.

2.2.title: Creating the organization: Cloud Identity, Workspace, or standalone
2.2.text:
An **organization resource** is created for you — you never "create an organization" with a command. There are
now two routes to one:

| Route | How the org appears | Principals it holds | Named after |
|:----------------------|:----------------------------------------------|:---------------------------|:-----------------|
| **Cloud Identity or Google Workspace** | Verify a domain, then the org is created when the first project or billing account is made by that customer | Managed users and groups in your domain, plus federated identities | The domain (`example.com`) |
| **Standalone organization** | Created automatically when a **new Free Trial** customer signs in to the console with a Google account and accepts the terms | Google accounts, and principals in a **workforce identity pool** ([§3.2](https://nirmata78.github.io/gcp-ace-simulator/theory/03-identity-access.html#s3-2)) | The user, e.g. `lara-brown-org` — **never a domain name** |

> New in the June 2026 guide — standalone organizations
>
> A standalone organization gives a new customer a real hierarchy — folders, org policies, org-level IAM —
> without a Cloud Identity super administrator or a verified domain. The signing-up user becomes **Organization
> Owner**. Facts worth holding: it is available **only to new Free Trial customers**, not to existing accounts;
> **one organization per user account**; its name cannot be a domain name, because domain names are reserved for
> Cloud Identity and Workspace organizations; other people are added by **invitation, which they must accept within
> 30 days**; a service account can never be an organization owner, and at least one active Google account must
> remain one. Workforce Identity Federation ([§3.2](https://nirmata78.github.io/gcp-ace-simulator/theory/03-identity-access.html#s3-2)) is how a standalone org lets people sign in with an external IdP.

**The first administrators.** In a Cloud Identity / Workspace org, the **super administrator** (Admin console) and
the **Organization Administrator** (`roles/resourcemanager.organizationAdmin`, IAM) are different roles in
different systems. The super admin manages users, groups and domain settings; the Organization Administrator
manages IAM on the resource hierarchy. Google's set-up guidance is to grant org-level roles to **groups** such as
`gcp-organization-admins@` rather than to individuals.

> **Super admin versus Organization Administrator.** *"Create users, reset passwords, manage groups"* is the Admin
> console and a Cloud Identity / Workspace admin role. *"Grant IAM roles on folders and projects"* is the
> Organization Administrator IAM role. Neither implies the other.

> **Google Cloud Setup** is the console's guided flow for a new organization: identity and groups, administrative
> access, billing, the folder hierarchy, a starter network (a Shared VPC host with subnets), central logging and
> monitoring, and a baseline of security org policies. It can apply the result directly or hand it to you as
> Terraform. This is the practical meaning of the guide's *"setting up cloud networking"* in Section 1 — the
> foundation network, not individual firewall rules.

2.3.title: Folders and projects in practice
2.3.text:
| Task | Command |
|:------------------------------------|:------------------------------------------------------------|
| Create a folder | `gcloud resource-manager folders create --display-name=finance --organization=ORG_ID` |
| Create a project in a folder | `gcloud projects create kestrel-fin-prod --folder=FOLDER_ID` |
| Move a project | `gcloud beta projects move P --folder=FOLDER_ID` |
| Delete / restore a project | `gcloud projects delete P` · `gcloud projects undelete P` |
| Protect a project from deletion | a **lien**: `gcloud alpha resource-manager liens create --project=P --restrictions=resourcemanager.projects.delete --reason=...` |

**Deleting a project** starts a **30-day pending-deletion** period: billing stops, resources are shut down, and
`gcloud projects undelete` brings it all back. After 30 days it is gone.

**The Resource Manager roles you should be able to name:**

| Role | For |
|:--------------------------------------------|:------------------------------------------------------------|
| `roles/resourcemanager.organizationAdmin` | Manage IAM and structure for the whole organization — very broad |
| `roles/resourcemanager.folderAdmin` | Full control of a folder and everything under it |
| `roles/resourcemanager.folderCreator` | Create folders |
| `roles/resourcemanager.projectCreator` | Create projects (usually granted on a folder) |
| `roles/resourcemanager.projectDeleter` | Delete projects |
| `roles/resourcemanager.projectMover` | Update and **move** projects between folders |
| `roles/browser` | See the hierarchy — folders and projects — but nothing inside them |

A move needs rights on the project, the source and the destination. **Project Mover granted on a common ancestor
(often the organization) covers all three in one binding**, which is why it beats Folder Admin or Organization
Administrator on a least-privilege question.

> **Historic default grants.** When a Cloud Identity / Workspace organization is created, every user in the domain is
> granted **Project Creator** and **Billing Account Creator** at the organization. Removing those two grants is a
> standard first governance step — it is the answer to *"users keep creating projects and billing accounts
> outside the folder structure"*.

2.4.title: APIs and services
2.4.text:
**APIs are enabled per project.** A new project has very little enabled, and a call to a disabled API fails with
*"API has not been used in project N before or it is disabled"* — an **enablement** problem, not a permission
problem.

| Task | Command |
|:------------------------------------|:----------------------------------------------------------------------|
| Enable an API | `gcloud services enable sqladmin.googleapis.com` |
| What is enabled | `gcloud services list --enabled` |

Enabling some APIs also creates **Google-managed service accounts** (service agents) that the product uses to act
in your project ([§3.9](https://nirmata78.github.io/gcp-ace-simulator/theory/03-identity-access.html#s3-9)). Enabling the Compute Engine API also creates the **default VPC network** unless the
organization policy `compute.skipDefaultNetworkCreation` is enforced — a common baseline, because the default
network ships with permissive firewall rules ([§4.4](https://nirmata78.github.io/gcp-ace-simulator/theory/04-networking.html#s4-4)).

> **Three error shapes, three different fixes.** *"API not enabled / not used before"* — enable the API.
> **403 / PERMISSION_DENIED** — an IAM grant is missing. **401 / UNAUTHENTICATED** — there are no valid
> credentials at all. The exam puts all three in one item often enough to learn the table.

2.5.title: Quotas and limits
2.5.text:
| Kind | Caps | Example | When hit |
|:----------------|:----------------------------------------|:------------------------------------------|:----------------------------|
| **Allocation quota** | How much may exist at once | vCPUs per region, GPUs per region, static IPs, VPC networks per project | Creation fails with a quota error |
| **Rate quota** | Requests per interval | API reads per minute | `429 RESOURCE_EXHAUSTED`; retry with exponential backoff |
| **System limit** | A fixed maximum, not adjustable | Maximum labels per resource | Redesign, do not request |

**Quotas are per project**, and many are **per region** (GPUs have both a per-region and an all-regions quota).
When a legitimate workload needs more, the answer is to **request an increase for that quota in that project** in
**Cloud Quotas** (IAM & Admin → Quotas & System Limits), or let the **quota adjuster** raise eligible quotas
automatically as usage approaches them. Spreading the workload across extra projects to dodge a quota is the
distractor.


> **A quota is a hard stop; a budget is only an alert ([§2.7](https://nirmata78.github.io/gcp-ace-simulator/theory/02-organization-projects-billing.html#s2-7)).** You can also *lower* a quota deliberately — for
> example BigQuery's query-usage-per-day quota — to cap consumption. That is the answer to *"make it impossible to
> exceed"*, where a budget is not.

> Free Trial accounts cannot use GPUs and have tight quotas; upgrading to a paid billing account is the fix, not a
> quota request. Quota increases can also depend on billing history for a new account (*verify* current rules).

2.6.title: Billing accounts and the roles around them
2.6.text:
A **Cloud Billing account** pays for projects. **A project is linked to at most one billing account; a billing
account can pay for many projects**, even across organizations. Two kinds exist: **self-serve** (card or bank
account, charged automatically) and **invoiced** (monthly invoice, for eligible customers). Unlinking a project's
billing account stops its paid services, and resources may be deleted.

| Role | Granted on | Lets the holder |
|:--------------------------------------|:------------------|:----------------------------------------------------|
| `roles/billing.admin` — Billing Account Administrator | Billing account | Everything: users, payment, links, budgets, exports |
| `roles/billing.user` — Billing Account User | Billing account | **Link projects to this account** |
| `roles/billing.viewer` — Billing Account Viewer | Billing account | Read costs and transactions |
| `roles/billing.costsManager` — Billing Account Costs Manager | Billing account | Budgets, exports, cost views — no payment control |
| `roles/billing.creator` — Billing Account Creator | Organization | Create new billing accounts |
| `roles/billing.projectManager` — Project Billing Manager | Project | Link and unlink **this project** |

> **Linking a project needs a grant on both sides:** permission on the **project** (Project Billing Manager, or
> Owner) **and** Billing Account User on the **billing account**. Owner of the project alone cannot attach it to an
> account it has no role on. This two-sided rule is the single most examined billing fact.

| Task | Command |
|:------------------------------------|:----------------------------------------------------------------------|
| Link a project to a billing account | `gcloud billing projects link P --billing-account=ID` |

2.7.title: Budgets, alerts and exports
2.7.text:
**A budget watches spend and notifies. It never stops anything.** Each budget has a **scope** (the whole billing
account, or selected projects, services or labels), an **amount** (fixed, or last month's spend), and **threshold
rules** on **actual** or **forecasted** spend — for example 50%, 90% and 100%.

| Notification route | Use |
|:----------------------------------|:------------------------------------------------------------|
| Email to billing admins and users | The default |
| Cloud Monitoring notification channels | Route to on-call tools, SMS, chat |
| **Pub/Sub topic** | **Programmatic response** — a function that scales down, notifies, or even unlinks billing |

> **"Automatically stop spending at the budget"** has no built-in switch. The supported pattern is a budget
> publishing to **Pub/Sub**, a **Cloud Run function** subscribed to it, and code that acts — for example disabling
> billing on the project. Say what that costs: disabling billing shuts services down and can delete resources. If the
> stem needs a *hard ceiling on a resource*, a **quota** is the tool.


### Billing export to BigQuery

The console's reports are for looking; **the BigQuery export is for querying**. There are three datasets:

| Export | Contains | Use |
|:----------------------|:----------------------------------------------------------------|:------------------------|
| **Standard usage cost** | Per-service, per-SKU, per-project cost with **labels** | Chargeback by team or cost centre |
| **Detailed usage cost** | The above **plus resource-level** rows (which VM, which bucket) | Per-resource analysis |
| **Pricing** | The list prices and your contract prices | Price analysis |

**Turn the export on early.** It is not a time machine: into a **multi-region** dataset (`US`, `EU`) the usage-cost
exports backfill only from the **start of the previous month**; into a **single-region** dataset, and for **pricing**,
nothing is backfilled. *"We need two years of queryable history"* is only possible if the export was on two years ago.
It is configured on the **billing account**, into a dataset in a project you choose.

2.8.title: Reading and predicting cost
2.8.text:
| Question | Tool |
|:----------------------------------------------|:------------------------------------------------------------|
| What **will** this architecture cost? (nothing built yet) | **Google Cloud Pricing Calculator** |
| What **did** it cost, by team? | **Billing export to BigQuery** + labels; billing reports for a glance |
| Tell me **when** spend crosses a line | **Budget** with threshold rules |
| How do I spend less on what I already run? | **Active Assist** recommendations ([§9.10](https://nirmata78.github.io/gcp-ace-simulator/theory/09-operations.html#s9-10)), CUD analysis, FinOps hub |

### Discounts

| Mechanism | Commitment | Notes |
|:----------------------|:----------------|:--------------------------------------------------------------|
| **Sustained use discounts** | None — automatic | For eligible machine series running much of the month. **E2 and several newer series do not receive them** (*verify*) |
| **Committed use discounts** — resource-based | 1 or 3 years of vCPU / memory / GPU in a region | Deepest discount for a steady footprint; billed whether used or not |
| **Committed use discounts** — spend-based (flexible) | 1 or 3 years of hourly spend | Applies across machine types and regions for a service |
| **Spot VMs** | None | Large discount, can be reclaimed any time ([§5.2](https://nirmata78.github.io/gcp-ace-simulator/theory/05-compute-engine.html#s5-2)) |
| **Free Trial / free tier** | — | $300 of credit for 90 days for new customers; small always-free usage (*verify*) |

> *"Steady, predictable, 24×7 for years"* — **committed use discount**, three years if the stem says so.
> *"Interruptible, restartable, cheapest"* — **Spot VMs**. *"No commitment, discount without doing anything"* —
> **sustained use discount**.

### Labels are the cost dimension

| Metadata | What it is | In the billing export? | Used by |
|:----------------|:----------------------------------------------|:----------|:--------------------------------|
| **Labels** | Free key–value pairs on resources | **Yes** | Cost attribution, filtering, automation |
| **Network tags** | Strings on VMs | **No** | VPC firewall rules and routes ([§4.3](https://nirmata78.github.io/gcp-ace-simulator/theory/04-networking.html#s4-3), [§4.4](https://nirmata78.github.io/gcp-ace-simulator/theory/04-networking.html#s4-4)) |
| **Tags** (resource-manager tags) | IAM-governed key–values attached to org, folders, projects, resources; inherited | — | Conditional IAM, org policy, Cloud NGFW ([§3.7](https://nirmata78.github.io/gcp-ace-simulator/theory/03-identity-access.html#s3-7)) |

2.9.title: Seeing everything: Cloud Asset Inventory and Gemini Cloud Assist
2.9.text:
**Cloud Asset Inventory** is the metadata database of every resource and policy in your organization — the
answer whenever a question needs a view *across* projects.

| Need | Capability |
|:------------------------------------------------|:----------------------------------------------------------|
| Find every VM with an external IP across the org | `gcloud asset search-all-resources --scope=organizations/ORG --query="..."` |
| Find every binding that grants `roles/owner` | `gcloud asset search-all-iam-policies --scope=organizations/ORG --query="policy:roles/owner"` |
| Who can do X on Y? | `gcloud asset analyze-iam-policy` — this is **Policy Analyzer** ([§3.8](https://nirmata78.github.io/gcp-ace-simulator/theory/03-identity-access.html#s3-8)) |
| Snapshot everything into BigQuery for SQL | `gcloud asset export --content-type=resource --bigquery-table=...` |
| React to changes in near real time | **Asset feeds** to a Pub/Sub topic |
| What did this resource look like last month? | Change **history** (about 35 days) with `gcloud asset get-history` |

Content types include `resource`, `iam-policy`, `org-policy`, `access-policy` and `os-inventory` (from VM
Manager, [§5.6](https://nirmata78.github.io/gcp-ace-simulator/theory/05-compute-engine.html#s5-6)). Reading it needs `roles/cloudasset.viewer` at the scope you query.

> New in the June 2026 guide — Asset Inventory with Gemini Cloud Assist
>
> **Gemini Cloud Assist** is the AI assistant in the console. For this objective it answers natural-language
> questions about your estate — *"which Compute Engine instances in folder Finance have external IP addresses?"*,
> *"summarise the resources in this project"* — and explains or drafts the `gcloud` / query to get the answer. It
> draws on Asset Inventory and your permissions: it **cannot show you what your IAM roles do not allow you to see**,
> and its output is a draft to verify, not an authority. It needs its API enabled and a role such as
> `roles/geminicloudassist.user`. The rest of its jobs are in [§8.5](https://nirmata78.github.io/gcp-ace-simulator/theory/08-tooling.html#s8-5) and [§9.10](https://nirmata78.github.io/gcp-ace-simulator/theory/09-operations.html#s9-10).

### More to recognise

- **Cloud Asset Inventory analyses, not just searches.** It returns the **effective** organization policy for every
  resource in scope, reports the IAM and policy effects of moving a project **before** you move it (project moves
  have no dry run), and runs **SQL** over asset data without a user-built BigQuery export.
- **Protect and verify.** A **lien** (`resourcemanager.projects.delete`) stops even an Owner deleting a project
  until the lien is removed. **Assured Workloads** applies a control package to a folder — data
  location **and** support-personnel controls; the `gcp.resourceLocations` constraint covers location only.
- **Organization policy beyond the catalogue.** `sql.restrictPublicIp` blocks public IPs on Cloud SQL
  (`sql.restrictAuthorizedNetworks` only blocks authorized networks). **Custom constraints** use CEL on resource
  fields when no predefined constraint fits — for example *every new GKE cluster must have Workload Identity
  Federation enabled*.
- **Quotas.** The **quota adjuster** requests increases automatically as usage nears a supported quota (it only
  raises). A **usage alert** from the Quotas page is a Cloud Monitoring alerting policy — a budget watches money,
  not quota.
- **Cost.** **Cost anomaly detection** in Cloud Billing flags spikes against historical patterns with no thresholds
  to set. **Gemini Cloud Assist in Cloud Billing** answers *"why did the bill go up?"* in natural language, within
  the user's billing permissions.
- **Everyday gcloud.** Named **configurations** (`gcloud config configurations create/activate`) switch account,
  project and region together. A **log scope** lets Logs Explorer query several projects' logs together without
  moving them.

3.1.title: Where human identities come from
3.1.text:
| Source | What it is | When it is the answer |
|:----------------------|:------------------------------------------------------------|:------------------------------|
| **Google account** | A personal account (Gmail or any email registered with Google) | Individuals, standalone orgs, Free Trial |
| **Cloud Identity** (Free or Premium) | Identity-as-a-service: managed users, groups, devices, SSO — without Workspace apps | The organization wants managed identities for Google Cloud only |
| **Google Workspace** | Cloud Identity plus Gmail, Drive and the rest | The company already runs on Workspace |
| **External IdP via Workforce Identity Federation** | Users stay in Entra ID, Okta, etc. and are **not** copied into Google | [§3.2](https://nirmata78.github.io/gcp-ace-simulator/theory/03-identity-access.html#s3-2) |

**Groups are the unit of access management.** Grant roles to `group:sre@example.com`, then manage people by
membership. A joiner becomes a membership change, not an IAM change, and the IAM policy stops churning. Groups can
contain users, service accounts and other groups.

### Managing users and groups — manually and automated

| Method | What it does |
|:------------------------------------|:------------------------------------------------------------------|
| **Admin console** (manual) | Create, suspend, delete users; create groups and manage membership |
| **Google Cloud Directory Sync (GCDS)** | **One-way** sync of users and groups **from Active Directory or LDAP into** Cloud Identity / Workspace, run on your own server on a schedule |
| **SAML / OIDC single sign-on** | Users authenticate at the corporate IdP; passwords never live at Google |
| **Automatic provisioning (SCIM)** from Entra ID, Okta and others | The IdP creates, updates and suspends Cloud Identity accounts as HR changes flow through it |
| **Directory API / scripts** | Programmatic account and group management |

> **Sync versus SSO.** GCDS or SCIM provisioning decides *which accounts exist* in Cloud Identity. SSO decides *where
> people type their password*. A typical enterprise uses both: accounts synced from AD, authentication at AD FS or
> Entra ID. And **Workforce Identity Federation replaces both** — nothing is synced at all.

### Suspend, then delete

| Action | Effect |
|:----------------|:----------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| **Suspend** |; sessions and OAuth tokens are revoked; data and group memberships are kept. **Reversible** |
| **Delete** | The account is removed. Transfer Drive and other data first. Restorable only for a short period (*verify*) |

> **A person who has left is removed at the identity layer, not in IAM.** Suspending the account makes every IAM
> binding, direct or via group, in every project, unusable at once — you cannot miss a binding you never had to
> find. IAM edits are for people who *stay* and whose access changes.

3.2.title: Workforce Identity Federation
3.2.text:
> New in the June 2026 guide — Workforce Identity Federation
>
> **Workforce Identity Federation lets people from an external identity provider — Microsoft Entra ID, Okta, AD FS,
> any OIDC or SAML 2.0 IdP — use Google Cloud without having a Google account and without being synchronised into
> Cloud Identity.** The IdP stays the source of truth: disable a user there and their Google Cloud access ends.

**The objects:**

| Object | What it is |
|:----------------------|:----------------------------------------------------------------------|
| **Workforce identity pool** | A container of external users, created at the **organization** level, location `global` |
| **Provider** | The trust with one IdP — OIDC or SAML — including **attribute mapping** (`google.subject`, `google.groups`, custom `attribute.*`) and an optional **attribute condition** limiting who may federate |
| **Principal identifiers** | How IAM names federated users in bindings |

```
principal://iam.googleapis.com/locations/global/workforcePools/POOL/subject/SUBJECT
principalSet://iam.googleapis.com/locations/global/workforcePools/POOL/group/GROUP_ID
principalSet://iam.googleapis.com/locations/global/workforcePools/POOL/attribute.dept/finance
principalSet://iam.googleapis.com/locations/global/workforcePools/POOL/*
```

**Granting access** uses those identifiers exactly like `user:` or `group:` — typically a `principalSet` for a
group coming from the IdP. **Signing in**: federated users reach a federated sign-in for the console, and
`gcloud` uses a login configuration file created for the pool. **Group bindings only work if the provider maps the
IdP's groups claim to `google.groups`** — otherwise the `principalSet .../group/...` matches nobody. The pool's
**session duration** (default 1 h, 15 min–12 h, e.g. `--session-duration=1800s`) sets how long console and gcloud
sessions from that pool last — per pool, so contractors can get shorter sessions than employees. Some products and features do not support
workforce identities (*verify* the supported-products list before choosing it).


> **Workforce versus Workload Identity Federation.** Same machinery, different subjects. **Workforce** is for
> **people** from an external IdP, pools live at the **organization**. **Workload** is for **software** outside
> Google Cloud — AWS, Azure, GitHub Actions, on-premises — pools live in a **project** ([§3.12](https://nirmata78.github.io/gcp-ace-simulator/theory/03-identity-access.html#s3-12)).

3.3.title: The IAM model and inheritance
3.3.text:
> **An allow policy binds a role to a set of principals, on a resource.** Every IAM item is a question about one
> of those three parts.

| Part | Examples | Notes |
|:----------------|:----------------------------------------------------------|:------------------------------------------|
| **Principal** | `user:` · `group:` · `serviceAccount:` · `domain:` · `principal://` / `principalSet://` · `allUsers` · `allAuthenticatedUsers` | Who |
| **Role** | `roles/storage.objectViewer` | A named bundle of **permissions** (`storage.objects.get`). You never grant a bare permission |
| **Resource** | Organization, folder, project, or an individual resource (bucket, topic, secret, service account...) | Where the policy is attached |
| **Condition** (optional) | A CEL expression on time, resource name/type or tags | [§3.6](https://nirmata78.github.io/gcp-ace-simulator/theory/03-identity-access.html#s3-6) |

An allow policy is a list of **bindings** plus an **etag** (for safe concurrent edits) and a **version** (3 is
needed when conditions are present). Each resource has at most one allow policy.

### Inheritance — the rules that decide most items

1. **Effective access is the union** of every binding that reaches the principal — directly, through any group, at
   the resource and at every ancestor up to the organization.
2. **A lower allow policy cannot remove a higher grant.** There is no "most specific wins" and no negative binding.
3. **Only two things subtract from what allow policies grant:** an **IAM deny policy** (removes permissions from
   principals) and an **organization policy** (removes configurations from everyone) — [§3.6](https://nirmata78.github.io/gcp-ace-simulator/theory/03-identity-access.html#s3-6) and [§3.7](https://nirmata78.github.io/gcp-ace-simulator/theory/03-identity-access.html#s3-7). A
   **principal access boundary** policy also caps *which resources* a principal may reach, but it never grants
   ([§3.13](https://nirmata78.github.io/gcp-ace-simulator/theory/03-identity-access.html#s3-13), *More to recognise*).
4. **`allUsers` means anyone on the internet, unauthenticated; `allAuthenticatedUsers` means anyone with any Google
   account** — effectively public too. Both are wrong answers unless the stem is about public content.

> *"Remove the user's project-level role so the folder grant no longer applies"* — impossible. The folder grant is
> still inherited. To take access away you remove the grant **where it was made**, remove the person from the
> **group** that carries it, or add a **deny** rule.

3.4.title: Roles: basic, predefined, custom
3.4.text:
| Kind | Examples | When |
|:------------|:----------------------------------------------|:------------------------------------------------------|
| **Basic** | `roles/owner`, `roles/editor`, `roles/viewer` | Legacy, cross-service, far too broad. **Almost never the answer** |
| **Predefined** | `roles/compute.instanceAdmin.v1`, `roles/pubsub.subscriber` | **The default correct answer.** Maintained by Google, per service |
| **Custom** | Your list of permissions | **Only when the need falls strictly between two predefined roles** |

**What Owner has that Editor lacks:** managing IAM on the resource (and a few billing associations). *"Who can grant
roles on this project?"* — an Owner or someone with a Security Admin-type role, never an Editor.

### Predefined roles worth naming on sight

| Area | Roles |
|:--------------|:------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| IAM | `iam.securityAdmin` (manage IAM policies) · `iam.roleAdmin` (custom roles) · `iam.serviceAccountAdmin` · `iam.serviceAccountUser` · `iam.serviceAccountTokenCreator` · `iam.workloadIdentityUser` |
| Compute | `compute.admin` · `compute.instanceAdmin.v1` · `compute.networkAdmin` · `compute.securityAdmin` (firewalls, SSL) · `compute.viewer` · `compute.osLogin` / `compute.osAdminLogin` |
| Storage | `storage.objectViewer` · `storage.objectCreator` · `storage.objectUser` · `storage.objectAdmin` · `storage.admin` |
| GKE | `container.admin` · `container.developer` · `container.viewer` |
| Run / functions | `run.admin` · `run.developer` · `run.invoker` · `cloudfunctions.developer` |
| Data | `bigquery.dataViewer` · `bigquery.dataEditor` · `bigquery.jobUser` · `bigquery.user` · `cloudsql.client` · `spanner.databaseUser` · `pubsub.publisher` · `pubsub.subscriber` |
| Operations | `logging.viewer` · `logging.privateLogViewer` (Data Access logs) · `logging.configWriter` · `monitoring.viewer` · `monitoring.editor` · `monitoring.metricWriter` · `logging.logWriter` |
| Secrets & keys | `secretmanager.secretAccessor` · `cloudkms.cryptoKeyEncrypterDecrypter` · `cloudkms.admin` |

> **`compute.networkAdmin` versus `compute.securityAdmin`.** Network Admin builds networks, subnets, routes and load
> balancers but **cannot change firewall rules or SSL certificates**; Security Admin manages firewall rules and
> certificates. The separation-of-duties question uses exactly this split.

### Custom roles

- Defined at the **organization** or **project** level — **not at a folder**. An org-level custom role can be
  granted anywhere in the org; a project-level one only in that project.
- Built from permissions whose custom-role support level is *supported* (some are *testing* or *not supported*).
- Carry a **launch stage** (`ALPHA`, `BETA`, `GA`, `DEPRECATED`, `DISABLED`).
- **You maintain them.** When Google adds a permission to a service, predefined roles gain it and your custom role
  does not — the stated reason to prefer predefined roles.

| Task | Command |
|:------------------------------------|:----------------------------------------------------------------------|
| Custom role in a project (or `--organization=ORG`) | `gcloud iam roles create vmOperator --project=P --permissions=compute.instances.get,...` |
| Start from a predefined role | `gcloud iam roles copy --source=roles/compute.viewer --destination=myViewer --dest-organization=ORG` |
| Add a permission to a custom role | `gcloud iam roles update vmOperator --project=P --add-permissions=compute.instances.start` |

3.5.title: Viewing and changing policies
3.5.text:
| Task | Command |
|:------------------------------------|:----------------------------------------------------------------------|
| Grant one role (additive, safe) | `gcloud projects add-iam-policy-binding P --member=group:sre@example.com --role=roles/compute.instanceAdmin.v1` |
| Remove one binding | `gcloud projects remove-iam-policy-binding P --member=user:x@example.com --role=roles/viewer` |
| Replace the whole policy | `gcloud projects get-iam-policy P` → edit → `gcloud projects set-iam-policy P policy.json` |
| The same on a folder, organization or bucket | `gcloud resource-manager folders add-iam-policy-binding` · `gcloud organizations add-iam-policy-binding` · `gcloud storage buckets add-iam-policy-binding` |

> **`set-iam-policy` replaces the whole policy.** It is a read–modify–write: get the policy, edit it, set it back
> with the same **etag** — if someone changed the policy in between, the etag no longer matches and the write is
> rejected rather than silently overwriting their change. For one grant, `add-iam-policy-binding` is the safer
> answer.

**Attaching a policy lower in the hierarchy** uses the same verbs on the resource itself — a bucket, a topic, a
secret, a service account. Resource-level bindings are how you grant access to *one* bucket rather than all of
them.

3.6.title: Conditions, deny policies and Privileged Access Manager
3.6.text:
### IAM conditions — scoping a grant

| Need | Condition |
|:----------------------------------------------|:------------------------------------------------------------------|
| Access that **expires** automatically | `request.time < timestamp("2026-12-31T00:00:00Z")` |
| Only business hours | `request.time.getHours("Europe/Warsaw") >= 9 && ...` |
| Only certain resources by name | `resource.name.startsWith("projects/_/buckets/fin-")` |
| Only resources carrying a tag | `resource.matchTag("ORG_ID/env", "prod")` |

| Task | Command |
|:------------------------------------|:----------------------------------------------------------------------|
| Grant that expires by itself | `add-iam-policy-binding ... --condition='expression=request.time < timestamp("2026-10-31T00:00:00Z"),title=audit-window'` |

*"The contractor's access must end on 31 October without anyone remembering to remove it"* is a condition.

### Deny policies — the IAM subtraction

A **deny policy** names principals, permissions they may never use, optional **exception principals**, and an
optional condition. It attaches to an **organization, folder or project** and is **evaluated before allow
policies**: a matching deny wins over every allow, everywhere below its attachment point.


Managing them needs `roles/iam.denyAdmin`. Deny policies name permissions in the form
`storage.googleapis.com/buckets.delete`, and the attachment point is URL-encoded (`/` becomes `%2F`).

> **Deny policy versus organization policy.** A **deny policy** removes *permissions* from *principals* —
> *"developers must never delete production buckets, whatever roles they hold"*. An **organization policy** removes
> *configurations* from *everyone* — *"no VM in this folder may have an external IP"*. Both bind project Owners.

### Privileged Access Manager

**Privileged Access Manager (PAM)** provides **just-in-time, time-bound elevation**: an administrator defines an
**entitlement** (which roles, on which resource, for how long, who may request, whether approval is needed); an
eligible user **requests a grant** with a justification, an approver approves, and the role is granted for the
window and then removed automatically, with the whole flow audited. It is the answer to *"engineers should hold
production admin rights only while working on an incident, with approval"* — standing Owner grants are the
distractor.

3.7.title: Organization policy and tags
3.7.text:
**The Organization Policy Service restricts what may be configured**, for every principal including Owners. A
policy sets a **constraint** on a node, and descendants inherit it.

| Constraint shape | Example | Effect |
|:----------------------|:----------------------------------------------|:------------------------------------------------|
| **Boolean** | `iam.disableServiceAccountKeyCreation` | On or off |
| **List** | `gcp.resourceLocations`, `compute.vmExternalIpAccess` | Allow or deny listed values |
| **Managed constraints** | Newer, typed versions of common constraints (e.g. `compute.managed.*`) | Same idea, better validation and dry-run support |
| **Custom constraints** | A CEL condition on a resource's fields, for supported services | *"No GKE cluster without Workload Identity"* |

**Inheritance:** a child node inherits the parent's policy unless its own policy **replaces** it; for list
constraints a child may instead **merge** with the parent. **Dry-run** policies and the **Policy Simulator** show
what a new policy would block before you enforce it. Changing org policies needs
`roles/orgpolicy.policyAdmin`, usually at the organization.

### Constraints worth recognising on sight

| Constraint | Stops |
|:------------------------------------------|:--------------------------------------------------------------|
| `gcp.resourceLocations` | Creating resources outside approved regions — **data residency** |
| `iam.allowedPolicyMemberDomains` | Granting roles to identities outside your organization — *domain restricted sharing* |
| `iam.disableServiceAccountKeyCreation` | Creating service-account keys |
| `iam.disableServiceAccountKeyUpload` | Uploading your own public keys |
| `iam.automaticIamGrantsForDefaultServiceAccounts` | The automatic **Editor** grant to default service accounts |
| `compute.vmExternalIpAccess` | VMs having external IPs (allow-list of VMs, or deny all) |
| `compute.requireOsLogin` | SSH keys in metadata — forces OS Login ([§5.5](https://nirmata78.github.io/gcp-ace-simulator/theory/05-compute-engine.html#s5-5)) |
| `compute.skipDefaultNetworkCreation` | Creation of the `default` VPC in new projects |
| `compute.restrictVpcPeering` / `compute.restrictSharedVpcHostProjects` | Uncontrolled network connections |
| `storage.uniformBucketLevelAccess` | Buckets using ACLs |
| `storage.publicAccessPrevention` | Buckets or objects being made public |
| `gcp.restrictNonCmekServices` | Resources created without customer-managed keys ([§7.14](https://nirmata78.github.io/gcp-ace-simulator/theory/07-storage-data.html#s7-14)) |

> **Secure by default.** Organizations created from 2024 onward have several of these enforced automatically —
> among them key creation disabled, uniform bucket-level access, public access prevention, domain restricted
> sharing, and no automatic Editor grant for default service accounts (*verify* the current list). That is why a
> brand-new org may refuse to create a service-account key.

> *"Prevent anyone — **including project owners** — from ..."* is an organization policy. The moment a stem says
> *including owners* or *even administrators*, stop reading IAM options.

### Tags — the IAM-governed metadata

**Tags** (resource-manager tags) are key–value pairs defined at the organization or a project, attached to
organizations, folders, projects and many resources, and **inherited** down the hierarchy. Unlike labels, **who
may attach a tag value is itself controlled by IAM** (`roles/resourcemanager.tagUser`), so tags can safely drive
policy:

- **Conditional IAM**: `resource.matchTag(...)` in a binding ([§3.6](https://nirmata78.github.io/gcp-ace-simulator/theory/03-identity-access.html#s3-6)).
- **Conditional org policy**: enforce a constraint only where `env=prod`.
- **Cloud NGFW**: *secure tags* select firewall-policy sources and targets ([§4.4](https://nirmata78.github.io/gcp-ace-simulator/theory/04-networking.html#s4-4)).

3.8.title: Troubleshooting and right-sizing access
3.8.text:
| Question | Tool |
|:----------------------------------------------|:----------------------------------------------------------|
| *Why* can (or can't) this principal do this action on this resource? | **Policy Troubleshooter** |
| *Who* can do X on Y? *What* can this principal reach? | **Policy Analyzer** (Asset Inventory) |
| Which roles are more than this principal actually uses? | **IAM role recommender** (Active Assist) — based on ~90 days of usage |
| Is this service account or key still used? | **Activity Analyzer** / service-account usage insights |
| What would a policy change break? | **Policy Simulator** |

3.9.title: Service accounts: kinds and lifecycle
3.9.text:
A **service account is both a principal and a resource.** You grant roles **to** it (what it can do) and roles
**on** it (who can use it).

| Kind | Address | Created by | Notes |
|:----------------------|:----------------------------------------------|:------------------|:--------------------------------|
| **User-managed** | `NAME@PROJECT_ID.iam.gserviceaccount.com` | You | The ones you design, one per workload |
| **Default** | Compute: `PROJECT_NUMBER-compute@developer.gserviceaccount.com`; App Engine: `PROJECT_ID@appspot.gserviceaccount.com` | Enabling the API | Historically granted **Editor** — replace with purpose-made accounts |
| **Google-managed (service agents)** | `service-PROJECT_NUMBER@gcp-sa-SERVICE.iam.gserviceaccount.com` (Cloud Storage: `...@gs-project-accounts...`) | Google, when the API is enabled or first used | The product's own identity **acting in your project** |

> New in the June 2026 guide — Google-managed service accounts
>
> **Service agents** are how Google services act on your resources: the Cloud Storage service agent publishes bucket
> notifications to Pub/Sub, the Compute Engine service agent attaches disks, a product's agent reads a CMEK key.
> They appear in IAM with a *Service Agent* role. Three things the exam uses: **do not remove their roles** (the
> product breaks); **grant them extra roles when a feature needs it** — most often
> `roles/cloudkms.cryptoKeyEncrypterDecrypter` for CMEK ([§7.14](https://nirmata78.github.io/gcp-ace-simulator/theory/07-storage-data.html#s7-14)) or `roles/pubsub.publisher` for Cloud Storage events
> ([§6.11](https://nirmata78.github.io/gcp-ace-simulator/theory/06-containers-serverless.html#s6-11)); and **force-create one** before first use with
> `gcloud beta services identity create --service=SERVICE.googleapis.com`.

| Task | Command |
|:------------------------------------|:----------------------------------------------------------------------|
| Create | `gcloud iam service-accounts create app-runtime` |
| Stop it now, reversibly | `gcloud iam service-accounts disable app-runtime@P.iam.gserviceaccount.com` |
| Delete; recover within 30 days | `gcloud iam service-accounts delete SA_EMAIL` · `gcloud iam service-accounts undelete UNIQUE_ID` |

> **Disable before delete.** Disabling stops the account immediately and is reversible. Deleting it leaves its role
> bindings behind as orphans, and a new account created with the **same name** is a **different principal** (a new
> unique ID) that does **not** inherit the old bindings. Undelete works for 30 days, by unique ID.

**The account ID is permanent.** The email `NAME@PROJECT_ID.iam.gserviceaccount.com` never changes; only the display
name and description can. "Renaming" a service account means creating a new one, granting it the same roles,
moving workloads to it, then disabling and deleting the old one.

3.10.title: Attaching and impersonating
3.10.text:
Two different ways to "use" a service account, guarded by two different roles granted **on** the account:

| Role on the service account | Lets the holder | Typical stem |
|:--------------------------------------|:------------------------------------------------|:----------------------------------|
| **`roles/iam.serviceAccountUser`** (`iam.serviceAccounts.actAs`) | **Attach** it to a resource they create — a VM, Cloud Run service, function, Dataflow job | *"Deploy a Cloud Run service that runs as `app@`"* |
| **`roles/iam.serviceAccountTokenCreator`** | **Mint tokens** for it — i.e. act **as** it right now | *"A CI identity must deploy as `deployer@` with no keys"* |

### Attaching — the normal case

A workload on Google Cloud runs **as** an attached service account and receives short-lived credentials from the
**metadata server** automatically. Nothing is stored; nothing rotates by hand.

| Task | Command |
|:------------------------------------|:----------------------------------------------------------------------|
| Run a VM as a service account | `gcloud compute instances create vm1 --service-account=SA_EMAIL --scopes=cloud-platform` |
| Run a Cloud Run service as one | `gcloud run deploy api --image=IMG --service-account=SA_EMAIL` |

**Attaching an account from another project** — a central `identities` project is a common design — also
requires that the organization policy `iam.disableCrossProjectServiceAccountUsage` is **not** enforced on the project
that owns the service account; where it is enforced, the attach fails however the IAM grants look.

**Access scopes** are a legacy VM-level filter applied *on top of* IAM. Best practice: the `cloud-platform` scope
plus narrow IAM roles on a dedicated service account. Changing a VM's service account or scopes requires the VM
to be **stopped**.

### Impersonating — acting as another identity

| Task | Command |
|:------------------------------------|:----------------------------------------------------------------------|
| Let `ci` impersonate `deployer` | `gcloud iam service-accounts add-iam-policy-binding deployer@P.iam.gserviceaccount.com --member=serviceAccount:ci@P.iam.gserviceaccount.com --role=roles/iam.serviceAccountTokenCreator` |
| Run one command as `deployer` | `gcloud compute instances list --impersonate-service-account=deployer@P.iam.gserviceaccount.com` |
| Make it the default for gcloud | `gcloud config set auth/impersonate_service_account SA_EMAIL` |

Impersonation issues **short-lived tokens**, writes **no key material**, and the audit log records **both** the
caller and the impersonated account — the original principal is in
`protoPayload.authenticationInfo.serviceAccountDelegationInfo`, which is how *"which engineer acted as `deploy-sa`?"* is
answered. It is also the recommended way for *humans* to use a privileged service
account — grant the engineer Token Creator on it rather than handing out a key.

> **Service Account User versus Token Creator.** *"Create a VM that runs as `sa@`"* needs **User**
> (`actAs`). *"Run this command as `sa@` from my terminal / pipeline"* needs **Token Creator**. Both are granted **on
> the service account**, not on the project, for least privilege.

3.11.title: Short-lived credentials, and keys as a last resort
3.11.text:
The **IAM Service Account Credentials API** (`iamcredentials.googleapis.com`) is what impersonation calls:

| Call | Produces | Used for |
|:----------------------|:--------------------------------------------------------|:------------------------------------------|
| `generateAccessToken` | OAuth 2.0 access token, **1 hour** by default (extendable to 12 h by org policy) | Calling Google APIs |
| `generateIdToken` | OIDC ID token for an **audience** | Calling Cloud Run, functions, IAP-protected apps |
| `signBlob` / `signJwt` | A signature by the account's Google-managed key | Signed URLs without a key file ([§7.4](https://nirmata78.github.io/gcp-ace-simulator/theory/07-storage-data.html#s7-4)), custom JWTs |

**ID tokens only:** `roles/iam.serviceAccountOpenIdTokenCreator` lets a caller mint **ID tokens** for the account —
enough to call Cloud Run or an IAP-protected app — but not access tokens or signatures. It is the least-privilege
choice when that is all a scheduler or caller needs.


### Application Default Credentials

Client libraries find credentials in this order: the file named by **`GOOGLE_APPLICATION_CREDENTIALS`**; the
user credentials written by **`gcloud auth application-default login`**; the **attached service account** via the
metadata server. On Google Cloud, the third needs no configuration at all — which is why "set
`GOOGLE_APPLICATION_CREDENTIALS` to a key file" is almost always the distractor.

### Service-account keys

A **user-managed key** is a long-lived private key that **never expires by default**, can be copied anywhere, and
is rotated only if you rotate it. Google's position, and the exam's: **a key is the last resort.**

| Situation | Keyless mechanism |
|:----------------------------------------------|:------------------------------------------------------|
| Workload on Google Cloud | **Attached** service account |
| One Google Cloud identity needs another's rights | **Impersonation** |
| Workload on AWS, Azure, GitHub, on-premises | **Workload Identity Federation** ([§3.12](https://nirmata78.github.io/gcp-ace-simulator/theory/03-identity-access.html#s3-12)) |
| Pod in GKE | **Workload Identity Federation for GKE** ([§6.8](https://nirmata78.github.io/gcp-ace-simulator/theory/06-containers-serverless.html#s6-8)) |
| Developer laptop | `gcloud auth application-default login` (+ impersonation) |
| Legacy system that supports none of these | A key — then restrict, rotate, monitor |

**Controls when keys must exist:** `iam.disableServiceAccountKeyCreation` (block them), an expiry constraint
(`iam.serviceAccountKeyExpiryHours`), rotation (`gcloud iam service-accounts keys create` / `delete`), and usage
monitoring (Activity Analyzer, Security Command Center findings).

> **"Store the JSON key in Secret Manager" does not satisfy "no key material".** It is still a long-lived key that
> anything able to read the secret can exfiltrate. Secret Manager is the right home for secrets Google *cannot* mint
> ([§3.13](https://nirmata78.github.io/gcp-ace-simulator/theory/03-identity-access.html#s3-13)); a service-account credential is something Google mints on demand.

3.12.title: Workload Identity Federation for external workloads
3.12.text:
> New in the June 2026 guide — provisioning Workload Identity Federation
>
> **Software running outside Google Cloud exchanges the credential it already has for a short-lived Google token.**
> An AWS role, an Azure managed identity, a GitHub Actions or GitLab OIDC token, a SAML assertion or an X.509
> certificate is presented to Google's **Security Token Service**, validated against a provider you configured, and
> exchanged — no service-account key ever leaves Google.

```
External credential (AWS role · OIDC token from GitHub/GitLab/Azure · SAML · X.509)
      |
      v
Workload identity pool (in a PROJECT)  --  provider: AWS | OIDC | SAML | X.509
      |   attribute mapping:   google.subject = assertion.sub, attribute.repository = ...
      |   attribute condition: assertion.repository == "kestrel/api"
      v
Google STS  -->  federated token  -->  (a) direct IAM grant to the principal, or
                                       (b) impersonate a service account (roles/iam.workloadIdentityUser)
```


The workload is given a **credential configuration file** — it contains no secret, only where to fetch the
external token and which pool and provider to use. **Creating and maintaining** pools and providers needs
`roles/iam.workloadIdentityPoolAdmin`; **using** one to act as a service account needs
`roles/iam.workloadIdentityUser` on that account — two different jobs, two different roles. Use the
service-account path (b) when an API does not accept federated principals directly.

**Kubernetes clusters outside Google Cloud** federate with an **OIDC provider** whose issuer is the cluster's
service-account token issuer. If Google cannot reach that issuer (a private, on-premises cluster), **upload the
cluster's JWKS** with `--jwk-json-path`; the control plane never needs to be exposed.

> **The attribute condition is the security boundary.** Without one, *any* identity the IdP can issue — any GitHub
> repository in the world, for a public issuer — could federate. *"Only pipelines from our repository"* is an
> attribute condition on the provider.

3.13.title: Secret Manager
3.13.text:
**Secret Manager stores secrets Google cannot mint for you** — a third-party API key, a database password, a TLS
private key from an outside CA.

| Concept | Meaning |
|:----------------------|:----------------------------------------------------------------------|
| **Secret** | The named container, with its own IAM policy, labels, replication policy |
| **Version** | The actual payload. Versions are immutable; states: enabled, disabled, destroyed |
| **`latest`** | An alias for the newest enabled version — rotation is *add a version* |
| **Replication** | Automatic (Google chooses) or user-managed (you pin regions); also regional secrets |
| **Rotation schedule** | Secret Manager **notifies** a Pub/Sub topic on schedule; **your code rotates** |
| **Expiration** | Delete the secret at a time or after a TTL |

| Role | Grants |
|:--------------------------------------|:----------------------------------------------------------|
| **`roles/secretmanager.secretAccessor`** | **Read the payload.** What a workload needs — grant it **on the one secret** |
| `roles/secretmanager.viewer` | See secrets and versions exist; **not** the payload |
| `roles/secretmanager.secretVersionManager` | Add, disable, destroy versions |
| `roles/secretmanager.admin` | Everything |

| Task | Command |
|:------------------------------------|:----------------------------------------------------------------------|
| Create a secret; add a version (rotate) | `gcloud secrets create db-password --data-file=-` · `gcloud secrets versions add db-password --data-file=-` |
| Read the current value | `gcloud secrets versions access latest --secret=db-password` |

**Consuming secrets:** Cloud Run and Cloud Run functions mount a secret **as an environment variable** (resolved
when an instance starts) or **as a file volume** (read at access time, so a new version is picked up without a
redeploy). GKE uses the Secret Manager add-on / CSI driver. Code can call the API directly.

> **Where a secret must not live, and why.** Baked into the image (cannot rotate without a rebuild), in instance
> **metadata** (readable by every process on the VM and visible in the console), in the repository, or in a plain
> bucket (no versioning semantics, no rotation notifications, generic audit only). Secret Manager is the managed
> product for the job — and a Kubernetes Secret is only base64 unless you add encryption.

### More to recognise

- **Workforce pools.** An **attribute condition** on the provider (`assertion.employee_type == 'staff'`) decides
  who may federate at all. **Disabling the pool** (`--disabled`) stops every federated user at once and can be
  undone. Custom attributes become principal sets: `principalSet://.../workforcePools/POOL/attribute.department/finance`.
  **Microsoft Entra ID** provisions Cloud Identity users through its enterprise application; GCDS is for LDAP /
  on-premises AD.
- **Limits and delegation in IAM.** An allow policy holds at most **1,500 principals** — use groups.
  **Principal access boundary** policies say which resources a set of principals is *eligible* to use; they never
  grant, and they block access outside the boundary whatever roles are granted. A condition on
  `iam.googleapis.com/modifiedGrantsByRole` lets a delegate grant **only** named roles. `request.time` conditions
  with a time zone give business-hours access; `resource.name.startsWith("projects/_/buckets/logs-")` scopes a
  project grant to matching buckets. **`roles/iam.securityReviewer`** reads every IAM policy without data access.
- **Service accounts in operation.** `iam.serviceAccountKeyExpiryHours` makes new keys expire. **Activity
  Analyzer** shows each key's last authentication. **HMAC keys** on a service account serve S3-compatible tools.
  Cloud Scheduler calls a private Cloud Run service with an **OIDC token** for an account holding
  `roles/run.invoker`. A VM's service account changes only while it is **stopped**. Autopilot has Workload
  Identity Federation for GKE on by default.
- **Workload identity federation in practice.** Separate **pools per environment**; **disable a provider**
  during an incident at the IdP; audit logs show the federated principal in
  `authenticationInfo.principalSubject`; a GitHub Actions job needs **`permissions: id-token: write`** or there is
  no token to exchange.

3.14.title: Part 3 recall card
3.14.text:
| Prompt | Answer |
|:------------------------------------------------|:--------------------------------------------------------|
| Leaver — revoke everything, now | **Suspend** the account (or disable it in the external IdP) |
| Sync AD users into Cloud Identity | **GCDS** (one-way) or SCIM provisioning from the IdP |
| Entra ID users, no copies in Google | **Workforce Identity Federation** (org-level pool) |
| GitHub Actions deploying, no keys | **Workload Identity Federation** + attribute condition |
| Remove an inherited grant from below | Impossible — remove it at the source, or **deny policy** |
| Access that expires by itself | **IAM condition** on `request.time` |
| Admin rights only during an incident, approved | **Privileged Access Manager** |
| Need between two predefined roles | **Custom role** (org or project, never folder) |
| Build networks but not touch firewalls | `compute.networkAdmin` (firewalls = `compute.securityAdmin`) |
| Nobody, including owners, may do X | **Organization policy** |
| Why can't Ana stop this VM? | **Policy Troubleshooter** |
| Who can read this bucket? | **Policy Analyzer** |
| Attach an SA to a VM / service | **Service Account User** on the SA |
| Act as an SA from CI or a terminal | **Token Creator** on the SA + impersonation |
| Product needs to use my KMS key | Grant the product's **service agent** the key role |
| Stop an SA now, reversibly | **Disable** it |
| Third-party password, rotate without redeploy | **Secret Manager**, `secretAccessor` on that secret, mounted as a volume |

4.1.title: The VPC model
4.1.text:
| Fact | Consequence |
|:----------------------------------------------|:--------------------------------------------------------------|
| A **VPC network is global** | One VPC spans all regions; VMs in different regions talk over internal IPs with no VPN or peering |
| **Subnets are regional** | A subnet exists in one region, across all its zones |
| VPCs are **isolated from each other** by default, even in one project | Connecting two needs peering, a VPN, NCC or Shared VPC ([§4.5](https://nirmata78.github.io/gcp-ace-simulator/theory/04-networking.html#s4-5)) |
| Firewall rules and routes belong to the **network** | They are global resources, scoped by targets |
| **Auto mode** creates one `/20` subnet per region from `10.128.0.0/9` | Convenient, overlapping with every other auto-mode VPC |
| **Custom mode** creates no subnets — you define them | **The production answer.** Auto mode can convert to custom, never back |

The **`default` network** in a new project is an auto-mode VPC with permissive firewall rules (internal traffic,
SSH, RDP, ICMP from anywhere). Production work starts on a custom-mode VPC, and the org policy
`compute.skipDefaultNetworkCreation` stops the default network appearing at all.

| Task | Command |
|:------------------------------------|:----------------------------------------------------------------------|
| Custom-mode VPC | `gcloud compute networks create vpc-prod --subnet-mode=custom` |
| Subnet with Private Google Access | `gcloud compute networks subnets create web-euc2 --network=vpc-prod --region=R --range=10.10.0.0/20 --enable-private-ip-google-access` |

4.2.title: Subnets and IP ranges
4.2.text:
- A subnet has one **primary IPv4 range** (RFC 1918 or other private ranges) and optional **secondary ranges** —
  used by GKE for Pod and Service IPs (alias IPs).
- **Four addresses in every primary range are reserved**: network, default gateway, second-to-last, and broadcast.
- Subnet ranges in one VPC, and across peered VPCs, **must not overlap**.
- Subnets can be **dual-stack** (IPv4 + IPv6) or IPv6-only (*recognise*).

### Resizing a subnet — expand only

| Task | Command |
|:------------------------------------|:----------------------------------------------------------------------|
| Grow a full subnet (never shrink) | `gcloud compute networks subnets expand-ip-range web-euc2 --region=R --prefix-length=19` |

**A subnet's primary range can be expanded (a shorter prefix), never shrunk**, without downtime, as long as the
larger range does not overlap anything. *"The subnet is out of addresses"* is `expand-ip-range`; *"we made it too
big"* has no fix except a new subnet and migration. Auto-mode subnets can grow up to `/16`.

> **Adding a subnet versus expanding one.** More addresses *in the same region for the same workloads* —
> expand. A **new region**, or a separate range for a different tier — create a new subnet in the existing VPC
> (`subnets create`). Creating a new VPC is almost never the answer to "out of IPs".

4.3.title: Routes
4.3.text:
Every packet leaving a VM is matched against the VPC's routing table.

| Route type | Created by | Notes |
|:----------------------|:------------------------------|:------------------------------------------------------------|
| **Subnet routes** | Automatically, per subnet range | Cannot be deleted; make every subnet reachable across the VPC |
| **Default route** `0.0.0.0/0` → default internet gateway | Automatically | Priority 1000. Delete it to cut all internet egress paths |
| **Custom static routes** | You | Destination, next hop, priority, optional **network tags** to apply to only some VMs |
| **Dynamic routes** | **Cloud Router** via BGP | Learned from VPN or Interconnect peers; regional or global per the VPC's routing mode |

**Next hops for a custom static route:** a VM instance (e.g. a firewall or NAT appliance), an internal IP, an
**internal passthrough Network Load Balancer** (for highly available appliances), a Classic VPN tunnel, or the
default internet gateway.

**Selection:** the **most specific prefix** wins; among equal prefixes, the **lowest priority number** wins; equal
priority spreads traffic (ECMP). Subnet routes cannot be overridden by a less specific custom route.

| Task | Command |
|:------------------------------------|:----------------------------------------------------------------------|
| Send a range through an appliance VM, for tagged VMs only | `gcloud compute routes create to-onprem --network=vpc-prod --destination-range=172.16.0.0/12 --next-hop-instance=fw-1 --tags=needs-inspection --priority=800` |

> New in the June 2026 guide — custom static routes
>
> The guide now names *adding custom static routes*. The usual stems: send traffic for a range through a
> **network virtual appliance** (next hop instance or, for HA, an internal passthrough NLB); route only **tagged**
> VMs through it; or give VMs with a special tag a **higher-priority** path. Remember that a route only *forwards*
> — the appliance VM also needs **IP forwarding** enabled (`--can-ip-forward` at creation), and firewall rules
> still apply.

4.4.title: Firewall rules and Cloud NGFW policies
4.4.text:
Firewalls are **distributed and stateful**: they are enforced at each VM's network interface, and return traffic
of an allowed connection is allowed automatically. Google Cloud's firewall product is now called **Cloud Next
Generation Firewall (Cloud NGFW)**, and it has two kinds of rule containers.

### VPC firewall rules — the classic kind

| Component | Values |
|:----------------------|:----------------------------------------------------------------------|
| Direction | **Ingress** or **egress** |
| Action | Allow or deny |
| **Priority** | **0–65535, lower wins**; default **1000**. Ties: deny beats allow |
| Targets | All instances · **network tags** · **service accounts** |
| Source (ingress) / destination (egress) | IP ranges; for ingress also source tags or source service accounts |
| Protocols and ports | `tcp:443`, `udp:53`, `icmp`, or all |
| Logging | Off by default; per rule ([§4.11](https://nirmata78.github.io/gcp-ace-simulator/theory/04-networking.html#s4-11)) |

**Implied rules**, present in every VPC and invisible in the list: **allow all egress** and **deny all ingress**,
both at the lowest priority (65535). Some traffic is outside the firewall's control altogether: the metadata
server (`169.254.169.254`) is always reachable, and **egress to TCP port 25 on external addresses is always
blocked**.

| Task | Command |
|:------------------------------------|:----------------------------------------------------------------------|
| HTTPS from anywhere to VMs tagged `web` | `gcloud compute firewall-rules create allow-web --network=vpc-prod --direction=INGRESS --action=ALLOW --rules=tcp:443 --source-ranges=0.0.0.0/0 --target-tags=web` |
| Load-balancer health checks to one service account's VMs | `... --rules=tcp:8080 --source-ranges=130.211.0.0/22,35.191.0.0/16 --target-service-accounts=SA_EMAIL` |
| Record what a rule matches | `gcloud compute firewall-rules update allow-web --enable-logging` |

> **Target by network tag versus by service account.** A **network tag** is a string that anyone able to edit the VM
> can add — adding `web` silently opens the VM to the web rule. A **target service account** can only be changed
> by someone who may attach that service account (and only while the VM is stopped). *"Ensure only the web tier's
> VMs receive this traffic, even if developers edit instances"* points at service accounts (or secure tags).

### Firewall policies — hierarchical, global and regional

| Policy | Attached to | Use |
|:----------------------------------|:------------------------------|:----------------------------------------------------|
| **Hierarchical firewall policy** | Organization or folder | Guardrails that apply to every VPC beneath — *"block this range everywhere"*, *"always allow the security scanner"* |
| **Global network firewall policy** | One VPC (all regions) | Modern replacement for VPC firewall rules; supports secure tags, FQDNs, geolocation, address groups |
| **Regional network firewall policy** | One VPC in one region | Region-specific rules |

Policy rules add a fourth action to allow and deny: **`goto_next`**, which hands evaluation down to the next level
(for example, an org policy delegating a decision to projects). Standard and Enterprise features add
**`apply_security_profile_group`** for intrusion prevention.
