**Evaluation order**, top to bottom, stopping at the first allow or deny:

```
1. Hierarchical policy at the organization  -->  2. hierarchical policies on folders (top down)
3. VPC firewall rules and the global network firewall policy (order configurable per network)
4. Regional network firewall policy          -->  5. implied rules (allow egress, deny ingress)
```

> New in the June 2026 guide — Cloud NGFW and secure tags
>
> **Secure tags** are resource-manager tags created with the firewall purpose and bound to a VPC. You attach tag
> *values* to VM instances (or GKE node pools), and firewall-**policy** rules select sources and targets by those
> values. Because attaching a tag value needs an IAM role (`roles/resourcemanager.tagUser` on the value), **a
> developer cannot open a VM to a rule simply by editing it** — the property network tags lack. And the mapping
> runs one way only: **network tags work only in VPC firewall rules; firewall policies use secure tags, not network
> tags.**
>
> **Cloud NGFW tiers:** **Essentials** — the foundational stateful firewall, policies, secure tags (no extra
> charge); **Standard** — adds FQDN objects, geolocation and threat-intelligence lists (charged on evaluated
> traffic); **Enterprise** — adds intrusion detection and prevention with TLS inspection, via firewall endpoints
> and security profiles.


**Operating policies.** Move an existing VPC's rules into a policy with the **migration tool** (it keeps evaluation order; rules using
network tags need tag-to-secure-tag mapping first), then **associate** the policy — a new policy does nothing until
associated. To record what a policy rule matches, set **`--enable-logging`** on that rule; flow logs sample and do not name the rule.

4.5.title: Shared VPC and VPC Network Peering
4.5.text:
| Need | Product | The deciding property |
|:----------------------------------------------|:------------------------|:----------------------------------------------------|
| **One network used by many projects**; a central team owns subnets, routes and firewalls; app teams keep their own projects, IAM and billing | **Shared VPC** | Host project + service projects, **one** network |
| **Two separate VPCs**, private connectivity, no gateways | **VPC Network Peering** | Native, full bandwidth, **non-transitive** |
| **Many VPCs** (and on-premises) in hub-and-spoke, with transitivity | **Network Connectivity Center** | A hub that makes spokes reach each other |

### Shared VPC

- The **host project** owns the VPC; **service projects** are attached and create resources in its subnets.
  Resources (and their bills) belong to the service project; the network belongs to the host.
- Requires an **organization**. A service project attaches to **one** host; a host cannot also be a service project.
- **Roles:** the **Shared VPC Admin** (`roles/compute.xpnAdmin`, granted at the org or a folder) enables hosts and
  attaches service projects. **Network User** (`roles/compute.networkUser`) on the host project — or on
  **individual subnets** for least privilege — lets service-project developers put resources in those subnets.

| Task | Command |
|:------------------------------------|:----------------------------------------------------------------------|
| Make the host project | `gcloud compute shared-vpc enable HOST_PROJECT` |
| Attach a service project | `gcloud compute shared-vpc associated-projects add SVC_PROJECT --host-project=HOST_PROJECT` |
| Least privilege: one subnet only | `gcloud compute networks subnets add-iam-policy-binding web-euc2 --region=R --member=group:team-a@example.com --role=roles/compute.networkUser` |

### VPC Network Peering

- **Both sides must create** the peering before it becomes active; the networks can be in different projects or
  organizations.
- **Non-transitive:** if A peers with B and B with C, **A cannot reach C**. Nor can a peer use your VPN or
  Interconnect to reach your on-premises network, unless custom routes are exported and imported.
- **No overlapping subnet ranges** between peers.
- **Subnet routes are exchanged automatically**; custom (static and dynamic) routes only if you enable export and
  import. **Firewall rules are not exchanged** — each side still controls its own ingress.
- Peering is also how **private services access** works (Cloud SQL, Memorystore private IP, [§4.7](https://nirmata78.github.io/gcp-ace-simulator/theory/04-networking.html#s4-7)), which is why
  those services inherit the non-transitivity.

| Task | Command |
|:------------------------------------|:----------------------------------------------------------------------|
| Peer two VPCs — run it on **both** sides | `gcloud compute networks peerings create a-to-b --network=vpc-a --peer-project=PB --peer-network=vpc-b` |

> **When a stem forgives a weakness, it is naming the product that has it.** *"Transitive routing is not required"*
> points straight at peering. *"No gateways or tunnels in the path"* eliminates VPN. *"A central network team must
> own the firewall rules"* is Shared VPC, not peering.

4.6.title: Hybrid connectivity: VPN, Interconnect, Cloud Router
4.6.text:
| Product | Path | Capacity | SLA | Right when |
|:----------------|:----------------|:----------------------|:------------------|:----------------------------|
| **HA VPN** | IPsec over the internet | ~3 Gbps per tunnel (*verify*); add tunnels | **99.99%** with two interfaces and two tunnels | Encrypted, quick to set up, moderate bandwidth |
| Classic VPN | IPsec, one interface | Same per tunnel | 99.9% | Legacy; static routing |
| **Dedicated Interconnect** | Your own circuits in a Google **colocation facility** | 10 or 100 Gbps circuits (400 Gbps in some locations, *verify*) | 99.9 / 99.99% by topology | High, steady bandwidth; you can reach a colo |
| **Partner Interconnect** | Through a service provider | 50 Mbps – 50 Gbps per attachment | 99.9 / 99.99% | You **cannot** reach a colo, or need less than 10 Gbps |
| **Cross-Cloud Interconnect** | Dedicated circuits to AWS, Azure, OCI, Alibaba | 10 / 100 Gbps | 99.9 / 99.99% | Private link to another cloud |
| Direct / Carrier Peering | To Google's edge | — | None | Reaching **Google public services** (Workspace, public APIs) — **not your VPC** |

**Cloud Router** is the regional BGP speaker for your VPC: it learns on-premises prefixes over VPN or
Interconnect and advertises your subnets back. HA VPN requires it. With the VPC's **dynamic routing mode set to
global**, routes learned in one region are usable from all regions.

> **Interconnect traffic is not encrypted by default.** Options: **MACsec** on Dedicated Interconnect, or **HA VPN
> over Cloud Interconnect** for IPsec on top of the private circuit. *"Private, high-bandwidth and encrypted"* is one
> of those two.


> **Do the bandwidth sum first.** *"2 Gbps, encrypted, next week"* — HA VPN. *"20 Gbps sustained, we are in an
> Equinix facility where Google is present"* — Dedicated Interconnect. *"5 Gbps, our data centre is nowhere near a
> Google facility"* — Partner Interconnect.

4.7.title: Private access to Google and to services
4.7.text:
| Need | Mechanism | How |
|:----------------------------------------------|:----------------------------------|:----------------------------------------------|
| VMs **without external IPs** reach Google APIs (Cloud Storage, BigQuery...) | **Private Google Access** | A **per-subnet** setting |
| **On-premises** hosts reach Google APIs privately over VPN / Interconnect | Private Google Access for on-premises | `private.googleapis.com` (`199.36.153.8/30`, most APIs) or `restricted.googleapis.com` (`199.36.153.4/30`, only APIs that support VPC Service Controls), via on-premises DNS and a Cloud Router **custom advertisement** of that range |
| Reach Google APIs at an **internal IP you choose** in your VPC | **Private Service Connect endpoint** for Google APIs | A PSC forwarding rule |
| Private IP for **Cloud SQL, Memorystore, Filestore, AlloyDB** | **Private services access** | Allocate a range; Google peers a service-producer VPC to yours |
| Consume a **specific service** (another team's, a partner's, a Google service) by internal IP, no peering | **Private Service Connect** (consumer endpoint → producer service attachment) | No overlapping-range problems, no transitivity issues |
| **Cloud Run / functions** reach resources on your VPC | **Direct VPC egress** (recommended) or a Serverless VPC Access connector | Per service |

> **Private Google Access versus Cloud NAT.** PGA reaches **Google APIs only**. Cloud NAT reaches **the internet**
> (package mirrors, a partner API). A private VM that needs only Cloud Storage and BigQuery needs PGA and nothing
> else; one that must `apt-get` from the internet needs Cloud NAT.

4.8.title: IP addresses, Cloud DNS and Cloud NAT
4.8.text:
### Addresses

| Type | Behaviour |
|:----------------------------------|:----------------------------------------------------------------|
| **Ephemeral** internal or external | Assigned at creation; an ephemeral **external** IP is released when the VM **stops** |
| **Static external, regional** | Reserved; for VMs and regional load balancers. **Billed while reserved and unused** |
| **Static external, global** | For global load balancers (Premium Tier only) |
| **Static internal** | A reserved address from a subnet — *"the licence server must always be `10.0.3.21`"* |

| Task | Command |
|:------------------------------------|:----------------------------------------------------------------------|
| Static IP for a global load balancer | `gcloud compute addresses create lb-ip --global` |
| Keep a VM's current ephemeral IP | `gcloud compute addresses create keep-me --addresses=34.118.1.2 --region=R` |
| Reserve a fixed internal IP | `gcloud compute addresses create lic-ip --region=R --subnet=app-euc2 --addresses=10.0.3.21` |

> **Private ranges can never be external IPs.** `10.x`, `172.16--31.x`, `192.168.x` are RFC 1918; an option
> assigning one as a VM's *external* address is invalid on sight.

### Cloud DNS

| Zone or policy | Does |
|:--------------------------------------|:----------------------------------------------------------------------|
| **Public zone** | Authoritative DNS on the internet for your domain; **DNSSEC** available; 100% SLA |
| **Private zone** | Names visible only to the **VPC networks you authorise** — `db.internal.kestrel.io` |
| **Forwarding zone** | Sends queries for a domain (e.g. `corp.local`) to **on-premises resolvers** |
| **Peering zone** | Resolves a domain using **another VPC's** DNS configuration |
| **Inbound server policy** | Gives the VPC resolver an address **on-premises clients can query** — so on-prem can resolve private zones |
| Response policy | Overrides answers for specific names — e.g. steer `*.googleapis.com` to private endpoints |

VMs also get **internal DNS** automatically: `VM_NAME.ZONE.c.PROJECT_ID.internal`.


> **Direction decides the DNS object.** Cloud VMs must resolve **on-premises** names — a **forwarding zone**.
> On-premises hosts must resolve **Cloud private** names — an **inbound server policy**.

### Cloud NAT

**Cloud NAT gives resources without external IPs outbound connectivity to the internet, and nothing inbound.** It
is a **regional**, software-defined service (no proxy VM, no single point of failure) configured on a **Cloud
Router**. It serves VMs, **private GKE nodes**, and serverless workloads using Direct VPC egress.

| Setting | Why it matters |
|:----------------------------------|:------------------------------------------------------------------|
| **Automatic vs manual (static) NAT IPs** | Manual IPs give a **fixed egress address** a partner can allow-list |
| Ports per VM | Too few ports cause dropped connections under load (*"OUT_OF_RESOURCES"*) |
| NAT logging | Translations and drops, in Cloud Logging |
| Public NAT vs Private NAT | Private NAT translates between VPCs or to on-premises with overlapping ranges |

| Task | Command |
|:------------------------------------|:----------------------------------------------------------------------|
| Cloud NAT for one region | `gcloud compute routers create nat-router --network=vpc-prod --region=R`, then `gcloud compute routers nats create nat-1 --router=nat-router --region=R --nat-all-subnet-ip-ranges --auto-allocate-nat-external-ips` |

4.9.title: Load balancing
4.9.text:
Four questions choose every load balancer: **external or internal · global or regional · HTTP(S) or any TCP/UDP
· proxy (terminates) or passthrough (preserves the client IP)**.

| Load balancer | Layer | Scope | Traffic | Client IP at backend | Typical use |
|:------------------------------|:-------|:----------------|:----------------|:--------------|:----------------------------|
| **Global external Application LB** | 7 | Global, **one anycast IP** | HTTP(S), HTTP/2, gRPC | No (`X-Forwarded-For`) | Public web app across regions; Cloud CDN, Cloud Armor |
| Regional external Application LB | 7 | Regional | HTTP(S) | No | Public HTTP in one region; Standard Tier possible |
| **Internal Application LB** (regional or cross-region) | 7 | Internal | HTTP(S) | No | Internal microservices, path routing |
| External proxy Network LB | 4 | Global or regional | TCP, SSL | No | Non-HTTP TCP needing TLS offload or global reach |
| Internal proxy Network LB | 4 | Internal | TCP | No | Internal TCP with a proxy |
| **External passthrough Network LB** | 4 | Regional | TCP, **UDP**, ESP, ICMP | **Yes** | Games, UDP, protocols needing the real client IP |
| **Internal passthrough Network LB** | 4 | Regional, internal | TCP, **UDP** | **Yes** | Internal TCP/UDP; next hop for appliances ([§4.3](https://nirmata78.github.io/gcp-ace-simulator/theory/04-networking.html#s4-3)) |

Envoy-based load balancers, such as the internal Application Load Balancer and the regional external one, need a
**proxy-only subnet** in each region they use (`--purpose=REGIONAL_MANAGED_PROXY`, *verify*): the proxies take
their addresses from it, so backend firewall rules must allow that range.

> **Three eliminations answer most load-balancer items.** *UDP* or *not HTTP* removes every Application LB.
> *Must see the client's source IP* removes every proxy — it is a **passthrough** LB. *One IP worldwide with
> failover between regions* is the **global external Application LB** (Premium Tier).

**The parts of an Application LB**, which the exam names: a **forwarding rule** (IP and port) → a **target proxy**
(HTTP or HTTPS, holding the **certificate**) → a **URL map** (host and path rules) → **backend services** (with
health checks, session affinity, Cloud CDN, Cloud Armor) → **backends**:

| Backend type | Points at |
|:----------------------------------|:------------------------------------------------------------------|
| **Instance group** (managed or unmanaged) | VMs |
| **Zonal NEG** | Pod or VM IP:port — GKE **container-native load balancing** |
| **Serverless NEG** | **Cloud Run**, Cloud Run functions, App Engine — the way to put them behind a global LB |
| Internet NEG | An external endpoint |
| Hybrid NEG | On-premises or other-cloud endpoints over hybrid connectivity |
| Private Service Connect NEG | A published service or Google API |

> **Health checks come from Google's probe ranges, `35.191.0.0/16` and `130.211.0.0/22`.** If no firewall rule allows
> them to the backends' serving port, every backend is marked unhealthy and the load balancer returns errors even
> though the VMs are fine. *"All backends unhealthy right after creating the LB"* is almost always this rule.

**Certificates:** **Google-managed certificates** (provisioned and renewed automatically once DNS points at the
LB, or via DNS authorisation in **Certificate Manager**) versus self-managed certificates you upload and renew.

4.10.title: Network Service Tiers, Cloud CDN and Cloud Armor
4.10.text:
| Tier | Path | Scope | Cost | Right when |
|:----------------|:----------------------------------------------|:------------------|:--------|:----------------------------|
| **Premium** (default) | Traffic enters and leaves **Google's backbone** at the edge closest to the user | **Global** — required for global LBs and global anycast IPs | Higher | Performance, global reach |
| **Standard** | Traffic rides the **public internet** to and from the region | **Regional only** | Lower egress price | Cost-sensitive, single-region, latency-tolerant |

Set per project default (`gcloud compute project-info update --default-network-tier=STANDARD`) or per resource on
IP addresses and forwarding rules.

> *"Lowest network cost, users in one region, performance not critical"* — **Standard Tier**. *"Single anycast IP
> for users on three continents"* — **Premium Tier** with a global external Application LB; Standard Tier cannot do
> it.

**Cloud CDN** caches responses at Google's edge; it is enabled on a **backend service or backend bucket** of a
global external Application LB. **Cloud Armor** is a WAF and DDoS policy attached to backend services of external
load balancers: preconfigured OWASP rules, IP and geo allow/deny, rate limiting, bot management, and **Adaptive
Protection** (ML-detected layer-7 attacks).

4.11.title: Seeing the network: flow logs, firewall logs, Connectivity Tests
4.11.text:
| Tool | Records or does | Use it for |
|:----------------------------------|:------------------------------------------------------------|:------------------------------|
| **VPC Flow Logs** | A **sample** of network flows (5-tuple, bytes, packets, latency, metadata), enabled per subnet or at network/attachment level | Traffic analysis, forensics, capacity and cost investigations |
| **Firewall Rules Logging** | One record per connection **allowed or denied by a specific rule** you enabled logging on | *"Is my rule matching? Which rule blocked this?"* |
| **Connectivity Tests** (Network Intelligence Center) | Simulates a packet from A to B through routes, firewalls, peering, VPN; can also probe the live data plane | *"Why can't VM A reach B?"* without touching production |
| Firewall Insights | Shadowed, overly permissive and unused rules | Cleaning up rules |
| Network Topology / Performance Dashboard | Visual topology; Google-measured latency and loss | Understanding and baselining |

> **Flow logs versus firewall logs.** Flow logs say **what traffic flowed** (sampled, per subnet). Firewall logs say
> **which rule decided** a connection. The **implied** deny-ingress rule cannot be logged — to log denied traffic,
> create an explicit low-priority deny rule with logging on. Both land in Cloud Logging and cost ingestion ([§9.7](https://nirmata78.github.io/gcp-ace-simulator/theory/09-operations.html#s9-7)).

| Task | Command |
|:------------------------------------|:----------------------------------------------------------------------|
| Turn on VPC Flow Logs for a subnet | `gcloud compute networks subnets update web-euc2 --region=R --enable-flow-logs` |

### More to recognise

- **Firewall operations.** An **address group** is a reusable list of IP ranges for policy rules. **Cloud NGFW
  Enterprise** adds intrusion prevention: a firewall endpoint, a security profile group and a rule with
  `apply_security_profile_group`. A firewall-purpose tag key is scoped to **one VPC** by its purpose data.
  `gcloud compute instances network-interfaces get-effective-firewalls` lists every rule and policy that applies
  to one VM.
- **Routing.** A **policy-based route** matches on **source** range and protocol and forwards to an internal
  passthrough load balancer — static routes match destinations only. A static route with **`--next-hop-ilb`**
  spreads over healthy appliances. Peered VPCs share **custom** (including VPN-learned) routes only when one side
  exports and the other imports them.
- **Connectivity.** **Network Connectivity Center** with **VPC spokes** gives any-to-any connectivity among many
  VPCs (peering is not transitive). **HA VPN to AWS** uses two AWS VPN connections and **four tunnels** for the
  99.99% topology. A **cross-region internal Application Load Balancer** fails internal traffic over between
  regions; a global external ALB with a **serverless NEG per region** does the same for Cloud Run.
- **Addresses and NAT.** Global load balancers need a **global** static address. A full GKE Pod range is extended
  by adding another secondary range and new node pools with `--pod-ipv4-range`. **Dynamic port allocation** on
  Cloud NAT fixes port exhaustion on a few busy VMs.

4.12.title: Part 4 recall card
4.12.text:
| Prompt | Answer |
|:------------------------------------------------|:--------------------------------------------------------|
| One VPC across regions? | Yes — VPC global, subnets regional |
| Subnet out of addresses | `subnets expand-ip-range` (never shrink) |
| Traffic for a range through an appliance VM | **Custom static route**, next hop instance (+ IP forwarding) |
| Lowest number wins? | Yes — priority 0–65535, default 1000 |
| Firewall targets developers cannot change by editing a VM | Service accounts, or **secure tags** in a firewall policy |
| Network tags in a firewall **policy**? | **No** — policies use secure tags |
| Guardrail rule for every VPC in a folder | **Hierarchical firewall policy** |
| Central team owns network, app teams own projects | **Shared VPC** |
| Two VPCs, private, non-transitive is fine | **VPC Network Peering** |
| Many VPCs, transitive hub | **Network Connectivity Center** |
| Encrypted, a few Gbps, fast to set up | **HA VPN** (99.99%) |
| 10+ Gbps, in a Google colo | **Dedicated Interconnect** |
| Cannot reach a colo | **Partner Interconnect** |
| Private VMs to Google APIs only | **Private Google Access** |
| Private VMs to the internet, nothing inbound | **Cloud NAT** |
| Fixed egress IP for a partner's allow-list | Cloud NAT with **static** NAT IPs |
| Cloud Run to a private Cloud SQL IP | **Direct VPC egress** |
| Cloud VMs resolve `corp.local` | **Forwarding zone** |
| On-prem resolves Cloud private zone | **Inbound server policy** |
| UDP, preserve client IP | **Passthrough** Network LB |
| One anycast IP, TLS at edge, multi-region | **Global external Application LB** (Premium Tier) |
| All backends unhealthy | Allow **35.191.0.0/16** and **130.211.0.0/22** |
| Cheapest egress, one region | **Standard Tier** |
| Why can't A reach B? | **Connectivity Tests** |

5.1.title: Choosing compute — the whole landscape
5.1.text:
Read the tree top to bottom and take the first exit that fits.

```
Is it an AI agent you want hosted, with sessions, memory and scaling managed for you?
    YES -> Agent Runtime on Gemini Enterprise Agent Platform            (§8.6)
Is it a container, or can it be one?
    NO  -> Do you need the OS: kernel modules, licensed software, lift-and-shift, Windows?
             YES -> Compute Engine VM (+ a managed instance group to scale and heal)
    YES -> Is it request- or event-driven and stateless?
             YES -> Cloud Run service (requests) / Cloud Run job (run to completion)
                    One small function per event?  -> Cloud Run functions
             NO  -> Do you need Kubernetes: operators, StatefulSets, DaemonSets, Helm, a mesh?
                      YES -> GKE Autopilot (Google runs the nodes)
                             GKE Standard  (you need node-level control)
Heavy parallel maths (training, large inference)? -> add GPUs or TPUs to the chosen platform (§5.9)
```

| Stem language | Points at |
|:------------------------------------------------------------|:------------------------------------------|
| "scale to zero", "pay nothing when idle", "spiky HTTP traffic" | **Cloud Run** |
| "one function per upload / message / event" | **Cloud Run functions** (with Eventarc) |
| "already on Kubernetes", "Helm charts", "operators", "DaemonSet" | **GKE** |
| "do not want to manage nodes, upgrades or node pools" | **GKE Autopilot** |
| "specific OS / kernel", "licensed software", "lift and shift", "Windows Server" | **Compute Engine** |
| "batch job that runs to completion" | **Cloud Run jobs**, or Batch on Compute Engine |
| "deploy our LangGraph / ADK agent with managed sessions and memory" | **Agent Runtime** |
| "train a large model", "matrix maths at scale" | **GPUs** or **TPUs** ([§5.9](https://nirmata78.github.io/gcp-ace-simulator/theory/05-compute-engine.html#s5-9)) |

> **Scale-to-zero distractors.** A GKE Standard cluster with a Horizontal Pod Autoscaler scales **Pods**, but the
> nodes keep running and billing. A managed instance group scaling on CPU needs running VMs to measure. App Engine
> **flexible** keeps at least one instance. Only Cloud Run, Cloud Run functions (and App Engine standard) idle to
> zero cost.

5.2.title: Machine families, custom types and provisioning models
5.2.text:
| Family | Series (examples — *verify* the current catalogue) | Use |
|:----------------------|:--------------------------------------------|:------------------------------------------------|
| **General purpose** | E2 (cost-optimised, shared-core `e2-micro`/`small`/`medium`), N2, N2D, N4, C3, C4, Arm-based C4A / T2A, Tau T2D | Most workloads; E2 for the cheapest general VM |
| **Compute-optimised** | C2, C2D, H3 | High clock, HPC, game servers |
| **Memory-optimised** | M1, M2, M3, X4 | SAP HANA, very large in-memory databases |
| **Storage-optimised** | Z3 | Very high local-SSD density |
| **Accelerator-optimised** | A2, A3, A4 (NVIDIA GPUs), G2 (L4 GPUs) | ML training and inference, graphics |

The exam tests the **category**, not model numbers: *"4 TB of RAM in one VM"* is memory-optimised; *"cheapest
possible dev box"* is E2; *"GPU for inference"* is accelerator-optimised or GPUs attached ([§5.9](https://nirmata78.github.io/gcp-ace-simulator/theory/05-compute-engine.html#s5-9)).

**Custom machine types** set vCPU and memory independently (on E2, N2, N2D, N4 and N1, among others) — the answer
to *"6 vCPUs and 40 GB; every predefined shape wastes one or the other"*. **Extended memory** goes beyond the
normal memory-per-vCPU ceiling.

### Provisioning models

| Model | Discount | Catch | Right for |
|:----------------------|:----------------|:------------------------------------------------------|:------------------------------|
| **Standard** (on-demand) | — | — | Default |
| **Spot VMs** | Large (60–91%, *verify*) | **Can be preempted at any time with ~30 s notice**; no SLA; no live migration; **no maximum runtime** | Fault-tolerant, checkpointing batch, CI runners, rendering |
| Preemptible VMs (legacy) | Large | Preemptible **and capped at 24 hours** | Superseded by Spot — recognise the name |
| Committed use | Up to ~55–70% (*verify*) | 1 or 3 years, billed regardless | Steady 24×7 footprint ([§2.8](https://nirmata78.github.io/gcp-ace-simulator/theory/02-organization-projects-billing.html#s2-8)) |
| Sole-tenant nodes | Premium | Most expensive | Physical isolation, bring-your-own-licence rules |

| Task | Command |
|:------------------------------------|:----------------------------------------------------------------------|
| Custom shape on a Spot VM | `gcloud compute instances create render-1 --machine-type=n2-custom-6-40960 --provisioning-model=SPOT --instance-termination-action=DELETE` |

**On preemption** a Spot VM is **stopped** or **deleted** (your `--instance-termination-action`); a shutdown script
gets the notice period to checkpoint. In a MIG, preempted VMs are recreated when capacity returns.

5.3.title: Launching an instance
5.3.text:
| Flag family | What it controls |
|:------------------------------------|:------------------------------------------------------------------|
| `--image-family` + `--image-project` | Boots the **latest non-deprecated** image in a family — `debian-cloud`, `ubuntu-os-cloud`, `windows-cloud`, or your own |
| Disks | Boot disk type and size; extra disks created or attached ([§5.4](https://nirmata78.github.io/gcp-ace-simulator/theory/05-compute-engine.html#s5-4)) |
| Network | Subnet, `--no-address` for no external IP, network tags |
| Identity | Service account and scopes ([§3.10](https://nirmata78.github.io/gcp-ace-simulator/theory/03-identity-access.html#s3-10)) |
| **Metadata** | Key–values read by the guest from the metadata server: `startup-script`, `shutdown-script`, `enable-oslogin`, `ssh-keys` |
| **Availability policy** | `--maintenance-policy=MIGRATE` (live-migrate during host maintenance) or `TERMINATE`; `--restart-on-failure` (automatic restart if the host crashes) |
| Protection | `--deletion-protection`; Shielded VM (secure boot, vTPM, integrity monitoring); Confidential VM (memory encryption) |

> **The availability policy is two settings.** *On host maintenance*: **MIGRATE** keeps the VM running by moving it
> to another host — the default — or **TERMINATE** stops it. *Automatic restart*: bring the VM back if the host
> fails. **GPU VMs must use TERMINATE** (they cannot live-migrate), and Spot VMs always terminate and never
> auto-restart.

**Changing a running VM:** the machine type, service account and scopes can be changed **only while the VM is
stopped**; disks can be attached live; labels, tags and metadata change live. A **stopped** VM, listed as
`TERMINATED`, keeps its disks (billed) and loses an ephemeral external IP; a **suspended** VM also keeps its memory state.

5.4.title: Disks: Persistent Disk, Hyperdisk and Local SSD
5.4.text:
| Type | Nature | Notes |
|:--------------------------------|:------------------------------------------|:--------------------------------------------------------|
| **pd-balanced** | SSD-backed network block storage | Good default for most boot and data disks |
| **pd-ssd** | Higher IOPS per GB | Databases on older machine series |
| **pd-standard** | HDD-backed | Cheapest, sequential throughput |
| pd-extreme | Provisioned IOPS | Top PD performance on some series |
| **Hyperdisk Balanced / Throughput / Extreme** | Network block storage with **performance (IOPS, throughput) provisioned independently of size** | The storage of the **newest machine series** — several (e.g. C4, N4) support **only** Hyperdisk (*verify* per series) |
| **Hyperdisk ML** | Read-only, attachable to **many VMs at once** | Serving model weights to a fleet |
| **Regional PD / Hyperdisk Balanced High Availability** | **Synchronously replicated across two zones** | Survives a zone failure; force-attach to a standby VM in the other zone |
| **Local SSD** | Physically attached, 375 GB partitions | **Highest performance, ephemeral**: data survives a reboot or live migration, **lost when the VM stops or is deleted** |

**Rules of thumb the exam uses:**

1. **Disks can be resized up, never down**, while attached. Grow the file system inside the guest afterwards.
2. **Local SSD plus a durability requirement is always wrong.** Use it for scratch, caches, temporary data.
3. **Regional disks are high availability; snapshots are backup.** *"Survive a zone failure with no data loss"* for
   a single-VM database is a regional disk, not a snapshot schedule.
4. **Zonal disks attach only to VMs in their zone.** To move one, snapshot it and create a disk elsewhere.

| Task | Command |
|:------------------------------------|:----------------------------------------------------------------------|
| Grow a disk (never shrink) | `gcloud compute disks resize data-2 --zone=Z --size=1TB` |
| Attach an existing disk | `gcloud compute instances attach-disk web-1 --disk=data-2 --zone=Z` |
| Regional disk, replicated in two zones | `gcloud compute disks create db-ha --region=R --replica-zones=R-a,R-b --type=pd-balanced` |

5.5.title: Connecting to instances: SSH keys, OS Login, IAP
5.5.text:
### Two ways Linux SSH access is authorised

| Method | How access is granted | Revoke by | Choose when |
|:----------------------|:----------------------------------------------|:------------------|:----------------------------|
| **Metadata-managed SSH keys** | Public keys in **project-wide** or **instance** metadata; `gcloud compute ssh` adds yours | Removing the key from metadata | Small, informal set-ups |
| **OS Login** | Linux accounts **tied to Google identities**; access is an **IAM role** | Removing the IAM role, or suspending the user | **The recommended answer** for teams |

**OS Login** is enabled with metadata `enable-oslogin=TRUE` (project or instance) or enforced org-wide with
`compute.requireOsLogin`. Access is then pure IAM:

| Role | Grants |
|:--------------------------------------|:----------------------------------------------------------|
| `roles/compute.osLogin` | SSH as a normal user |
| `roles/compute.osAdminLogin` | SSH with **sudo** |
| `roles/iam.serviceAccountUser` on the VM's service account | Also needed when the VM runs as a service account |
| `roles/compute.osLoginExternalUser` (on the org) | Users from **outside** your organization |

Add **`enable-oslogin-2fa=TRUE`** to require two-step verification. OS Login is Linux-only; Windows uses RDP with a
password generated by `gcloud compute reset-windows-password`.

> **Project-wide SSH keys reach every VM in the project** that does not block them. *"A contractor's key must work
> on one VM only"* — instance-level key with `block-project-ssh-keys=TRUE`, or better, OS Login with an IAM binding
> on that one instance.

### Reaching a VM with no external IP

| Mechanism | Needs |
|:----------------------------------|:------------------------------------------------------------------|
| **IAP TCP forwarding** | `gcloud compute ssh vm --tunnel-through-iap`; a firewall rule allowing **`35.235.240.0/20`** on 22 (or 3389); **`roles/iap.tunnelResourceAccessor`** |
| Bastion host | A VM with an external IP you harden and patch — the assembled alternative |
| VPN / Interconnect | Private path from on-premises |
| **Serial console** | Boot problems, broken networking: `gcloud compute connect-to-serial-port vm`, metadata `serial-port-enable=TRUE` |

> *"SSH to VMs with no public IP, per-user authorisation, no bastion"* — **IAP TCP forwarding + OS Login**.
> *"The VM does not boot / sshd is dead"* — **serial console**.

5.6.title: Inventory and VM Manager
5.6.text:
### Viewing what is running


A project-level list is `gcloud compute instances list`; **across projects** it is Cloud Asset Inventory ([§2.9](https://nirmata78.github.io/gcp-ace-simulator/theory/02-organization-projects-billing.html#s2-9)).

### VM Manager

**VM Manager** is a suite for running a fleet of VMs, driven by the **OS Config agent** (pre-installed in most
Google public images). Enable it with the OS Config API and metadata `enable-osconfig=TRUE`.

| Component | Does |
|:----------------------------------|:----------------------------------------------------------------|
| **OS inventory management** | Collects installed packages, OS version, available updates — per VM, queryable, exported to Asset Inventory |
| **Patch management** | **Patch jobs** (run now) and **patch deployments** (scheduled), filtered by labels or zones, with pre/post scripts, a **rollout** (zone by zone or concurrent, with a **disruption budget** capping how many VMs patch at once) and **patch compliance** reporting |
| **OS policies** | Declare desired state — packages installed, files, services, scripts — and the agent enforces it; assigned to VMs by filters |


> *"Patch 400 Linux VMs every Sunday, and report which are non-compliant"* — **VM Manager patch deployment**. *"Make
> sure the Ops Agent is installed on every VM labelled `env=prod`"* — an **OS policy assignment**. A cron job on
> each VM is the assembled distractor.

5.7.title: Snapshots, images and machine images
5.7.text:
| Artefact | Captures | Use it to |
|:----------------------|:--------------------------------------------------------|:------------------------------------------------|
| **Snapshot** | **One disk's data**, incrementally | Back up a disk; restore or clone **that disk**, in any zone or region |
| **Custom image** | **One disk**, as a **bootable** image | Boot new VMs from a golden state; **what an instance template references** |
| **Machine image** | **All of a VM's disks plus its configuration** — machine type, metadata, labels, tags, network, service account | Clone, back up or move a **whole VM** |
| Instance template | A **specification**, no data | Tell a MIG what to create ([§5.8](https://nirmata78.github.io/gcp-ace-simulator/theory/05-compute-engine.html#s5-8)) |

> **Snapshot = one disk's data. Image = one bootable disk. Machine image = the whole VM. Template = a recipe.**

### Snapshots

- **Incremental**: the first is full, later ones store changed blocks; deleting one never breaks the others.
- Stored **multi-regionally or regionally** (you choose), so a disk can be created from them anywhere.
- **Snapshot schedules** are resource policies attached to disks, with retention — the managed answer to *"back up
  these disks nightly, keep 14 days"*. A cron job running `gcloud` is the assembled distractor.
- **Archive snapshots** cost less to store and more to restore; **instant snapshots** are fast, in-place,
  point-in-time copies for rollback — **not** a backup, since they live with the disk.
- For application consistency, quiesce the application or use **VSS** on Windows.

### Images

- **Image families** point at the newest non-deprecated image — build `hardened-v7`, add it to family
  `hardened`, and every template using the family picks it up.
- **Deprecation states**: `DEPRECATED` (warn), `OBSOLETE` (no new use), `DELETED`.
- **Share** images across projects by granting `roles/compute.imageUser` on the image project.
- The **golden-image** pattern: *"every VM must boot already hardened, with no configuration step at start-up"* —
  bake a custom image; a startup script is configuration at boot and can fail.

| Task | Command |
|:------------------------------------|:----------------------------------------------------------------------|
| Nightly snapshots, kept 14 days | `gcloud compute resource-policies create snapshot-schedule nightly --region=R --daily-schedule --start-time=02:00 --max-retention-days=14`, then `gcloud compute disks add-resource-policies data-2 --resource-policies=nightly --zone=Z` |
| Snapshot now; restore in another zone | `gcloud compute snapshots create snap-1 --source-disk=data-2 --source-disk-zone=Z` · `gcloud compute disks create data-2-copy --source-snapshot=snap-1 --zone=Z2` |
| Custom image in a family | `gcloud compute images create hardened-v7 --source-disk=golden --source-disk-zone=Z --family=hardened` |
| Whole VM: every disk plus its configuration | `gcloud compute machine-images create web-1-mi --source-instance=web-1 --source-instance-zone=Z` |

> *"Recreate this VM — with all three data disks and its configuration — in another zone, fewest steps"* is a
> **machine image**. Three snapshots move the data but lose the machine type, metadata, tags and service account;
> a custom image contains only one disk.

5.8.title: Instance templates and managed instance groups
5.8.text:
**An instance template is immutable.** To change what a group creates, make a **new** template and roll it out.
Templates are **global** or **regional** (a regional template keeps its dependencies in one region).

### MIG versus unmanaged instance group

| | Managed (MIG) | Unmanaged |
|:----------------------|:------------------------------------------------|:------------------------------------|
| Instances | Identical, **from a template** | Any VMs you add by hand |
| Autoscaling, autohealing, rolling updates | **Yes** | No |
| Use | Almost everything | Load-balancing a heterogeneous legacy set |

**Zonal MIGs** keep all VMs in one zone; **regional MIGs** spread them across zones (three by default) and survive
a zone outage — the answer to *"must stay up if a zone fails"*.

### The four MIG features, and which problem each solves

| Feature | Solves |
|:----------------------------------|:------------------------------------------------------------------|
| **Autohealing** (a health check on the MIG) | The VM is up but **the application is broken** — the MIG **recreates** it |
| **Autoscaling** | Not enough or too much **capacity** — changes the **count** |
| **Updates** (rolling, canary) | Rolling a **new template** out without an outage |
| **Regional distribution** | Surviving a **zone** failure |

> **MIG health check versus load-balancer health check.** A load balancer's health check only **stops sending
> traffic** to a failing instance — the broken VM keeps running forever. The MIG's **autohealing** health check
> **recreates** it. Give autohealing an **initial delay** long enough for boot, or it will kill instances in a loop.

### Autoscaling

| Signal | Example |
|:----------------------------------|:------------------------------------------------------------------|
| **CPU utilisation** | Target 60% average |
| **Load-balancing serving capacity** | Utilisation or requests per second per instance behind an HTTP(S) LB |
| **Cloud Monitoring metric** | Per-instance or per-group, e.g. Pub/Sub backlog |
| **Schedules** | Scale up at 08:00 on weekdays |

Other controls: **min and max** replicas, the **initialisation period** (how long a new VM is ignored while it
warms up), **scale-in controls** (limit how fast it shrinks), and **predictive** autoscaling for CPU patterns.

### Updating a group

| Task | Command |
|:------------------------------------|:----------------------------------------------------------------------|
| Autoscale on CPU | `gcloud compute instance-groups managed set-autoscaling web-mig --region=R --min-num-replicas=3 --max-num-replicas=12 --target-cpu-utilization=0.6` |
| Autohealing | `gcloud compute instance-groups managed update web-mig --region=R --health-check=hc-http --initial-delay=300` |
| Canary: 20% on the new template | `gcloud compute instance-groups managed rolling-action start-update web-mig --region=R --version=template=web-v1 --canary-version=template=web-v2,target-size=20%` |
| Full rollout with no capacity loss | `... rolling-action start-update web-mig --region=R --version=template=web-v2 --max-surge=3 --max-unavailable=0` |
| Restart or recreate every VM | `... rolling-action restart web-mig` · `... rolling-action replace web-mig` |

| Knob | Effect |
|:----------------------------------|:------------------------------------------------------------------|
| `--max-surge` | Extra instances created above target during the update (capacity kept) |
| `--max-unavailable` | How many may be down at once (0 = never below target) |
| `--type=proactive` / `opportunistic` | Replace now, or only when instances are recreated anyway |
| `--replacement-method=substitute` / `recreate` | New names, or keep names (needed for stateful MIGs) |
| `--canary-version=...,target-size=N%` | Send part of the group to the new template first |
| **Rollback** | Another `start-update` back to the old template |

**Stateful MIGs** preserve per-instance disks, metadata and IPs across recreation — MIG management for workloads
like databases or legacy apps that need stable identity.

5.9.title: GPUs and TPUs
5.9.text:
> New in the June 2026 guide — GPUs and TPUs
>
> The guide asks you to **identify whether to use GPUs or TPUs**, and to **attach** them. The choice is about the
> workload; the attaching is about a handful of hard constraints.

| | **GPUs** (NVIDIA) | **TPUs** (Google) |
|:----------------------|:------------------------------------------------|:------------------------------------------------|
| What | General-purpose parallel processors | ASICs built for large matrix / tensor operations |
| Frameworks | Anything CUDA: PyTorch, TensorFlow, JAX, RAPIDS, custom kernels | **JAX, PyTorch/XLA, TensorFlow** via the XLA compiler |
| Strong at | Broad model variety, custom ops, inference, graphics, rendering, video, smaller jobs | **Large-scale training and serving** of big models, cost per unit of throughput at scale |
| Where | Compute Engine (attached or accelerator-optimised series), GKE node pools, Cloud Run | **Cloud TPU VMs**, **GKE TPU node pools**, Agent Platform training |
| Unit | 1–8+ GPUs per VM | Chips, hosts, **slices** (e.g. `v5litepod-8`), multislice |

> *"Rendering"*, *"video transcoding"*, *"our model uses custom CUDA kernels"*, *"a few GPUs for inference"* —
> **GPU**. *"Train a very large transformer in JAX as cheaply as possible at scale"* — **TPU**. When the stem gives
> no framework constraint and the workload is general, GPU is the safer answer.

### Attaching GPUs — the constraints

- **Accelerator-optimised series** (A2, A3, A4, G2) come with GPUs built into the machine type — one A100 40GB is
  **`a2-highgpu-1g`**, the 80GB A100 is `a2-ultragpu-*`; you choose the machine type, not `--accelerator`. **N1** VMs
  take attached GPUs (`--accelerator=type=nvidia-tesla-t4,count=1`); A100s cannot be attached to N1, and E2/C3 take
  no GPUs.
- **Graphics desktops** (CAD, 3D) — NVIDIA GPUs such as the L4 with **RTX Virtual Workstation** images. TPUs never
  render graphics.
- **Very large training** across thousands of chips — a **multi-host TPU slice**, joined by the inter-chip
  interconnect.
- **GKE Autopilot**: the Pod asks — `nodeSelector: cloud.google.com/gke-accelerator: nvidia-l4` plus
  `resources.limits: nvidia.com/gpu: 1`; Autopilot provisions the node and drivers.
- **`--maintenance-policy=TERMINATE`** — GPU VMs cannot live-migrate.
- **Drivers**: use a GPU-ready image (Deep Learning VM) or install NVIDIA drivers; GKE can install them for you.
- **Quota**: per region **and** an all-regions GPU quota; request both ([§2.5](https://nirmata78.github.io/gcp-ace-simulator/theory/02-organization-projects-billing.html#s2-5)).
- **Availability**: GPU and TPU types exist only in certain **zones** ([§1.4](https://nirmata78.github.io/gcp-ace-simulator/theory/01-exam-locations-tools.html#s1-4)). *"The create call fails in this zone"*
  — check `accelerator-types list` and choose another zone.
- Spot pricing applies to both GPUs and TPUs for interruptible work.

| Task | Command |
|:------------------------------------|:----------------------------------------------------------------------|
| GPU attached to an N1 VM | `gcloud compute instances create train-1 --machine-type=n1-standard-8 --accelerator=type=nvidia-tesla-t4,count=2 --maintenance-policy=TERMINATE` |
| GPU built into the machine type (G2, A2, A3) | `gcloud compute instances create infer-1 --machine-type=g2-standard-8 --maintenance-policy=TERMINATE` |
| Which zones offer a GPU | `gcloud compute accelerator-types list --filter="name~l4"` |

### More to recognise

- **Compute choices beyond the big four.** **Batch** runs arrays of tasks on VMs it creates and deletes.
  **VMware Engine** moves vSphere estates unchanged. **Sole-tenant nodes** give dedicated hosts for per-core
  licences. **Oracle Database@Google Cloud** runs Exadata inside Google Cloud regions.
- **Capacity and placement.** A **future reservation** holds capacity for a known date (quota is permission, a
  commitment is a discount, neither is capacity). **Dynamic Workload Scheduler flex-start** obtains a set of GPUs
  together when capacity appears, without pre-emption during the run. A regional MIG's **target distribution shape
  `ANY`** places VMs wherever a zone has capacity. Spot VMs with **`--instance-termination-action=STOP`** keep
  their disks for a later restart.
- **Disks and security.** **Hyperdisk Balanced High Availability** is the synchronous two-zone disk for
  Hyperdisk-only machine series. **Hyperdisk Storage Pools** pool capacity and performance across many disks.
  **Confidential VM** encrypts memory in use. **OS policy assignments** in VM Manager enforce desired state
  (packages, files) continuously.

5.10.text:

6.1.title: GKE architecture and cluster modes
6.1.text:
A GKE cluster is a **Google-managed control plane** (API server, scheduler, etcd) plus **nodes** — Compute Engine
VMs running your Pods. The two modes differ in who owns those nodes.

| | **Autopilot** | **Standard** |
|:------------------------------|:------------------------------------------------|:------------------------------------------------|
| Nodes | **Google** provisions, scales, upgrades, repairs and secures them | **You** configure node pools (with automation you enable) |
| You pay for | **Pod resource requests** (CPU, memory, storage) | **Nodes**, whether Pods fill them or not |
| Topology | Always **regional** | Zonal, multi-zonal or regional |
| Node access, privileged Pods, custom node config | Restricted | Allowed |
| Best-practice defaults (Workload Identity, Shielded nodes, auto-upgrade) | **On and enforced** | Available, you choose |
| Right when | *"We do not want to manage nodes"* | Node-level control, special hardware set-ups, DaemonSets that need host access |

> **"Do not want to manage nodes" is Autopilot — not Standard with node auto-provisioning and autoscaling.**
> Automation on a Standard cluster changes how much work the nodes are, not who owns them or how you are billed.

### Cluster topology and access

| Choice | Meaning |
|:----------------------------------|:------------------------------------------------------------------|
| **Zonal** | One control-plane replica in one zone — a zone outage takes the control plane |
| **Regional** | Control plane replicated across **three zones**; nodes spread across them. `--num-nodes` is **per zone**, so `--num-nodes=2` creates **six** nodes |
| **Private nodes** | Nodes have **internal IPs only** (`--enable-private-nodes`); they need **Cloud NAT** to pull images from the internet, and Private Google Access for Artifact Registry |
| **Control-plane endpoint** | Public endpoint limited by **authorized networks**, a private endpoint only (`--enable-private-endpoint`), or the **DNS-based endpoint** secured by IAM |
| **VPC-native** | Pods and Services take IPs from subnet **secondary ranges** (alias IPs) — the default |
| **Release channel** | Rapid · **Regular** (default) · Stable · Extended; with maintenance windows and exclusions. An exclusion's scope is *no upgrades*, *no minor upgrades* or *no minor or node upgrades* (control-plane patches still allowed); channel clusters can't turn off node auto-upgrade |

| Task | Command |
|:------------------------------------|:----------------------------------------------------------------------|
| Autopilot cluster | `gcloud container clusters create-auto shop --location=R` |
| Standard regional cluster — `--num-nodes` is per zone | `gcloud container clusters create batch --location=R --num-nodes=1 --release-channel=regular` |
| Private nodes, control plane limited to a range | `... --enable-private-nodes --enable-master-authorized-networks --master-authorized-networks=203.0.113.0/24` |

6.2.title: kubectl and cluster access
6.2.text:
`gcloud` manages the **cluster** (create, resize, upgrade, delete, node pools); **`kubectl` manages what runs in it**
(Deployments, Services, Pods). `get-credentials` is the bridge: it writes a kubeconfig entry.

| Task | Command |
|:------------------------------------|:----------------------------------------------------------------------|
| kubectl and its auth plugin | `gcloud components install kubectl gke-gcloud-auth-plugin` |
| Point kubectl at a cluster | `gcloud container clusters get-credentials shop --location=R` |

**kubectl authenticates with the `gke-gcloud-auth-plugin`**, which uses your gcloud credentials — a missing plugin
is the modern *"kubectl cannot authenticate"* error. Cloud Shell has both pre-installed.

**Authorisation is two layers.** **IAM** grants cluster-wide Kubernetes rights at the project
(`roles/container.viewer`, `container.developer`, `container.admin`). **Kubernetes RBAC** (Roles and RoleBindings)
grants rights **per namespace**, and can bind Google Groups. *"Team A may deploy only in namespace `team-a`"* is
RBAC.

### Viewing cluster inventory

| Task | Command |
|:------------------------------------|:----------------------------------------------------------------------|
| What runs, and where | `kubectl get pods -o wide` · `kubectl get deployments,services -n shop` |
| Why a Pod is not running (events) | `kubectl describe pod POD` |
| Logs of the crashed container | `kubectl logs POD --previous` |
| Live CPU and memory | `kubectl top pods` |
| The cluster's node pools | `gcloud container node-pools list --cluster=shop --location=R` |

6.3.title: Workloads
6.3.text:
| Object | For |
|:------------------------------|:------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| **Pod** | One or more containers sharing a network namespace; the smallest unit |
| **Deployment** | **Stateless** replicas, rolling updates, rollback. **The default** |
| **StatefulSet** | **Stable names** (`db-0`, `db-1`), **per-Pod persistent volumes** (`volumeClaimTemplates`), ordered start-up — databases, queues |
| **DaemonSet** | **One Pod per node** — log shippers, node agents |
| **Job / CronJob** | Run to completion, once or on a schedule |
| **ConfigMap / Secret** | Configuration injected as env vars or files (a Secret is only base64 unless encrypted) |
| **PersistentVolumeClaim** | A request for storage, provisioned by a **StorageClass** (`standard-rwo` = balanced PD; Filestore for ReadWriteMany) |

| Task | Command |
|:------------------------------------|:----------------------------------------------------------------------|
| Create and expose imperatively | `kubectl create deployment web --image=IMG` · `kubectl expose deployment web --port=80 --target-port=8080` |
| Apply manifests (the normal way) | `kubectl apply -f k8s/` |
| New image, watch it, roll it back | `kubectl set image deployment/web web=IMG:1.5` · `kubectl rollout status deployment/web` · `kubectl rollout undo deployment/web` |
| Scale by hand | `kubectl scale deployment web --replicas=6` |

> *"Each replica needs its own disk and a stable hostname"* — **StatefulSet**. *"Run exactly one collector on every
> node, including new ones"* — **DaemonSet**. *"Nightly clean-up at 02:00"* — **CronJob**.

6.4.title: Exposing workloads and splitting traffic
6.4.text:
| Object | Gives you | Load balancer |
|:------------------------------|:----------------------------------------------------------|:------------------------------------------|
| Service **ClusterIP** (default) | A stable internal virtual IP inside the cluster | None |
| Service **NodePort** | A port on every node's IP | None |
| Service **LoadBalancer** | An IP for **one** Service | An external **passthrough Network LB** — or an internal one with the annotation `networking.gke.io/load-balancer-type: "Internal"` |
| **Ingress** | **One** HTTP(S) entry point with **host and path rules** to many Services | An **Application LB** (external; `gce-internal` class for internal) |
| **Gateway API** (Gateway + HTTPRoute) | Ingress's successor: role separation, header matching, **weighted traffic splitting** | An Application LB chosen by GatewayClass |

GKE uses **container-native load balancing** — the LB targets Pod IPs directly through NEGs — which removes a hop
and makes health checks per Pod.

> **Path or host routing, or one IP for many Services, means Ingress or Gateway.** A `LoadBalancer` Service is one IP
> for one Service at layer 4 — three apps behind *"one external IP routed by URL path"* is one Ingress, not three
> LoadBalancer Services.

### Traffic splitting on GKE

> New in the June 2026 guide — traffic splitting now includes GKE
>
> Cloud Run and Cloud Run functions split traffic between **revisions** natively ([§6.10](https://nirmata78.github.io/gcp-ace-simulator/theory/06-containers-serverless.html#s6-10)). On GKE, the native
> mechanism is the **Gateway API**: an `HTTPRoute` whose `backendRefs` carry **weights** sends, say, 90% to the
> Service in front of v1 and 10% to the Service in front of v2. The older approximation — two Deployments behind
> one Service, split by replica counts — is coarse and ties the split to capacity.

6.5.title: Scaling Pods and nodes; Autopilot resource requests
6.5.text:
| Layer | Mechanism | Scales |
|:----------------------|:------------------------------------------|:------------------------------------------------------|
| Pods, horizontally | **HorizontalPodAutoscaler** | Replica count on CPU, memory, custom or external metrics |
| Pods, vertically | **VerticalPodAutoscaler** | Each Pod's **requests** — recommend only, or apply by recreating Pods |
| Nodes (Standard) | **Cluster autoscaler** per node pool; **node auto-provisioning** creates pools | Node count to fit pending Pods |
| Nodes (Autopilot) | Automatic | Whatever the Pods request |

| Task | Command |
|:------------------------------------|:----------------------------------------------------------------------|
| Horizontal Pod Autoscaler | `kubectl autoscale deployment web --cpu-percent=60 --min=3 --max=30` |
| Vertical Pod Autoscaling (Standard) | `gcloud container clusters update batch --location=R --enable-vertical-pod-autoscaling` |
| Cluster autoscaler on a node pool | `gcloud container node-pools update default-pool --cluster=batch --location=R --enable-autoscaling --min-nodes=1 --max-nodes=10` |

> **HPA versus VPA.** HPA adds Pods; VPA resizes them. Do not let both act on the **same CPU or memory metric** for
> one workload — they fight. A common pattern is HPA on a custom metric (requests per second) with VPA managing
> requests, or VPA in *recommendation* mode only.

> New in the June 2026 guide — managing Autopilot Pod resource requests
>
> **In Autopilot, resource requests are the bill and the scheduling input**, so the platform enforces them:
>
> - A container with **no requests** gets **defaults** applied (for the general-purpose compute class, on the order
>   of 0.5 vCPU and 2 GiB — *verify*).
> - Requests below the **minimums**, or with a **CPU-to-memory ratio** outside the allowed range, are **adjusted
>   upward** automatically; values are rounded to allowed increments. `kubectl get pod -o yaml` shows the result, and
>   a warning explains the change.
> - **Limits** equal requests unless the cluster supports **Pod bursting** (recent versions, cgroup v2): then a
>   **limit above the request** lets the Pod use spare node capacity while you pay only for the request.
> - **Hardware per workload, not per pool**: Arm with `nodeSelector: kubernetes.io/arch: arm64` (an arm64 image; older
>   versions also name an Arm compute class); a machine family with the **Performance** class plus
>   `cloud.google.com/machine-family: c3`. Autopilot has no node pools to create.
> - **Compute classes** select hardware: the default general-purpose class, **Balanced**, **Scale-Out**,
>   **Performance**, **Accelerator** — requested with a `nodeSelector` of `cloud.google.com/compute-class`; Spot Pods
>   with `cloud.google.com/gke-spot: "true"`.
>
> *"Autopilot Pods cost more than expected"* — look for missing or oversized requests, and use VPA
> recommendations to right-size them. *"A Pod was scheduled with more memory than we asked for"* — ratio or
> minimum enforcement.

6.6.title: Node pools and upgrades (Standard)
6.6.text:
A **node pool** is a group of identically configured nodes — a managed instance group under the hood.

| Task | How |
|:------------------------------------------|:----------------------------------------------------------------|
| Add capacity of a **new kind** (GPUs, high memory, Spot, Arm) | `gcloud container node-pools create` with the new machine type and labels / taints |
| Change machine type of existing nodes | `gcloud container node-pools update --machine-type` recreates the nodes with the pool's upgrade strategy (*verify*). To test first and keep a fallback, **create a new pool**, cordon and drain the old one, delete it later |
| Resize | `gcloud container clusters resize CLUSTER --node-pool=POOL --num-nodes=N` |
| Autoscale | `--enable-autoscaling --min-nodes --max-nodes` (per zone), or `--total-min-nodes` / `--total-max-nodes` |
| Keep workloads on the right pool | **Node labels + `nodeSelector` / affinity**; **taints + tolerations** to keep everything else off |
| Remove | `gcloud container node-pools delete` (Pods are rescheduled elsewhere) |
| Upgrades | **Surge** upgrades (`max-surge`, `max-unavailable`) or **blue-green** upgrades per pool |

6.7.title: Artifact Registry and image access
6.7.text:
**Artifact Registry** stores container images and language packages (Maven, npm, Python, Go, apt, yum, Helm charts
as OCI). **Container Registry is shut down** — `gcr.io` paths are now served by Artifact Registry. Repositories are
**regional or multi-regional** and addressed as `LOCATION-docker.pkg.dev/PROJECT/REPO/IMAGE:TAG`.

| Mode | Is |
|:----------------|:----------------------------------------------------------------------|
| **Standard** | Your own artefacts |
| **Remote** | A caching proxy of an upstream (Docker Hub, Maven Central, PyPI) — builds survive upstream rate limits and outages |
| **Virtual** | One endpoint aggregating several repositories |

**Cleanup policies** delete old versions automatically; **Artifact Analysis** scans images for vulnerabilities.

| Role | Grants |
|:--------------------------------------|:----------------------------------------------------|
| `roles/artifactregistry.reader` | Pull |
| `roles/artifactregistry.writer` | Push and pull |
| `roles/artifactregistry.repoAdmin` / `admin` | Manage repositories and artefacts |

| Task | Command |
|:------------------------------------|:----------------------------------------------------------------------|
| Docker repository | `gcloud artifacts repositories create shop --repository-format=docker --location=R` |
| Let the local Docker CLI push to it | `gcloud auth configure-docker R-docker.pkg.dev` |

### Configuring GKE to pull from Artifact Registry

**Nodes pull images as the node pool's service account.** No `imagePullSecrets` are needed; what is needed is
**`roles/artifactregistry.reader` for that service account** on the repository (or its project).

- **Same project, default Compute Engine service account with Editor** — it just works (and is too broad).
- **Recommended: a minimal custom node service account** (`roles/container.defaultNodeServiceAccount`) — then you
  **must grant it `artifactregistry.reader`** explicitly.
- **Repository in another project** — grant the node service account reader **on that repository**.
- **Private nodes** reach Artifact Registry through **Private Google Access**; pulling from Docker Hub needs Cloud
  NAT, or a **remote repository**.

> *"Pods are stuck in `ImagePullBackOff` with 403 from `pkg.dev`"* is the node service account lacking
> `artifactregistry.reader` — not a missing `docker login`, not a public repository, and not a service-account key
> in an `imagePullSecret`.

6.8.title: Workload Identity Federation for GKE
6.8.text:
> New in the June 2026 guide — a Google Cloud service account with a GKE application
>
> **Pods authenticate to Google APIs as a Kubernetes service account (KSA) that IAM recognises**, so no key is mounted
> and Pods do not borrow the node's identity. It is enabled by default on Autopilot; on Standard, enable a
> **workload pool** on the cluster and the **GKE metadata server** on node pools.

**Two ways to grant access, both keyless:**

| Step | What you configure |
|:------------------------------------|:----------------------------------------------------------------------|
| Enable it (Standard; on by default in Autopilot) | `gcloud container clusters update batch --location=R --workload-pool=P.svc.id.goog` |
| (a) Grant IAM straight to the Kubernetes service account | member `principal://iam.googleapis.com/projects/NUM/locations/global/workloadIdentityPools/P.svc.id.goog/subject/ns/shop/sa/web` |
| (b) Let it impersonate a Google service account | `roles/iam.workloadIdentityUser` on the Google SA for member `serviceAccount:P.svc.id.goog[shop/web]`, then annotate the KSA with `iam.gke.io/gcp-service-account=GSA_EMAIL` |

The Pod spec names `serviceAccountName: web`. Client libraries then find credentials through ADC with no change.

> **Node service account versus workload identity.** The **node** service account is for the node's own jobs —
> pulling images, writing logs and metrics. **Application** access to Cloud Storage, Pub/Sub or BigQuery belongs to
> the **Pod's** identity through Workload Identity Federation for GKE. Granting app roles to the node account gives
> them to every Pod on the node.

One limitation is worth knowing: **Pods that use the host network (`hostNetwork: true`) cannot use Workload Identity
Federation for GKE** — they reach the node's metadata server and act as the node's service account.

6.9.title: Cloud Run services and jobs
6.9.text:
**Cloud Run runs containers without servers or clusters**, billed per use, scaling automatically — to zero when
idle.

| Resource | Is |
|:----------------------|:----------------------------------------------------------------------|
| **Service** | Serves **requests** (HTTP, gRPC, WebSockets) at a stable HTTPS URL; scales on load |
| **Job** | Runs **tasks to completion** — in parallel, with retries — on demand or on a schedule via Cloud Scheduler |
| **Worker pool** | Always-on, non-request workloads such as queue consumers (*recognise*) |
| **Revision** | An **immutable** snapshot of a service's code and configuration, created by every deploy |

### Deploying

| Route | Steps | When |
|:--------------------------|:------------------------------|:----------------------------|
| **`gcloud run deploy SVC --source .`** | **One**: Cloud Build builds (Dockerfile or buildpacks), stores in Artifact Registry, deploys | *"Fewest steps from source to a URL"* |
| `gcloud run deploy SVC --image=IMAGE` | One | The image already exists |
| `docker build` + `push` + `deploy` | Three, plus a local Docker daemon | You need control of the build |
| Cloud Build trigger / Cloud Deploy pipeline | A pipeline | **Continuous** delivery on every commit |

| Task | Command |
|:------------------------------------|:----------------------------------------------------------------------|
| Deploy from source, private, as its own identity | `gcloud run deploy api --source . --region=R --no-allow-unauthenticated --service-account=SA_EMAIL` |
| Run-to-completion job | `gcloud run jobs create nightly-export --image=IMG --tasks=20 --max-retries=3` · `gcloud run jobs execute nightly-export` |

### Access and networking

| Setting | Options |
|:----------------------------------|:------------------------------------------------------------------|
| **Authentication** | *Require authentication* — callers need **`roles/run.invoker`** and send an **ID token**; or *allow unauthenticated* (`allUsers` invoker) for public sites |
| **Ingress** | `all` · `internal` (VPC and some Google sources only) · `internal-and-cloud-load-balancing` |
| **Egress to a VPC** | **Direct VPC egress** (recommended) or a Serverless VPC Access connector — for private IPs such as Cloud SQL or Memorystore |
| **Static outbound IP** | Route all egress through the VPC and **Cloud NAT** with a static address |
| **Custom domain / CDN / WAF** | A **global external Application LB with a serverless NEG** — then Cloud CDN, Cloud Armor, IAP (enable IAP on the backend service and grant users **IAP-secured Web App User**, `roles/iap.httpsResourceAccessor`; the same works for MIG backends) |
| **Identity** | A **dedicated service account** per service, never the default Compute account |
| **Secrets** | `--set-secrets=DB_PASS=db-password:latest` (env) or `/secrets/db=db-password:latest` (volume) ([§3.13](https://nirmata78.github.io/gcp-ace-simulator/theory/03-identity-access.html#s3-13)). An env var is resolved when the instance **starts**; a volume is read from Secret Manager **each time the file is read**, so it picks up rotation without a deploy. The runtime service account needs **Secret Accessor** on the secret |

> *"Service A must call private service B"* — grant **B's `run.invoker` to A's service account**; A attaches an ID
> token for B's URL. Making B public and checking a header is the distractor.

6.10.title: Cloud Run revisions, traffic and scaling
6.10.text:
**Every deploy creates a revision, and by default sends it 100% of traffic immediately.** A gradual rollout is a
deliberate two-step:

| Task | Command |
|:------------------------------------|:----------------------------------------------------------------------|
| 1. Deploy at 0%, reachable on its own tag URL | `gcloud run deploy api --image=IMG:v2 --no-traffic --tag=canary` |
| 2. Send it 10% | `gcloud run services update-traffic api --to-tags=canary=10` |
| Promote; roll back | `gcloud run services update-traffic api --to-latest` · `... --to-revisions=api-00041-xyz=100` |

> **Revisions are immutable and stay addressable**, so a canary is a traffic percentage and a rollback is one
> command that points traffic back — no rebuild, no DNS change. DNS weighting against a native split is always the
> wrong answer: it is cached, coarse and slow to reverse.

### Autoscaling settings

| Setting | Meaning | Default |
|:----------------------------------|:------------------------------------------------------------------|:------------|
| **Minimum instances** | Kept warm to avoid **cold starts**; above 0, the service no longer idles to zero cost | 0 |
| **Maximum instances** | Ceiling — protects a database from connection storms and caps cost | 100 (*verify*) |
| **Concurrency** | Requests handled **at once by one instance** | 80 (max 1000) |
| **Billing / CPU allocation** | **Request-based** (CPU only while handling requests) or **instance-based** (CPU always, for background work) | Request-based |
| Startup CPU boost | Extra CPU during start-up | Off |
| Request timeout | Per request | 5 min (up to 60) |

| Task | Command |
|:------------------------------------|:----------------------------------------------------------------------|
| Warm instances, a cap, requests per instance | `gcloud run services update api --min-instances=2 --max-instances=40 --concurrency=50` |
| CPU outside requests (instance-based billing) | `gcloud run services update worker --no-cpu-throttling` |

> *"First request after idle is slow"* — **minimum instances** (or startup CPU boost). *"The database runs out of
> connections at peak"* — **maximum instances** and/or lower **concurrency**. *"A single-threaded app misbehaves
> under load"* — **concurrency 1**. *"Work continues after the response is sent"* — **instance-based billing**.

6.11.title: Cloud Run functions and events
6.11.text:
**Cloud Run functions** (formerly Cloud Functions) are functions deployed **as Cloud Run services** — you write a
handler; Google builds and runs the container. So revisions, traffic splitting, scaling, concurrency, VPC egress
and IAM work exactly as in [§6.9](https://nirmata78.github.io/gcp-ace-simulator/theory/06-containers-serverless.html#s6-9)–[§6.10](https://nirmata78.github.io/gcp-ace-simulator/theory/06-containers-serverless.html#s6-10).

| Task | Command |
|:------------------------------------|:----------------------------------------------------------------------|
| Fire on every upload to a bucket | `gcloud functions deploy thumb --gen2 --runtime=python312 --trigger-event-filters="type=google.cloud.storage.object.v1.finalized" --trigger-event-filters="bucket=lumen-uploads"` |
| Fire on a Pub/Sub message; on HTTP | `--trigger-topic=orders` · `--trigger-http` |

### Where events come from

| Source | Mechanism | Notes |
|:------------------------------------------|:----------------------------------------|:------------------------------------------------|
| **HTTP** | Direct request | Authenticated with an ID token unless public |
| **Pub/Sub message** | Eventarc creates a **push subscription** | At-least-once; make handlers idempotent |
| **Cloud Storage** object *finalized*, *deleted*, *archived*, *metadataUpdated* | Eventarc, via Pub/Sub under the hood | The trigger must be in the **bucket's region**; the **Cloud Storage service agent needs `roles/pubsub.publisher`** |
| **Eventarc direct events** from Google services | Eventarc trigger | Filtered by event type and attributes |
| **Cloud Audit Log events** — *"when anyone creates a VM"* | Eventarc on an audit log entry | Needs the relevant audit log type **enabled** (Data Access for reads) |
| Third-party / custom | Eventarc channels, Eventarc Advanced buses | *Recognise* |

**Eventarc** routes events from sources to targets — Cloud Run services, functions, GKE services, Workflows. A
trigger has **filters**, a **destination**, and a **service account** that needs `roles/eventarc.eventReceiver`
and `roles/run.invoker` on the target.


> **"The function never fires on uploads."** Check, in order: the trigger's region matches the bucket's; the Cloud
> Storage **service agent** has `pubsub.publisher`; the trigger service account can invoke the function; the event
> type is `finalized`, not `metadataUpdated`. Polling the bucket from a VM is the assembled distractor.

**Deploying from Cloud Run.** A function can also be deployed with the Cloud Run command itself —
`gcloud run deploy thumb --source . --function=make_thumbnail --base-image=python312 --region=R` — which makes
the "a function *is* a Cloud Run service" point concrete.

**Retries.** Event-driven functions may enable **retry on failure** — useful for transient errors, dangerous
without idempotency, because a permanent bug then retries until the event expires.

6.12.title: App Engine, Cloud Build and delivery
6.12.text:
### App Engine — recognise it

App Engine is the original serverless platform. **One App Engine application per project, and its region can
never change.** **Standard** environment: sandboxed runtimes, scales to zero, fast start. **Flexible**: containers on
VMs, **minimum one instance**, no scale-to-zero. Services have **versions**; traffic splits between versions by
percentage, and `gcloud app deploy --no-promote` deploys without moving traffic.

| Task | Command |
|:------------------------------------|:----------------------------------------------------------------------|
| Deploy without moving traffic | `gcloud app deploy --no-promote --version=v7` |
| Split traffic 90/10 | `gcloud app services set-traffic default --splits=v6=0.9,v7=0.1` |

Where App Engine appears on the current exam it is mostly a distractor for *"scale to zero"* (flexible cannot) or
*"a new region"* (the region is permanent).

### Cloud Build and Cloud Deploy

**Cloud Build** runs a `cloudbuild.yaml` of container **steps** — build, test, push, deploy — on **triggers**
(push to a branch, tag, pull request) or on demand. It runs as a **service account**; best practice is a
**user-specified** service account with only the roles the pipeline needs (for example `run.developer` plus
`iam.serviceAccountUser` on the runtime account). **Cloud Deploy** adds managed release pipelines to GKE and Cloud
Run, with promotion between targets, approvals and **canary** strategies.

| Task | Command |
|:------------------------------------|:----------------------------------------------------------------------|
| Build and push an image without local Docker | `gcloud builds submit --tag=R-docker.pkg.dev/P/shop/web:1.6 .` |

### More to recognise

- **Operating GKE.** Enrol production in the **Stable** release channel. The control plane's **DNS-based
  endpoint** is authorised by IAM, so no bastion or IP allow-list is needed. A **PodDisruptionBudget** limits
  evictions during drains. **Blue-green node pool upgrades** keep old nodes for a soak period. Environment
  variables from a ConfigMap change only after **`kubectl rollout restart`**. `kubectl get pods -A
  –field-selector=status.phase=Pending` lists every Pending Pod. An HPA on the external metric
  **`num_undelivered_messages`** scales Pub/Sub consumers. HPA utilisation is usage divided by **request**, so
  oversized requests delay scaling.
- **Sharing accelerators.** **GPU time-sharing** gives several Pods turns on one GPU; **multi-instance GPUs**
  partition an A100/H100 into isolated slices with their own memory.
- **Images and serverless.** An Artifact Registry **remote repository** caches Docker Hub and avoids its rate
  limits. Cloud Run **maximum instances** protects a database's connection limit. **Direct VPC egress** reaches
  private IPs without connector instances. Cloud Run functions react to **Firestore document events** through
  Eventarc. Choose the **snapshot storage location** explicitly when residency requires a region.

6.13.title: Part 6 recall card
6.13.text:
| Prompt | Answer |
|:------------------------------------------------|:--------------------------------------------------------|
| No node management | **Autopilot** (always regional) |
| Regional Standard, `--num-nodes=2` | **Six** nodes (per zone × 3) |
| Nodes with internal IPs only | `--enable-private-nodes` (+ Cloud NAT for internet pulls) |

| One Pod on every node | **DaemonSet** |
| One IP, path routing to many Services | **Ingress** or **Gateway** |
| 10% to v2 on GKE | **Gateway API HTTPRoute weights** |
| More replicas on load | **HPA**; right-size requests: **VPA** |
| Autopilot Pod got more memory than requested | **Minimum / ratio enforcement** on requests |
| Change node machine type | `node-pools update --machine-type` recreates nodes (upgrade strategy); to keep a fallback, **new node pool**, drain old |
| `ImagePullBackOff` 403 from `pkg.dev` | Node SA needs **`artifactregistry.reader`** |
| Pod reads a bucket, no key | **Workload Identity Federation for GKE** |
| Source to URL, one command | `gcloud run deploy --source .` |
| Canary 10% on Cloud Run | `--no-traffic --tag`, then `update-traffic --to-tags=tag=10` |
| Cold starts | **Min instances** |
| DB connection storms | **Max instances** / lower concurrency |
| Service A calls private service B | A's SA gets **`run.invoker`** on B; ID token |
| Custom domain + Cloud Armor for Cloud Run | Global external ALB + **serverless NEG** |
