| React to "VM created" anywhere | **Eventarc** audit-log trigger |

7.1.title: Choosing a storage product
7.1.text:
Start with the **access model** the application needs; the product follows.

| Access model | Product | Pick it when the stem says |
|:----------------------|:------------------------------------|:--------------------------------------------------------|
| **Objects** over HTTP(S), any size, any number | **Cloud Storage** | "files", "images", "backups", "data lake", "static website", "archive" |
| **Block** device for one VM (or read-many) | **Persistent Disk / Hyperdisk** ([§5.4](https://nirmata78.github.io/gcp-ace-simulator/theory/05-compute-engine.html#s5-4)) | "boot disk", "database on a VM" |
| **Shared POSIX file system (NFS)** for many VMs or Pods | **Filestore** | "shared file system", "lift-and-shift app that expects NFS", "ReadWriteMany in GKE" |
| **Enterprise NAS: NFS and SMB**, Windows shares, NetApp features | **Google Cloud NetApp Volumes** | "SMB", "Windows file shares", "migrate our NetApp ONTAP", snapshots and cross-region replication of volumes |
| **Parallel file system** with very high throughput for thousands of clients | **Google Cloud Managed Lustre** | "AI training data loading", "HPC scratch", "checkpoints from thousands of GPUs" |
| Ephemeral, ultra-fast local scratch | **Local SSD** | "temporary", "cache", "scratch" |

> New in the June 2026 guide — the file-storage family
>
> **Filestore** is managed NFS in tiers from basic HDD to **zonal**, **regional** (survives a zone) and enterprise
> instances. **NetApp Volumes** is NetApp's storage run by Google — NFSv3/v4.1 **and SMB**, with Active Directory
> integration, volume snapshots, backups and replication — the answer whenever **Windows/SMB** or **NetApp** appears.
> **Managed Lustre** is a fully managed **parallel** file system for AI/ML and HPC, where aggregate throughput to
> many clients matters more than anything else. None of them is object storage, and none is the answer to "cheap
> archive".

7.2.title: Cloud Storage: buckets, locations, classes
7.2.text:
| Concept | Fact |
|:----------------------|:----------------------------------------------------------------------|
| **Bucket names** | **Globally unique**, immutable; a bucket's **location** is also fixed at creation |
| **Objects** | Immutable: a change writes a new object (or a new *generation*); no partial updates |
| Consistency | **Strong** read-after-write and list consistency |
| **Location type** | **Region** · **dual-region** (two regions — a predefined pair, or a **configurable** pair you choose within one continent, e.g. `--location=EU --placement=europe-west3,europe-central2`; optional **turbo replication** — replicated within 15 minutes) · **multi-region** (`US`, `EU`, `ASIA`) |
| Storage class | A bucket **default**, overridable **per object** |

### The four classes

| Class | Designed for | **Minimum storage duration** | Storage price | Retrieval fee |
|:----------------|:------------------------------|:--------------|:----------|:----------|
| **Standard** | Frequently accessed, "hot" | **None** | Highest | None |
| **Nearline** | About **once a month** | **30 days** | Lower | Low |
| **Coldline** | About **once a quarter** | **90 days** | Lower still | Higher |
| **Archive** | **Once a year or less** | **365 days** | **Lowest** | Highest |

**Memorise 0 / 30 / 90 / 365.** Deleting, overwriting or moving an object before its minimum is billed as if it
had stayed the full minimum (the **early-deletion charge**).

> **All four classes have the same millisecond latency to the first byte.** There is no thaw, no restore step, no
> waiting — that is a different cloud's archive model. Classes differ only in **storage price, retrieval price,
> minimum duration** (and availability SLA). A stem that says *"read once a year but must be available immediately
> when requested"* is still **Archive**; the "immediately" clause decides nothing.

**Autoclass** moves each object between classes automatically based on its access pattern, with no retrieval or
early-deletion charges — the answer to *"access patterns are unknown or change"*. It replaces lifecycle class
transitions on that bucket.

| Task | Command |
|:------------------------------------|:----------------------------------------------------------------------|
| Bucket with a location and default class | `gcloud storage buckets create gs://kestrel-archive --location=EU --default-storage-class=ARCHIVE --uniform-bucket-level-access` |
| Let Autoclass choose the class | `gcloud storage buckets create gs://kestrel-media --location=EUR4 --enable-autoclass` |
| Copy; mirror a directory | `gcloud storage cp -r ./exports gs://kestrel-archive/2026/` · `gcloud storage rsync ./site gs://kestrel-web --recursive` |
| Change one object's class | `gcloud storage objects update gs://B/big.mov --storage-class=COLDLINE` |

7.3.title: Lifecycle, versioning, soft delete and retention
7.3.text:
| Feature | Does | Typical stem |
|:------------------------------|:------------------------------------------------------------|:------------------------------------------|
| **Lifecycle rules** | **Delete** objects, or **SetStorageClass** to a colder class, by age, date, number of newer versions, current class, prefix... | "Nearline after 30 days, delete after a year" |
| **Object versioning** | Keeps **noncurrent versions** when an object is overwritten or deleted | "recover a file someone overwrote" |
| **Soft delete** | Keeps **deleted** objects restorable for a window — **7 days by default** on new buckets, configurable (up to 90) | "undo an accidental delete from yesterday" |
| **Retention policy** | Objects **cannot be deleted or overwritten** until they reach the retention age | "keep every record for 7 years" |
| **Bucket Lock** | **Locks** the retention policy **permanently** — it can be lengthened, never shortened or removed | "WORM", "regulator requires immutability, even from admins" |
| **Object holds** / **object retention lock** | Per-object holds (temporary or event-based) and per-object retention settings | "legal hold on these files" |

| Task | Command |
|:------------------------------------|:----------------------------------------------------------------------|
| Lifecycle rules (a JSON file of `SetStorageClass` / `Delete` actions on conditions such as `age`, `isLive`, `numNewerVersions`) | `gcloud storage buckets update gs://B --lifecycle-file=lifecycle.json` |
| Versioning; soft-delete window | `gcloud storage buckets update gs://B --versioning` · `... --soft-delete-duration=30d` |
| Retention policy, then lock it (irreversible) | `... --retention-period=7y` · `... --lock-retention-period` |
| Hold one object | `gcloud storage objects update gs://B/contract.pdf --temporary-hold` |


> **Versioning, soft delete and a locked retention policy protect against different things.** Versioning and soft
> delete protect against **accidents** — someone with permission can still remove versions. A **locked retention
> policy** protects against **intent**: nobody, including an Owner, can delete the object early, and nobody can
> unlock the policy. Lifecycle rules only move objects to **colder** classes; they never warm them up, and changes
> can take up to 24 hours to act.
>
> **Lifecycle on a versioned bucket.** `Delete` on a live object makes it noncurrent, and its `age` still counts from
> creation. A plain `age` rule therefore deletes the noncurrent version too, on a later run. With `isLive: true` the rule
> never matches noncurrent versions, so they stay and stay billed until another rule removes them, such as
> `daysSinceNoncurrentTime`. `numNewerVersions` never matches the newest noncurrent version once the live one is gone.

7.4.title: Securing objects
7.4.text:
| Mechanism | Use |
|:------------------------------------------|:------------------------------------------------------------------|
| **Uniform bucket-level access** | **IAM only**, no object ACLs — the recommended setting. Reversible for 90 days, then permanent |
| Fine-grained access | IAM plus per-object **ACLs** — legacy needs only |
| **Public access prevention** | Blocks `allUsers` / `allAuthenticatedUsers` on the bucket (also enforceable by org policy) |
| **Signed URL** | **Time-limited** access to one object for someone **with no Google identity** — download or upload; V4 URLs last at most 7 days |
| Signed policy document | Browser **form uploads** with constraints (size, type) |
| HMAC keys | S3-compatible access for tools that speak the S3 API |
| CMEK default key | Customer-managed encryption for the bucket ([§7.14](https://nirmata78.github.io/gcp-ace-simulator/theory/07-storage-data.html#s7-14)) |

| Role | Grants |
|:--------------------------------------|:----------------------------------------------------------|
| `roles/storage.objectViewer` | Read and list objects |
| `roles/storage.objectCreator` | Create objects — **not** read, overwrite or delete them |
| `roles/storage.objectUser` | Read, create, update, delete objects |
| `roles/storage.objectAdmin` | Full control of **objects**, not bucket settings |
| `roles/storage.admin` | Full control of buckets **and** objects |

| Task | Command |
|:------------------------------------|:----------------------------------------------------------------------|
| Read access to one bucket | `gcloud storage buckets add-iam-policy-binding gs://B --member=group:analysts@example.com --role=roles/storage.objectViewer` |
| Time-limited link, no key file | `gcloud storage sign-url gs://B/report.pdf --duration=2h --impersonate-service-account=SA_EMAIL` |

> *"A partner with no Google account must download one file this week"* — **signed URL**. *"A drop box where
> uploaders must not read each other's files"* — **`objectCreator`**. *"Manage objects but never change the
> bucket's settings"* — **`objectAdmin`**, not `admin`.

7.5.title: Estimating storage cost
7.5.text:
| Product | You pay for | Levers |
|:----------------------|:------------------------------------------------------------|:------------------------------------------------|
| **Cloud Storage** | GB-months by class and location · **operations** (Class A writes/lists cost more than Class B reads) · **retrieval** (Nearline and colder) · early deletion · network egress and inter-region replication | Class, lifecycle, Autoclass, location |
| **Persistent Disk / Hyperdisk** | **Provisioned** size (not used size); Hyperdisk also provisioned IOPS and throughput; snapshots by stored data | Right-size; delete unattached disks |
| **Cloud SQL / AlloyDB** | Instance vCPU and memory · storage · **HA roughly doubles** the instance · backups beyond the free allowance | Size, HA only where needed, committed use |
| **BigQuery** | **Storage** (active vs **long-term** after 90 days unmodified at about half price; logical or physical billing) · **compute**: on-demand **per TiB scanned** or capacity **slots** (editions) | Partition, cluster, select only needed columns |
| **Spanner / Bigtable** | Compute capacity (nodes / processing units) · storage · replication | Autoscaling |

**Tools:** the **Pricing Calculator** before building; a BigQuery **dry run** before querying; **billing export**
after; **Storage Insights** and Active Assist recommendations to find waste.
To put a hard limit on BigQuery on-demand spend, set **custom quotas** on query usage per day, per project or per user:
once reached, further queries fail until the next day. A budget only alerts.

| Task | Command |
|:------------------------------------|:----------------------------------------------------------------------|
| Bytes a query would scan, free | `bq query --use_legacy_sql=false --dry_run 'SELECT ...'` |
| Hard cap on one query's cost | `bq query --maximum_bytes_billed=10000000000 'SELECT ...'` |

> **`LIMIT` does not reduce BigQuery on-demand cost** — the bytes scanned are the columns read across the
> partitions touched. Selecting fewer columns, filtering on the **partition** column, and **clustering** are what
> reduce it. `--maximum_bytes_billed` makes an expensive query **fail** instead of running.

7.6.title: Choosing a database
7.6.text:
| Product | Model | Scale and consistency | Pick it when the stem says |
|:----------------|:----------------------------------|:----------------------------------|:------------------------------------------|
| **Cloud SQL** | Managed MySQL, PostgreSQL, SQL Server | **One primary for writes**; read replicas | "managed relational", "migrate our MySQL/Postgres/SQL Server", "regional is fine" |
| **AlloyDB** | **PostgreSQL-compatible**, high performance | One primary + **read pools**; columnar engine for analytics | "Postgres, much faster", "transactions and analytics on the same data" |
| **Spanner** | Relational, SQL, **horizontally scalable** | **Strong (external) consistency, global**, up to 99.999% | "**global** relational", "scale **writes**", "strong consistency across regions" |
| **Bigtable** | Wide-column NoSQL, **row-key and range** access | Millions of ops/s, single-digit ms, petabytes | "time series", "IoT", "hundreds of thousands of writes/s", "ad-tech", "key lookups" |
| **Firestore** | **Document** NoSQL, serverless | Strong consistency, auto-scaling; real-time listeners, offline SDKs | "mobile / web app", "documents", "sync clients in real time" |
| **BigQuery** | Serverless **analytical warehouse**, columnar | Scans terabytes–petabytes | "analytics", "data warehouse", "SQL over huge datasets", "BI dashboards" |
| **Memorystore** | Managed **Redis, Valkey, Memcached** | Sub-millisecond, in memory | "cache", "session store", "leaderboard" |

> **Four eliminations decide most database items.**
> **1.** Cloud SQL and AlloyDB **cannot scale writes horizontally** — any stem about write throughput beyond one
> primary, or relational data spanning continents with strong consistency, is **Spanner**.
> **2.** BigQuery is **not** a low-latency point-lookup or OLTP store.
> **3.** Bigtable has **no joins, no multi-row transactions, no secondary indexes** in the relational sense — design
> is row-key design.
> **4.** Memorystore is a **cache**, never the system of record.

7.7.title: Cloud SQL and AlloyDB
7.7.text:
### Cloud SQL

| Topic | Fact |
|:------------------------------|:----------------------------------------------------------------------|
| Editions | **Enterprise** and **Enterprise Plus** (higher SLA, data cache, near-zero-downtime maintenance) |
| **High availability** | A **regional** instance: synchronous **standby in another zone**, automatic failover. **The standby serves no reads** |
| **Read replicas** | **Asynchronous** copies for **read scaling**, in the same or **another region**; a cross-region replica can be **promoted** for DR |
| **Backups** | **Automated** daily (retention configurable, default 7) and **on-demand**; restoring **to an instance overwrites it** |
| **Point-in-time recovery** | Needs **binary logging** (MySQL) or **WAL archiving** (PostgreSQL) enabled **beforehand**; recovers by **cloning to a new instance** at a timestamp |
| Connecting | **Cloud SQL Auth Proxy** or language **connectors** (IAM-authorised, TLS, no IP allow-lists) · **private IP** via private services access or PSC · public IP with authorized networks (discouraged) · **IAM database authentication** |
| Storage | Automatic storage increase; storage **cannot shrink** |
| Maintenance | Maintenance window and deny periods you set |

| Task | Command |
|:------------------------------------|:----------------------------------------------------------------------|
| HA primary, PITR, private IP only | `gcloud sql instances create orders --database-version=POSTGRES_16 --region=R --availability-type=REGIONAL --enable-point-in-time-recovery --no-assign-ip --network=vpc-prod` |
| Read replica (in another region: DR) | `gcloud sql instances create orders-replica --master-instance-name=orders --region=R2` |
| Restore to a moment, as a new instance | `gcloud sql instances clone orders orders-restored --point-in-time='2026-09-20T14:04:00Z'` |
| Make the replica the primary | `gcloud sql instances promote-replica orders-replica` |
| Connect; export | `gcloud sql connect orders --user=postgres` · `gcloud sql export sql orders gs://B/orders.sql.gz --database=shop` |

> **High availability is not read capacity, and a replica is not a backup.** HA's standby exists only to take over
> from a failed zone. A read replica serves reads — and **replicates a destructive `DELETE` within seconds**, so it
> cannot undo one. *"A bad statement ran at 14:05; lose the least data"* is **PITR to a new instance** at 14:04,
> leaving the damaged original untouched for comparison.

### AlloyDB for PostgreSQL

A **cluster** holds a **primary instance** (highly available by default across zones) and optional **read pool
instances** that scale reads. Its **columnar engine** accelerates analytical queries on live transactional data.
**Continuous backup and recovery** allows restore to any point in its window (14 days by default, *verify*) plus
scheduled backups; **cross-region secondary clusters** provide DR. It connects like Cloud SQL (Auth Proxy, private
IP, PSC). *AlloyDB Omni* runs the same engine anywhere.

7.8.title: Spanner, Bigtable and Firestore
7.8.text:
### Spanner

- An **instance** has a **configuration** — **regional** (99.99%), **dual-region** or **multi-region** (99.999%) —
  and **compute capacity** in **nodes** or **processing units** (1 node = 1,000 PU; small instances from 100 PU).
  Managed **autoscaling** adjusts capacity.
- **GoogleSQL** or **PostgreSQL** dialect; ACID transactions across rows, tables and regions; **interleaved tables**
  to co-locate parent and child rows.
- **Hotspots:** a monotonically increasing primary key (a timestamp, a sequence) sends all inserts to one split —
  use UUIDv4, bit-reversed sequences or a hashed prefix.
- **Backups** (full and incremental; copies to other regions) and **PITR** within the version-retention period (up
  to 7 days).


### Bigtable

- An **instance** has one or more **clusters** (one per zone; several clusters = **replication**, across regions if
  you like), each with **nodes** that scale throughput linearly; SSD or HDD storage.
- **App profiles** route traffic: **single-cluster routing** (strong read-your-writes) or **multi-cluster routing**
  (automatic failover, **eventual** consistency between clusters).
- **Row-key design is everything**: queries are by key or key range. Avoid keys that start with a timestamp or a
  sequential ID (hotspots); use `device#reverse_timestamp` shapes; keep related data adjacent.
- Tables are sparse; time-series data is often "tall and narrow". **Backups** per table restore into a new table.
- Data access with **`cbt`** or client libraries; Bigtable also supports **GoogleSQL** queries (*recognise*).


### Firestore

- **Native mode** (documents in collections, real-time listeners, offline mobile/web SDKs) or **Datastore mode**
  (server workloads using the Datastore API).
- **Firestore with MongoDB compatibility** (Enterprise edition) accepts **standard MongoDB drivers and MQL** on
  serverless Firestore — *"move a MongoDB app to a serverless managed database with minimal code change"*.
- The **location** — a region or a multi-region such as `eur3` — is **permanent**. A project can hold several
  **named databases**.
- **Indexes**: single-field indexes are automatic; **composite indexes** must be created for multi-field queries
  (the error message links to create one). **TTL policies** delete expired documents.
- **Recovery**: **PITR** (when enabled, reads and exports as of any minute in the last 7 days), **scheduled
  backups** (daily or weekly, restore into a **new** database), and managed **export/import** to Cloud Storage.

7.9.title: BigQuery
7.9.text:
| Concept | Fact |
|:------------------------------|:----------------------------------------------------------------------|
| Hierarchy | Project → **dataset** (has a **location** — a region or `US`/`EU` multi-region, fixed) → tables, views, materialized views |
| **Partitioning** | By ingestion time, a date/timestamp column, or an integer range — queries filtering on it scan less; partition expiration drops old data |
| **Clustering** | Sorts data within partitions by up to four columns — cheaper filters and aggregations on them |
| **Compute pricing** | **On-demand** (per TiB scanned) or **capacity** (**editions**: slots in reservations, with autoscaling) |
| **Storage pricing** | Active vs **long-term** (unmodified 90 days, about half price); logical or physical billing |
| **Time travel** | Query or restore a table as of up to **7 days** ago (configurable 2–7), then **7 days of fail-safe** |
| Table snapshots / clones | Cheap point-in-time copies |
| Access | `bigquery.dataViewer` on the **data** + `bigquery.jobUser` on the **project that runs the query** |

### Jobs, and reviewing their status

Every load, query, export and copy is a **job**.

| Task | Command |
|:------------------------------------|:----------------------------------------------------------------------|
| Recent jobs; one job's state and bytes | `bq ls -j -a` · `bq show -j JOB_ID` |
| The most expensive queries | `region-eu.INFORMATION_SCHEMA.JOBS`, ordered by `total_bytes_billed` |

> *"Which queries cost the most yesterday?"* — `INFORMATION_SCHEMA.JOBS`. *"Did last night's load succeed?"* —
> `bq show -j` or the console's job history. *"Stop analysts running a 50 TB query by mistake"* —
> **maximum bytes billed** or a **custom query quota**; a budget only alerts afterwards.

7.10.title: Memorystore and Database Center
7.10.text:
**Memorystore** runs **Redis** (standalone Basic tier, or Standard tier with a replica and automatic failover),
**Redis Cluster**, **Valkey** and **Memcached**, reached over private networking. Typical jobs: caching query
results, session state, rate limiting, leaderboards. Persistence options exist on some offerings, but the exam's
rule stands: **a cache in front of a database, not the database**.

> New in the June 2026 guide — Database Center
>
> **Database Center** is one console view of the **whole database fleet** across projects — Cloud SQL, AlloyDB,
> Spanner, Bigtable, Firestore, Memorystore. It inventories every instance and surfaces **health, availability,
> security and cost issues**: no automated backups, no HA, outdated versions, public IPs, missing deletion protection,
> over-provisioning. It needs no agents, and Gemini can answer fleet questions in natural language (*"which Cloud SQL
> instances in production have no backups?"*). *"One place to see and fix risk across all our databases"* is Database
> Center; a spreadsheet or per-product consoles are the distractors.

7.11.title: Loading and moving data
7.11.text:
**Do the arithmetic before comparing tools.** 1 Gbps moves about **10 TB per day** at full, uncontended speed; 100
Mbps about **1 TB per day**.

```
Volume / usable bandwidth = days.  Acceptable?
   NO  -->  Transfer Appliance (ship a device, load it on site, send it back)
   YES -->  Where is the data?
              Another cloud (S3, Azure Blob), HTTP URLs, another bucket  -->  Storage Transfer Service
              On-premises file systems                                   -->  STS with agents
              Small, one-off, scripted                                    -->  gcloud storage cp / rsync
              Into BigQuery, recurring from SaaS / GCS / S3  -->  BigQuery Data Transfer Service
```

| Tool | Right when |
|:----------------------------------|:------------------------------------------------------------------|
| **`gcloud storage cp / rsync`** | Small or scripted transfers; parallel composite uploads for big files are automatic |
| **Storage Transfer Service** | Large or **recurring** transfers from other clouds, URL lists, on-premises (with **agent pools**), or between buckets; scheduling, retries, integrity checks, bandwidth limits |
| **Transfer Appliance** | Hundreds of TB or more, a **thin or busy link**, or a deadline the network cannot meet |
| **`bq load`** | One-off or batch loads of CSV, JSON, Avro, Parquet, ORC **from Cloud Storage** — batch loading is free |
| **External tables / BigLake** | **Query in place** without loading |
| **BigQuery Data Transfer Service** | **Scheduled** loads into BigQuery from SaaS, Cloud Storage, S3, other warehouses |
| **Storage Write API**, Pub/Sub BigQuery subscriptions, Dataflow | **Streaming** into BigQuery |
| **Datastream** | Change data capture from MySQL, PostgreSQL, Oracle into BigQuery or Cloud Storage |
| **Database Migration Service** | Migrating databases into Cloud SQL / AlloyDB |

| Task | Command |
|:------------------------------------|:----------------------------------------------------------------------|
| Load files into a table | `bq load --source_format=PARQUET --autodetect sales.orders gs://kestrel-lake/orders/*.parquet` |

7.12.title: Messaging and pipelines: Pub/Sub, Managed Kafka, Dataflow
7.12.text:
### Pub/Sub

| Concept | Fact |
|:----------------------------------|:------------------------------------------------------------------|
| **Topic** | Where publishers send messages; a global resource (with an optional message-storage-location policy) |
| **Subscription** | **Each subscription gets every message**; subscribers **sharing** one subscription **split** the messages |
| Delivery types | **Pull** (StreamingPull), **push** to an HTTPS endpoint (with OIDC auth), or **export** straight into **BigQuery** or **Cloud Storage** |
| Acknowledgement | At-least-once by default; **ack deadline** 10 s default, up to 600 s; **exactly-once** available for pull |
| Retention | Unacked messages kept **7 days** by default (up to 31); topics can retain messages for replay |
| Failure handling | Retry policy (immediate or exponential backoff); **dead-letter topic** after N delivery attempts. The **Pub/Sub service agent** forwards the messages, so it needs **Publisher** on the dead-letter topic and **Subscriber** on the source subscription |
| Ordering | **Ordering keys** preserve order per key |
| Replay | **Snapshots** and **seek** to a time |

> **Fan-out needs one subscription per consumer.** Four services that must each process every order need **four
> subscriptions** on one topic. Four workers sharing **one** subscription compete, and each message goes to one of
> them — that is load-balancing, not fan-out.

> New in the June 2026 guide — Managed Service for Apache Kafka
>
> **Managed Service for Apache Kafka** runs Apache Kafka clusters for you — sizing in vCPU and memory, automatic
> broker management and rebalancing, topics and partitions, Kafka Connect clusters — speaking the **native Kafka
> protocol**. Choose it when you already have **Kafka clients, connectors or skills**, need **partition-ordered
> logs** replayed by **offset**, or are migrating from self-managed Kafka. Choose **Pub/Sub** for a serverless,
> global service with per-message acknowledgement and no partitions to plan.

### Dataflow

**Dataflow runs Apache Beam pipelines** — batch and streaming, one programming model — as a managed,
autoscaling service. **Templates** (classic and Flex, and Google-provided ones such as *Pub/Sub to BigQuery*) let
people launch pipelines without code.

| Job action | Effect |
|:----------------------|:----------------------------------------------------------------------|
| **Drain** | Stop reading new input, **finish in-flight data**, then stop — **no data loss** |
| **Cancel** | Stop **immediately**; in-flight data is lost |
| **Update** | Replace a running streaming job with compatible new code, keeping state |


Job health is in the **Dataflow monitoring UI** (job graph, stage throughput, **system lag**, **data freshness**,
worker logs), with metrics in Cloud Monitoring. Workers run as a service account that needs `roles/dataflow.worker`.

**Recognise the neighbours:** **Dataproc** (managed Spark and Hadoop — *lift-and-shift existing Spark jobs*),
**Cloud Composer** (managed Airflow — *orchestrate a DAG of dependent steps*), **Workflows** (orchestrate API
calls), **Cloud Scheduler** (managed cron — *one job on a timer*), **Cloud Tasks** (queued calls with rate
limits).

7.13.title: Backup, restore and multi-region redundancy
7.13.text:
### Backup and restore

| Service | Backup mechanisms | Restores to |
|:----------------------|:------------------------------------------------------------|:------------------------------------------|
| Compute Engine | Snapshot schedules, machine images, **Backup and DR Service** | New disk / VM |
| Cloud Storage | Versioning, soft delete, retention, dual-/multi-region | Previous generation, undeleted object |
| **Cloud SQL** | Automated + on-demand backups, **PITR** | Same instance (overwrites) or **clone** to a new one |
| **AlloyDB** | Continuous backup + scheduled backups | **New cluster** at a point in time |
| **Spanner** | Backups (full / incremental, cross-region copies), PITR ≤ 7 days | New database |
| **Bigtable** | Table backups | New table |
| **Firestore** | PITR (7 days), scheduled backups, export/import | **New database** / imported data |
| BigQuery | Time travel, fail-safe, table snapshots, dataset replication | Table as of a time |

**Backup and DR Service** centralises backup policy for VMs, disks, databases and file shares, with **backup
vaults** that make backups immutable and indelible for a set period — the answer to *"backups ransomware cannot
delete"*.

### Multi-region redundancy across data solutions

| Product | Multi-region option | What it gives |
|:----------------------|:------------------------------------------------------------|:------------------------------------------|
| Cloud Storage | **Dual-region** (turbo replication: RPO 15 min) or **multi-region** bucket | Data survives a region; no failover action. Default replication: 99.9% of new objects in 1 h, **RPO 12 h**; turbo is **dual-region only** |
| Cloud SQL | **Cross-region read replica**, promoted on disaster. **Enterprise Plus advanced DR**: a designated **DR replica**, **switchover** (planned, zero loss) and **replica failover** (outage), plus a **write endpoint** — a DNS name that follows the primary | Minutes of RPO; apps need no reconfiguration with the write endpoint |
| Cloud SQL backups | **Custom backup location** (another region or a multi-region) | Backups outlive the instance's region, no replica needed |
| AlloyDB | **Cross-region secondary cluster** (HA alone is two zones of one region) | Promote on disaster |
| **Spanner** | **Multi-region** or **dual-region** configuration (two regions in one country, e.g. `dual-region-germany1`) | Synchronous, strongly consistent, **99.999%** for both (regional: 99.99%). Move the **default leader** to where writes originate — no data moves |
| Bigtable | **Clusters in several regions** + multi-cluster routing; **backup copies** to another region's cluster | Automatic failover, **eventual consistency** — read-your-writes needs a **single-cluster routing** app profile |
| Firestore | **Multi-region location** (`nam5`, `eur3`) — also for **Firestore with MongoDB compatibility** | Synchronous replication, automatic, 99.999% |
| BigQuery | **Cross-region dataset replication** (read-only secondary, promotable); **managed disaster recovery** (Enterprise Plus **failover reservation** — slots fail over with the data) | **Trap:** a **multi-region dataset** (`US`, `EU`) is stored in **one region** of that geography — **no cross-region redundancy** by itself |
| Persistent Disk | **Asynchronous Replication** to a disk in a second region | Target **RPO ≈ 1 minute**; fail over by attaching the secondary disk |
| Filestore | **Regional tier** (zones); **backups stored in another region** (restorable anywhere) | Regional = zone failures only; cross-region backup = region loss |
| NetApp Volumes | **Volume replication** to a storage pool in another region | Destination is read-only until replication is stopped |
| Memorystore | Cross-region replicas on some offerings (*verify*) | Promote on disaster |

> *"Zero RPO, automatic failover, relational, across regions"* — **Spanner multi-region**; *"... and the data must
> stay in one country"* — **Spanner dual-region**. *"Survive a region with a few minutes' data loss, keep Postgres"*
> — **cross-region replica** (Cloud SQL) or **secondary cluster** (AlloyDB). *"Objects must be readable if a region
> is lost, and replicated within 15 minutes"* — **dual-region with turbo replication**. *"The data came back but the
> jobs had no slots"* — **BigQuery managed disaster recovery**. *"Apps had to be reconfigured after failover"* —
> **Cloud SQL write endpoint**.

7.14.title: Encryption and customer-managed keys
7.14.text:
**Everything at rest is encrypted by default with Google-managed keys**, using envelope encryption; you cannot
turn it off. The questions are about what to choose when default is not enough.

| Model | Key held by | Rotation | Revocation | Choose when |
|:------------------------------|:------------------------------|:----------------|:----------------------------|:------------------------------|
| **Google-managed** (default) | Google | Automatic | Not available to you | No stated key requirement |
| **CMEK** — customer-managed | **You, in Cloud KMS** | **On a schedule you set** | **Disable or destroy the key version** | "we must control, rotate and be able to revoke the key" |
| **CSEK** — customer-supplied | You, sent **with every request** | Manual | Stop supplying it | Cloud Storage and Compute Engine only; you keep raw keys |
| **Cloud EKM** | **An external key manager** outside Google | Yours | Yours | "Keys must never be stored in Google Cloud" |
| Client-side | You, before upload | Yours | Yours | Provider must never see plaintext |

### Cloud KMS vocabulary

```
Key ring   location is permanent: a region, a multi-region (eu, us) or global
  +-- Key           purpose (symmetric encrypt/decrypt, asymmetric sign, MAC); rotation period;
                    protection level: SOFTWARE | HSM (FIPS 140-2 Level 3) | EXTERNAL | EXTERNAL_VPC
        +-- Key version   the key material; enabled | disabled | scheduled for destruction | destroyed
```

> New in the June 2026 guide — configuring CMEK
>
> **Three rules make CMEK work, and each is a favourite distractor.**
> **1. The service agent needs the key.** The product's **Google-managed service account** — not your user, not your
> workload's service account — needs **`roles/cloudkms.cryptoKeyEncrypterDecrypter`** on the key ([§3.9](https://nirmata78.github.io/gcp-ace-simulator/theory/03-identity-access.html#s3-9)).
> **2. Locations must match.** The key's location must be compatible with the resource's: a bucket in `EU` needs a
> key in `eu` (or a region inside it, per product rules); a regional Cloud SQL instance needs a key in that region.
> **3. Rotation is not re-encryption.** Rotating creates a **new primary version** for new data; existing data stays
> readable with the older versions, which must stay enabled. **Disabling** a version makes data encrypted with it
> unreadable (reversible); **destroying** it is permanent after the scheduled-destruction delay (30 days by default)
> — *crypto-shredding*.
>
> **Cloud KMS Autokey** creates key rings and keys for CMEK automatically, per resource, in a dedicated key project
> — the answer to *"enforce CMEK everywhere without hand-creating hundreds of keys"*, paired with the org policy
> `gcp.restrictNonCmekServices`, which **blocks creating** resources in the listed services unless they use CMEK
> (preventive, unlike an alert on audit logs). A **BigQuery dataset in the `EU` multi-region needs a key in `eu`** —
> a `europe-west1` key fails with a location error however the permissions are set.

| Task | Command |
|:------------------------------------|:----------------------------------------------------------------------|
| Key ring and key (HSM, 90-day rotation) | `gcloud kms keyrings create data-eu --location=europe-central2` · `gcloud kms keys create sql-key --keyring=data-eu --location=europe-central2 --purpose=encryption --rotation-period=90d --protection-level=hsm` |
| Let the product use the key | grant `roles/cloudkms.cryptoKeyEncrypterDecrypter` on the key to the product's **service agent** — create it first if absent: `gcloud beta services identity create --service=sqladmin.googleapis.com` |
| Use the key | `gcloud sql instances create ... --disk-encryption-key=KEY` · `gcloud storage buckets update gs://B --default-encryption-key=KEY` |
| Stop data being readable | `gcloud kms keys versions disable 3 --key=sql-key --keyring=data-eu --location=europe-central2` |

### More to recognise

- **More redundancy mechanics.** **Filestore instance replication** keeps a standby in another region (about
  30-minute RPO; promote the replica). **Memorystore Standard Tier** fails over between zones of **one** region.
  Watch a Cloud SQL replica's **replication lag** — it is the data you would lose. Spanner **custom instance
  configurations** add **read-only replicas** for distant readers; Spanner and Bigtable **backups can be copied**
  to another region. A BigQuery **dataset copy** (Data Transfer Service) is a one-off or scheduled copy, not a
  replica. A Firestore location is **permanent** — a new database and an export/import change it. A second
  Bigtable cluster also **isolates batch reads** from serving traffic.
- **Newer data products.** Spanner's **PostgreSQL interface**; AlloyDB **vector search** (pgvector, ScaNN) beside
  operational rows; **Memorystore for Valkey** (open-source, Redis-compatible); a Pub/Sub **BigQuery
  subscription** writes messages to a table with no pipeline; **Dataflow templates** run standard pipelines
  from parameters.
- **Newer storage features.** **Hierarchical namespace** buckets give real folders and atomic renames.
  **Anywhere Cache** is a zonal SSD read cache in front of a bucket. **Autoclass** moves each object by its own
  access. **Storage Transfer Service agents** copy from on-premises file systems. **Soft delete** keeps deleted
  objects (7 days by default) even without versioning.
- **Operating data.** A Backup and DR **backup vault** with enforced minimum retention holds backups nobody can
  delete early. Spanner **`version_retention_period`** (up to 7 days) allows reads at a past timestamp. BigQuery
  **`EXTERNAL_QUERY`** joins live Cloud SQL rows. The **physical** storage billing model bills compressed bytes.
  Database Center also covers **databases on Compute Engine VMs**. Rotating a key never re-encrypts: **rewrite**
  old data onto the new version; a version scheduled for destruction can be **restored** during the delay.

7.15.title: Part 7 recall card
7.15.text:
| Prompt | Answer |
|:------------------------------------------------|:--------------------------------------------------------|
| Minimum durations | **0 / 30 / 90 / 365** days |
| Read once a year, needed "immediately" | **Archive** — same latency as Standard |
| Unknown access pattern | **Autoclass** |
| Undo yesterday's accidental delete | **Soft delete** (7 days default) or versioning |
| Immutable for 7 years, even for admins | **Retention policy + Bucket Lock** |
| File for someone with no Google account | **Signed URL** (impersonated signer, no key file) |
| Upload-only drop box | `storage.objectCreator` |
| SMB shares for Windows | **NetApp Volumes** |
| NFS for many VMs / RWX in GKE | **Filestore** |
| Feed thousands of GPUs with training data | **Managed Lustre** |
| Global relational, scale writes, strong consistency | **Spanner** |
| Time series, 500k writes/s, key lookups | **Bigtable** (design the row key) |
| Mobile app, real-time sync | **Firestore** |
| Warehouse SQL over TBs | **BigQuery** |
| Postgres plus analytics on live data | **AlloyDB** |
| Bad DELETE at 14:05 | Cloud SQL **PITR clone** to 14:04 |
| HA standby serves reads? | **No** — use a read replica |
| Cut BigQuery cost | Partition, cluster, fewer columns; `LIMIT` does not help |
| Which queries were expensive? | `INFORMATION_SCHEMA.JOBS` |
| Fleet-wide database risk view | **Database Center** |
| 500 TB over 100 Mbps | **Transfer Appliance** (≈ 500 days otherwise) |
| S3 to Cloud Storage nightly | **Storage Transfer Service** |
| Four consumers each get every message | **Four subscriptions** |
| Existing Kafka clients, offsets | **Managed Service for Apache Kafka** |
| Stop a streaming job without losing data | Dataflow **drain** |
| CMEK: resource cannot use the key | Grant the **service agent** `cryptoKeyEncrypterDecrypter` |
| Make CMEK data unreadable now | **Disable** the key version |

8.1.title: Infrastructure as code: the model
8.1.text:
**Infrastructure as code (IaC)** describes infrastructure in version-controlled files and lets a tool make reality
match them. The exam prefers it over console clicks and shell scripts for anything repeatable, and it prefers
**declarative** tools.

| Property | Declarative IaC (Terraform, Config Connector) | A script of `gcloud` commands |
|:------------------------------|:------------------------------------------------|:------------------------------------------------|
| You write | The **desired end state** | The **steps** |
| Re-running | **Idempotent** — changes only what differs | Fails or duplicates |
| Preview | **Plan / diff before apply** | None |
| Drift | **Detected** on the next plan | Invisible |
| Review | Pull request on a readable diff | Review of imperative code |

> **Deployment Manager is deprecated** — never choose it for new work. **Console export** gives a one-time copy, not a
> maintained definition. **A shell script** is repeatable but not declarative. When an option offers Terraform (or
> Infrastructure Manager) against any of these, Terraform wins.

8.2.title: Terraform on Google Cloud
8.2.text:
| Concept | Meaning |
|:------------------------------|:----------------------------------------------------------------------|
| **Provider** | The plug-in that talks to an API — `google` and `google-beta` |
| **Resource** / **data source** | Something Terraform manages / something it only reads |
| **Module** | A reusable package of resources with inputs and outputs |
| **State** | Terraform's record of what it manages — the mapping from code to real resource IDs |
| **Plan** / **apply** | Compute the diff / execute it |

**State is the heart of it, and the exam's Terraform items are mostly about state:**

- **Store it remotely** in a **Cloud Storage backend** — shared by the team, with **locking** so two applies cannot
  run at once. Local state on laptops is the classic failure: two engineers, two truths.
- **State contains secrets and resource details.** Restrict the bucket, enable **versioning** to recover a corrupted
  state, never commit it to git.
- **One state per environment** (separate directories or backends) limits the blast radius of a mistake.
- **Existing resources** made by hand are brought under management with **`import`** blocks or `terraform import`
  — not by deleting and recreating them.
- **Pin** provider and module versions so a plan today means the same tomorrow.

| Task | How |
|:------------------------------------|:----------------------------------------------------------------------|
| Remote state, with locking | a `backend "gcs"` block naming a bucket and a prefix |
| Pin the provider | `version = "~> 7.0"` for `hashicorp/google` |
| The loop | `terraform init` → `terraform plan -out=tfplan` → `terraform apply tfplan` |
| Adopt a resource made by hand | an `import` block, or `terraform import ADDRESS ID` |


**Infrastructure Manager** is Google's managed service that **runs Terraform for you**: it stores state, runs
plans (*previews*) and applies (*revisions*) as a service account, and records history — Terraform without owning
the runner or the state bucket.

8.3.title: Blueprints and Kubernetes-native tools
8.3.text:
| Tool | What it is | Choose it when |
|:------------------------------|:------------------------------------------------------------------|:------------------------------|
| **Cloud Foundation Toolkit (CFT)** | Google-maintained **Terraform modules and blueprints** (project factory, network, GKE...) | *"Use Google's tested modules rather than writing from scratch"* |
| **Fabric FAST** | An opinionated, staged **landing-zone** built from Cloud Foundation Fabric modules: bootstrap (org, automation, billing, logging) → resource management (folders) → networking and security → project factory | *"Stand up an enterprise-grade organization foundation quickly, following Google's practices"* |
| **Config Connector** | A Kubernetes add-on that manages Google Cloud resources as **Kubernetes custom resources**, continuously **reconciling** them | *"Teams manage their Cloud SQL and buckets with the same YAML and GitOps flow as their apps"* |
| **Config Controller** | Hosted Config Connector + Config Sync + Policy Controller | A managed control plane for that model |
| **Helm** | The **package manager for Kubernetes**: **charts** (templated manifests), **values**, **releases** with history | *"Install and upgrade the same application across many clusters, with rollback"* |



> **Terraform versus Config Connector.** Both are declarative. **Terraform** reconciles **when you run it**.
> **Config Connector** reconciles **continuously** inside a cluster — a console change is reverted automatically —
> and fits teams already working in Kubernetes YAML. **Helm** deploys *applications* into Kubernetes; it does not
> create the cluster or cloud resources (unless charts contain Config Connector objects).

8.4.title: Making changes the recommended way
8.4.text:
1. **Everything in version control**; changes by **pull request** with the `plan` output attached for review.
2. **Apply from a pipeline**, not a laptop — Cloud Build or another CI running as a **dedicated deploy service
   account**, reached by **impersonation** or **Workload Identity Federation**, never a key ([§3.10](https://nirmata78.github.io/gcp-ace-simulator/theory/03-identity-access.html#s3-10), [§3.12](https://nirmata78.github.io/gcp-ace-simulator/theory/03-identity-access.html#s3-12)).
3. **Least privilege per stage** — the networking pipeline cannot touch IAM on the org; separate states per
   environment.
4. **No manual console changes** in managed environments; if one happens, the next `plan` shows the **drift** —
   revert it in code or adopt it into code.
5. **Policy as code** — organization policies as guardrails, plus plan validation (Policy Controller, `gcloud
   beta terraform vet`) before apply.
6. **Promote the same code** dev → staging → prod with different variables, not three copies.

8.5.title: AI-assisted planning and implementation
8.5.text:
> New in the June 2026 guide — AI-assisted tooling
>
> The June 2026 guide describes an Associate Cloud Engineer as someone who works **"supported by AI tooling"**, and
> names four tools. Expect *"which tool fits this task"* items and items about **using them safely**, not trivia about
> their menus.

| Tool | Where it lives | What it is for |
|:------------------------------|:------------------------------|:----------------------------------------------------------------|
| **Gemini Cloud Assist** | The **Google Cloud console** (and APIs) | Ask about **your** resources in natural language; generate `gcloud` and Terraform; **troubleshoot** with investigations over logs, metrics and config changes; explain log entries; draft alerting policies and queries; cost and optimisation insights; design architectures |
| **Gemini CLI** / **Antigravity CLI** | Your **terminal** | An AI agent that reads your code and files, runs shell commands (with your approval), scaffolds projects, writes IaC and can provision resources. In 2026 Google moved Gemini CLI's capabilities into the Antigravity CLI |
| **Google Antigravity** | A desktop **agent-first development platform** (IDE, CLI, SDK) | Agents that plan and carry out multi-step development tasks across editor, terminal and browser |
| **Application Design Center** | The console | Platform teams publish **approved, Terraform-backed application templates**; developers design on a **visual canvas** (AI-assisted), then deploy; results are registered as **App Hub applications** |

> *"Ask which of my VMs have public IPs, from the console"* — **Gemini Cloud Assist**. *"From my terminal, have an
> agent generate and apply the Terraform for this service"* — **Gemini CLI / Antigravity CLI**. *"The platform team
> wants developers to deploy only from governed, reusable architecture templates"* — **Application Design Center**.
> *"An agentic IDE"* — **Antigravity**.

> **The rules that do not change because an AI wrote it.** Generated commands and IaC are **drafts**: review the plan
> before applying. The assistant acts **with your permissions**, so least privilege still governs what it can see and
> change. Prefer generated **code** that goes through the normal review and pipeline over an agent making direct
> changes to production. Never paste secrets into prompts.

**Configuring the tools — three mechanics worth recognising.** A **`GEMINI.md`** file in the repository gives
Gemini CLI **standing instructions** (conventions, modules to use, what never to do) in every session. Extra tools
reach Gemini CLI through **MCP servers** registered under `mcpServers` in `.gemini/settings.json`. In the other
direction, **Gemini Cloud Assist exposes a remote MCP server**, so a third-party MCP-capable assistant can use it
with the signed-in user's permissions. Gemini Cloud Assist itself needs **`geminicloudassist.googleapis.com`**
enabled and **`roles/geminicloudassist.user`** for its users; *describe an app in a sentence and get a design to
refine and deploy* is Gemini Cloud Assist in **Application Design Center**.

8.6.title: AI and developer platforms
8.6.text:
> New in the June 2026 guide — agents, notebooks and workstations
>
> **Vertex AI is now Gemini Enterprise Agent Platform** (renamed April 2026; services unchanged). The guide names
> three of its operations tasks plus Cloud Workstations. Old names still appear in documentation and older material:
> *Vertex AI Agent Engine* → **Agent Runtime**; *Vertex AI Workbench* → **Agent Platform Workbench**.

### Agent Runtime

**Agent Runtime** (on Gemini Enterprise Agent Platform) is a **managed runtime for AI agents** built with the Agent
Development Kit (ADK), LangChain/LangGraph and other frameworks. You deploy the agent; it provides **scaling,
sessions, memory, identity, tracing and logging**, including long-running agents. It is the compute answer for
*"host our agent without building the serving infrastructure"* — the alternative is packaging the agent yourself
on Cloud Run or GKE.

Deploying is done from the Agent Platform SDK (or console): package the agent, **deploy** it to a region, give it a
**service identity** with only the roles its tools need, then query it through its endpoint and watch it in Cloud
Trace and Logging.

- The deployment names the agent's **`requirements`** (only those packages are installed — *"ModuleNotFoundError
  after deploy"* means a missing requirement) and a **Cloud Storage staging bucket**. Keep the bucket in the agent's
  project; a bucket elsewhere needs a read grant to the **Agent Platform service agent**.
- **Release a new version by updating** the existing Agent Runtime resource: callers keep its resource name.

### Notebooks: Workbench and BigQuery

| Surface | What it is | Operational points |
|:------------------------------|:------------------------------------------------------------|:--------------------------------------------|
| **Agent Platform Workbench** instances | Managed **JupyterLab on a Compute Engine VM** you configure (machine type, GPUs, disks, network) | **Idle shutdown** to stop paying for idle notebooks; start/stop, custom containers. **Access mode**: **single-user** (`--instance-owners`, one individual account, not a group) or **service-account** (anyone who can act as the instance's service account). **Upgrade** rebuilds the boot disk and **keeps the data disk** (`/home/jupyter`) |
| **BigQuery notebooks** (Colab Enterprise in BigQuery Studio) | Serverless notebooks next to your data | **Runtime templates** define the machine an admin allows; notebooks can be **scheduled**; notebooks are **code assets with version history, shared individually** — no project-wide BigQuery role needed to collaborate on one |


> *"Data scientists leave notebook VMs running all weekend"* — **idle shutdown** on Workbench instances (or
> serverless notebooks in BigQuery). *"Notebook needs a GPU"* — a Workbench instance with an attached GPU, in a zone
> that offers it.

### Cloud Workstations

**Cloud Workstations** gives developers **managed development environments** in Google Cloud, reached from a browser
IDE or a local IDE over a tunnel. Administrators define them in layers:

```
Workstation cluster   (a region + VPC subnet: where workstations run, private networking)
  +-- Workstation configuration   (machine type, container image with tools, persistent disk,
  |                                idle and running timeouts, who may use it)
        +-- Workstation            (one developer's instance of that configuration)
```

It answers *"source code must not live on laptops"*, *"standardise every developer's toolchain"*, *"developers
need access to private resources on the VPC"*. Access is IAM, images come from Artifact Registry, and **idle
timeouts** control cost.

- **Self-service**: **`roles/workstations.workstationCreator`** on a configuration lets developers create
  workstations from it; creators get **`roles/workstations.user`** on their own. Neither lets them edit the
  configuration.
- **Standard tooling**: extend a Cloud Workstations **base image**, push it to Artifact Registry, set it as the
  configuration's container image.
- **Only `/home` persists** (the persistent disk). Anything written elsewhere is recreated from the image on every
  start — *"my clone in /opt vanished overnight"*.


### More to recognise

- **Agents.** **Agent Identity** gives each deployed agent its own principal, tied to its lifecycle, so grants and
  audit logs are per agent — and deleting the agent **does not** remove bindings to that principal.
- **Notebooks.** An administrator's **runtime template** fixes the network, subnet and public-IP setting for
  Colab Enterprise runtimes.
- **Workstations.** A **private cluster** (private gateway) is reached only through Private Service Connect.
  GPUs are declared on the **configuration** (N1, A2 or A3 machine types only).
- **Tooling.** Store Terraform state in a **`gcs` backend** (shared, locked, versioned). A console create form's
  **Equivalent code** shows the gcloud, Terraform or REST version of your settings.

9.1.title: Google Cloud Observability, and setting it up
9.1.text:
| Product | Answers |
|:------------------------------|:----------------------------------------------------------------------|
| **Cloud Monitoring** | Metrics, dashboards, **alerting policies**, uptime checks, SLOs |
| **Cloud Logging** | Log collection, storage, routing, querying, log-based metrics |
| **Cloud Trace** | Where time goes across services in one request |
| **Cloud Profiler** | Where CPU and memory go **inside** one service |
| **Error Reporting** | Groups and counts **exceptions** from logs, and notifies on new ones |
| **Ops Agent** | Collects **guest** metrics and logs from VMs |
| **Managed Service for Prometheus** | Prometheus metrics, collected and stored for you, queried in PromQL |
| **Personalized Service Health / Cloud Hub** | Google-side incidents affecting you / an application-centric operations view |

**Setting it up** (the Section 1 objective) means: the Logging and Monitoring APIs enabled (they are by default in
new projects); a **metrics scope** that lets one project see metrics from many; **log routing and retention**
decided (buckets, sinks, org-level defaults — including the **default storage location** of new projects' log
buckets, `gcloud logging settings update --organization=ORG_ID --storage-location=R`, for data residency); **agents** on VMs; **Managed Prometheus** on GKE (enabled by default
on new clusters); **notification channels** created once and reused by alerts.

### Metrics scopes

A **metrics scope** makes one **scoping project** able to chart and alert on metrics of many **monitored
projects** — *"one dashboard over twelve projects"*. Keep the scoping project free of workloads; add projects in
**Monitoring → Settings**. The Logging equivalent is an **aggregated sink** or a **log scope** / Log Analytics view
across projects ([§9.5](https://nirmata78.github.io/gcp-ace-simulator/theory/09-operations.html#s9-5)).

9.2.title: Metrics and the Ops Agent
9.2.text:
Metrics are identified by type; the **prefix tells you where they come from**:

| Prefix | Source |
|:----------------------------------|:------------------------------------------------------------------|
| `compute.googleapis.com/...` | The **hypervisor** — CPU utilisation, disk and network I/O. No agent needed |
| `agent.googleapis.com/...` | The **Ops Agent** — **memory**, swap, disk space used, processes |
| `workload.googleapis.com/...` | Application metrics via the Ops Agent's OpenTelemetry / third-party receivers |
| `custom.googleapis.com/...` | **Custom metrics** you write through the Monitoring API |
| `logging.googleapis.com/user/...` | **Log-based metrics** you define |
| `prometheus.googleapis.com/...` | **Managed Service for Prometheus** |

> **The hypervisor cannot see inside the guest.** CPU appears on every VM's charts; **memory and disk-space
> utilisation appear only after the Ops Agent is installed.** *"Memory is missing from the dashboard"* — install the
> Ops Agent.

**The Ops Agent** combines Fluent Bit (logs) and an OpenTelemetry collector (metrics) in one agent, replacing the
legacy Logging and Monitoring agents. It is configured in `/etc/google-cloud-ops-agent/config.yaml`, has
**integrations** for common applications (nginx, MySQL, PostgreSQL, JVM, Redis...), and its VM's service account
needs **`roles/logging.logWriter`** and **`roles/monitoring.metricWriter`**. To install on a fleet, use an **OS
policy** through VM Manager ([§5.6](https://nirmata78.github.io/gcp-ace-simulator/theory/05-compute-engine.html#s5-6)) or the console's agent-install flow, not a script run by hand on each VM.

9.3.title: Alerting, uptime checks and SLOs
9.3.text:
> **Only an alerting policy notifies anyone.** Dashboards, uptime checks, log-based metrics and SLOs measure; an
> alerting policy decides and sends.

| Part of an alerting policy | Meaning |
|:----------------------------------|:------------------------------------------------------------------|
| **Condition** | Metric threshold · metric **absence** · **forecast** · **PromQL** query · **log match** (log-based alert) |
| **Duration / retest window** | How long the condition must hold — *"for 5 minutes"* avoids flapping |
| **Notification channels** | Email, SMS, mobile app, Slack, PagerDuty, webhooks, **Pub/Sub** — defined once, reused |
| Documentation | Markdown sent with the notification — the runbook link |
| Incident | Opened when the condition fires; closes automatically when it clears |

| Requirement | Construct |
|:----------------------------------------------|:------------------------------------------------------------------|
| Page when p95 latency > 800 ms for 5 minutes | **Alerting policy**, threshold condition on the latency metric, 5-min duration |
| Tell us if the public endpoint is unreachable from several regions | **Uptime check + an alerting policy on it** |
| Notify **each time** a specific error line appears | **Log-based alert** (alerting policy with a log-match condition) |
| Alert when an error line appears **more than 50 times in 10 minutes** | **Log-based metric (counter) + a metric alerting policy** |
| Alert when the error budget burns too fast | **SLO** + **burn-rate** alerting policy |
| Alert when a metric **stops arriving** | **Metric-absence** condition |

> **Log-based alert versus log-based metric.** A **log-based alert** notifies on individual matching entries (with a
> notification rate limit) — the simplest answer to *"tell us whenever X is logged"*. A **log-based metric** turns
> matching entries into a **time series** — needed for **rates and thresholds** (*"more than N per window"*),
> charts, and SLOs. Error Reporting groups exceptions but cannot express *"more than 50 in 10 minutes of this plain
> line"*.

**Uptime checks** probe HTTP(S), TCP or ICMP endpoints from several Google locations (or privately, inside a VPC),
and chart availability and latency; they alert only through an attached policy. **SLOs** are defined on a
**service** with an **SLI** (availability or latency), a target and a window (rolling or calendar); the **error
budget** is the allowed failure; a **burn-rate** alert fires when the budget is being consumed too fast.

9.4.title: Custom metrics and Managed Service for Prometheus
9.4.text:
| Way in | When |
|:------------------------------------------|:------------------------------------------------------------------|
| **Log-based metric** | The signal is already in logs — no code change |
| **OpenTelemetry** (SDK → Ops Agent / collector / OTLP endpoint) | New instrumentation; vendor-neutral |
| **Monitoring API** `timeSeries.create` → `custom.googleapis.com/...` | Direct writes from code |
| **Prometheus exporters / `/metrics` endpoints** | Kubernetes and Prometheus-ecosystem apps → Managed Service for Prometheus |

**Managed Service for Prometheus** stores Prometheus metrics in Google's global time-series store (Monarch),
retains them long-term, and lets you query with **PromQL** in Metrics Explorer, alerting policies and Grafana.

| Collection mode | How |
|:----------------------------------|:------------------------------------------------------------------|
| **Managed collection** (GKE, the default on new clusters) | You declare **`PodMonitoring`** / `ClusterPodMonitoring` resources; Google runs the collectors |
| Self-deployed collection | A drop-in replacement Prometheus binary you run |
| On VMs | The **Ops Agent's Prometheus receiver** |

9.5.title: Cloud Logging: routing, buckets, Log Analytics
9.5.text:
```
Log entries --> Log Router --> sinks (inclusion filter, exclusion filters)
                                 |-- _Required bucket   400 days, cannot change, free
                                 |-- _Default bucket    30 days by default, configurable
                                 |-- custom log bucket  your region, retention (1 day - 10 years), CMEK
                                 |-- BigQuery dataset   query constantly, join with other data
                                 |-- Cloud Storage      cheap long-term archive
                                 |-- Pub/Sub topic      stream out: SIEM, Splunk, on-premises
                                 |-- another project    central logging project
```

| Bucket | Retention | Holds |
|:----------------------|:------------------------------|:------------------------------------------------------------|
| **`_Required`** | **400 days, fixed, free** | **Admin Activity** and **System Event** audit logs (and Access Transparency) |
| **`_Default`** | **30 days** by default, configurable | Everything else not excluded — including **Data Access** audit logs |
| **Custom buckets** | You choose (1–3,650 days), can be **locked** | Anything a sink routes there |

**Sinks** live on a project, folder, organization or billing account. An **aggregated sink** on a folder or
organization with `--include-children` routes every project's logs beneath it — the answer to *"central logging
for all projects"*. Each sink has a **writer identity** (a service account) that **must be granted write access at
the destination** (`bigquery.dataEditor`, `storage.objectCreator`, `pubsub.publisher`, or `logging.bucketWriter`)
— a sink that "does nothing" usually lacks this grant.

**Exclusion filters** drop entries **before storage** — the lever for the logging bill (*"we do not need debug
logs from dev"*). Routing is free; ingestion and retention beyond the defaults cost money.

**Log views** restrict who sees which logs **inside** a bucket (`roles/logging.viewAccessor` on a view).

### Log Analytics

Upgrading a log bucket to **Log Analytics** lets you query logs with **SQL**, and optionally create a **linked
BigQuery dataset** that queries the same data **from BigQuery without copying it**. *"Analysts want SQL over our
logs and to join them with business data, without a second pipeline"* — Log Analytics with a linked dataset.

| Task | Command |
|:------------------------------------|:----------------------------------------------------------------------|
| Central bucket with Log Analytics | `gcloud logging buckets create central --location=europe-west4 --retention-days=365 --enable-analytics` |
| Every project's logs into it | `gcloud logging sinks create all-to-central logging.googleapis.com/projects/LOGS_P/locations/europe-west4/buckets/central --organization=ORG_ID --include-children` |
| Who to grant on the destination | the sink's `writerIdentity`: `gcloud logging sinks describe all-to-central` |
| Stop paying for debug logs | `gcloud logging sinks update _Default --add-exclusion=name=no-debug,filter='severity<INFO'` |
| Keep `_Default` longer | `gcloud logging buckets update _Default --location=global --retention-days=90` |

### Exporting to external systems

| Destination | Right when |
|:----------------------------------|:------------------------------------------------------------------|
| **Pub/Sub** | Stream to a **SIEM**, Splunk (via a Dataflow template), or an **on-premises** collector |
| **BigQuery** | Query constantly, join, dashboard |
| **Cloud Storage** | **Retain cheaply for years**, read rarely — with lifecycle to Archive |
| A log bucket with long retention | Keep logs in Logging's own tools and Log Analytics |

9.6.title: Reading logs
9.6.text:
**Logs Explorer** (and `gcloud logging read`) use the Logging query language:

```
resource.type="gce_instance" AND severity>=ERROR
resource.type="cloud_run_revision" AND resource.labels.service_name="api"
logName="projects/P/logs/cloudaudit.googleapis.com%2Factivity"
protoPayload.methodName="v1.compute.firewalls.patch"
protoPayload.authenticationInfo.principalEmail="mara@kestrel.io"
jsonPayload.orderId="A-1042"          textPayload:"timeout"          httpRequest.status>=500
timestamp>="2026-09-20T14:00:00Z" AND timestamp<"2026-09-20T15:00:00Z"
```

`=` equals, `:` has / contains, `=~` regular expression, `AND` / `OR` / `NOT`.

**A log entry's fields**, which "view log message details" means: `logName`; `resource` (type and labels —
which VM, service, cluster); `timestamp` and `receiveTimestamp`; `severity`; `insertId`; `labels`; `trace` and
`spanId` (link to Cloud Trace); `httpRequest`; and one payload — `textPayload`, `jsonPayload`, or **`protoPayload`
for audit logs** (`methodName`, `serviceName`, `resourceName`, `authenticationInfo.principalEmail`, `status`).

| Task | Command |
|:------------------------------------|:----------------------------------------------------------------------|
| Query logs from the CLI | `gcloud logging read 'resource.type="k8s_container" AND severity>=ERROR' --freshness=1h` |

9.7.title: Audit, flow and firewall logs
9.7.text:
| Audit log type | Records | Default | Cost | Bucket |
|:--------------------|:------------------------------------|:------------------------|:--------------|:------------|
| **Admin Activity** | Calls that **change** configuration or metadata | **Always on; cannot be disabled** | Free | `_Required` |
| **Data Access** | Calls that **read** configuration, or **read or write user data** | **Off** (except **BigQuery**, on) | Charged | `_Default` |
| **System Event** | Google-initiated changes (live migration, autoscaler) | Always on | Free | `_Required` |
| **Policy Denied** | Requests **denied by a security policy** (e.g. VPC Service Controls) | On | Charged (can exclude) | `_Default` |

**Enabling Data Access logs** is part of the IAM policy (`auditConfigs`) at the organization, folder or project, per
service and per type — `ADMIN_READ`, `DATA_READ`, `DATA_WRITE` — with optional **exempted principals** (e.g. a
noisy batch service account). Console: **IAM & Admin → Audit Logs**. Reading Data Access logs needs
**`roles/logging.privateLogViewer`**.

> *"Who changed this firewall rule?"* — **Admin Activity**, always there. *"Who read these objects?"* — **Data
> Access**, which exists **only if it was enabled before** the reads. *"We have no record of who downloaded the file"*
> usually means Data Access logging was never turned on.

**VPC Flow Logs** (sampled flows per subnet or network) and **Firewall Rules Logging** (per rule, allowed or denied
connections) are not audit logs, but the guide groups them here because they answer the same kind of question —
*what happened on the network* — and are configured and read the same way, in Cloud Logging ([§4.11](https://nirmata78.github.io/gcp-ace-simulator/theory/04-networking.html#s4-11)). Both are
charged by volume: tune sampling and aggregation for flow logs, and log only the rules you need.

9.8.title: Diagnosing an application
9.8.text:
| Symptom | Tool |
|:----------------------------------------------|:------------------------------------------------------------------|
| A request is slow — **which service** in the chain? | **Cloud Trace** (spans per service; automatic for Cloud Run and App Engine requests, OpenTelemetry elsewhere) |
| One service is slow or expensive — **why, inside the code**? | **Cloud Profiler** (continuous CPU, heap, thread and contention profiles in production, low overhead) |
| A new **exception** started appearing | **Error Reporting** (groups stack traces, counts, first seen, notifies) |
| The **database** is slow — which queries, from which app or user? | **Query Insights** (Cloud SQL, AlloyDB): top queries, load, plans, tags |
| A slow query needs an index | **Index advisor** (Cloud SQL, AlloyDB) recommends indexes from the real workload |
| **What changed?** | Admin Activity audit logs; deploy history; **Gemini Cloud Assist investigations**, which correlate logs, metrics and config changes |
| Is it **Google**? | **Personalized Service Health** ([§9.9](https://nirmata78.github.io/gcp-ace-simulator/theory/09-operations.html#s9-9)) |

> **Trace tells you *which*; Profiler tells you *why*.** A latency jump across four services is Trace first. CPU
> utilisation tells you neither — a service can be slow while idle, waiting on a dependency.

9.9.title: Service health and Cloud Hub
9.9.text:
> New in the June 2026 guide — Personalized Service Health and Cloud Hub
>
> **The public Google Cloud Service Health dashboard** lists broad incidents for everyone. **Personalized Service
> Health** shows the incidents and planned events **that affect your projects and products** — per project, and in
> an **organization-level view across every project** — with history, an API and logs — and you can **alert on them** with Cloud Monitoring alerting policies. *"Tell on-call automatically when
> a Google incident affects our Cloud SQL instances in europe-west4"* is Personalized Service Health with an alerting
> policy, not someone watching the status page. Least-privilege access to it is
> **`roles/servicehealth.viewer`** on the project or organization (the Service Health API must be enabled); basic
> Viewer also works but grants far more.
>
> **Cloud Hub** is an **application-centric operations home** in the console: for applications defined in **App Hub**
> (their services and workloads) it brings together **health** (open alerts, Service Health events), **active events
> and maintenance**, deployments, cost and optimisation, and support cases. *"One view of the health of our checkout
> application across its projects"* — Cloud Hub.

9.10.title: Optimising: Active Assist and Gemini Cloud Assist
9.10.text:
**Active Assist** is the family of **recommenders** that analyse usage and suggest changes, each with estimated
savings or risk reduction:

| Recommender | Suggests |
|:----------------------------------|:------------------------------------------------------------------|
| **VM machine-type (rightsizing)** | A smaller or larger machine type from observed use |
| **Idle resources** | Idle VMs, unattached disks, unused static IPs, old images |
| **Committed use discounts** | Commitments that fit your steady usage |
| **IAM role recommender** | Removing permissions a principal has not used (~90 days) |
| **Unattended project** | Projects nobody uses — delete or reclaim |
| Cloud SQL / GKE | Over-provisioned instances, idle clusters, container requests |
| Firewall Insights | Shadowed and unused rules |

They appear in the **Recommendation Hub**, on resource pages, in the **FinOps hub**, and via the Recommender API.


**Gemini Cloud Assist for Cloud Monitoring** helps you **build and read** observability in natural language:
drafting PromQL and alerting conditions, explaining a chart or a log entry, summarising an incident, and running
**investigations** that propose likely root causes. As in [§8.5](https://nirmata78.github.io/gcp-ace-simulator/theory/08-tooling.html#s8-5), its output is a starting point you verify, bounded
by your permissions.

### More to recognise

- **Alerting that matches intent.** An **SLO burn-rate** alert pages on fast error-budget consumption, not on
  every blip. A **synthetic monitor** runs a scripted, multi-step journey on a schedule. A **private uptime check**
  reaches an internal endpoint through **Service Directory**.
- **Open standards.** Grafana keeps its **PromQL** dashboards against Managed Service for Prometheus. An
  **OpenTelemetry Collector** exports OTLP metrics and traces to Cloud Monitoring and Cloud Trace.
- **Cost and clarity.** Lower **VPC Flow Logs** sampling and lengthen aggregation to cut volume. **Explain this log
  entry** asks Gemini Cloud Assist what an entry means. Cloud Hub's **Deployments** page shows failed App Hub
  deployments; its **Optimization** page shows cost per project or application.

10.1.title: Confusion pairs
10.1.text:
| A | B | What separates them |
|:--------------------------|:--------------------------|:----------------------------------------------------------------|
| **Budget** | **Quota** | Budget **alerts**, never caps · quota **hard-stops** |
| **Label** | **Network tag** | Cost attribution, in the billing export · firewall/route matching, never in billing |
| **Network tag** | **Secure tag** | Anyone who edits the VM can set it; VPC rules only · IAM-controlled; firewall **policies** |
| **Super admin** | **Organization Administrator** | Users, groups, domain (Admin console) · IAM on the hierarchy |
| **GCDS / SCIM** | **Workforce Identity Federation** | Copy identities into Cloud Identity · no copies; IdP stays the source |
| **Workforce** federation | **Workload** federation | People, org-level pool · software outside Google, project-level pool |
| **IAM allow** | **Organization policy** | Who may act · what may be configured, **including by owners** |
| **Allow policy** | **Deny policy** | Additive union · subtracts, **evaluated first** |
| **IAM condition** | **PAM** | Grant with a built-in expiry or scope · request-and-approve, just-in-time elevation |
| **Policy Troubleshooter** | **Policy Analyzer** | *Why* can this principal (not) do it · *who* can do it |
| Service Account **User** | Service Account **Token Creator** | **Attach** an SA to a resource · **act as** it now |
| **Default SA** | **Service agent** | Your workload's legacy identity (Editor) · Google's product acting in your project |
| **Disable SA** | **Delete SA** | Reversible, bindings intact · orphaned bindings; same name ≠ same principal |
| **Secret Manager** | **SA key** | Secrets Google cannot mint · a credential Google mints on demand — don't store one |
| **`gcloud auth login`** | **`application-default login`** | Credentials for the CLI · for client-library code |
| **VPC** | **Subnet** | Global · regional |
| **Expand subnet** | **New subnet** | More IPs, same range, never shrink · another region or tier |
| **Shared VPC** | **Peering** | One network, many projects · two networks joined |
| **Peering** | **NCC** | Non-transitive pair · transitive hub |
| **HA VPN** | **Interconnect** | Encrypted over internet, quick, a few Gbps · private circuits, 10–100 Gbps, not encrypted by default |
| **Dedicated** | **Partner** Interconnect | You are in a Google colo · you are not |
| **Interconnect** | **Direct Peering** | Private VPC reach · Google public services only |
| **Private Google Access** | **Cloud NAT** | Google APIs only · the internet |
| **PSC** | **Private services access** | Endpoint to a service, no peering · peered producer VPC (Cloud SQL private IP) |
| **Forwarding zone** | **Inbound server policy** | Cloud resolves on-prem names · on-prem resolves Cloud names |
| **Proxy** LB | **Passthrough** LB | Terminates, rewrites client IP · preserves client IP |
| **Application** LB | **Network** LB | HTTP(S) at layer 7 · any TCP/UDP at layer 4 |
| **Premium** tier | **Standard** tier | Google backbone, global · public internet, regional, cheaper |
| **Flow logs** | **Firewall logs** | What traffic flowed (sampled) · which rule decided |
| **Spot** | **Preemptible** | No max runtime · 24-hour cap (legacy) |
| **MIGRATE** | **TERMINATE** | Live-migrate during maintenance · stop (required for GPUs) |
| **Snapshot** | **Image** | One disk's data · one bootable disk |
| **Image** | **Machine image** | One disk · all disks + VM configuration |

10.3.title: The command atlas
10.3.text:
The grammar: `gcloud GROUP [SUBGROUP] VERB NAME --flags`; scope by `--zone`, `--region`, `--global` or
`--location`. The exam tests the **verb and the deciding flag**, not full invocations — this is the index of the
ones worth recognising, each shown in context earlier.

| Area | Commands worth recognising |
|:--------------------|:----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| Context | `gcloud config configurations create/activate` · `gcloud config set project P` · `gcloud auth login` (CLI) versus `gcloud auth application-default login` (code) · `gcloud components install kubectl` |
| Hierarchy, billing | `gcloud projects create/delete/undelete` · `gcloud beta projects move P --folder=F` · `gcloud services enable API` · `gcloud billing projects link P --billing-account=B` |
| IAM | `gcloud projects add-iam-policy-binding P --member=M --role=R [--condition=...]` · `set-iam-policy` replaces everything · `gcloud iam roles create/copy/update` |
| Service accounts | `gcloud iam service-accounts create/disable/delete/undelete` · `--impersonate-service-account=SA` · Token Creator on the SA to impersonate it |
| Network | `gcloud compute networks create --subnet-mode=custom` · `subnets expand-ip-range` · `firewall-rules create --target-tags/--target-service-accounts` · `shared-vpc enable` · `networks peerings create` (both sides) · `addresses create` · `routers nats create` |
| Compute | `gcloud compute instances create --provisioning-model=SPOT` · `disks resize` · `snapshots/images/machine-images create` · `instance-groups managed set-autoscaling` · `rolling-action start-update --canary-version / --max-surge` |
| GKE | `gcloud container clusters create-auto` versus `create --num-nodes` (per zone) · `get-credentials` · `node-pools update --enable-autoscaling` · `kubectl apply/rollout undo/scale/autoscale/describe/logs --previous` |
| Serverless | `gcloud run deploy --source . / --image` · `--no-traffic --tag` then `services update-traffic --to-tags` · `--min-instances` · `gcloud functions deploy --trigger-event-filters/--trigger-topic/--trigger-http` · `gcloud app deploy --no-promote` · `gcloud builds submit --tag` |
| Storage and data | `gcloud storage buckets create --default-storage-class` · `buckets update --lifecycle-file/--versioning/--retention-period` · `gcloud storage cp/rsync/sign-url` · `bq query --dry_run` · `bq load` · `gcloud sql instances create --availability-type=REGIONAL` · `sql instances clone --point-in-time` · `promote-replica` |
| Keys and secrets | `gcloud kms keyrings/keys create` · `gcloud beta services identity create --service=S` · `gcloud secrets versions access latest` |
| Operations | `gcloud logging sinks create ... --include-children` · the sink's `writerIdentity` · `gcloud logging buckets create --enable-analytics` · `gcloud logging read FILTER` |
